19780-report-of-the-national-library-ser:
New Zealand's National Library Service reported yearly on its work. This report covers the Service as a whole and its four divisions. They were the Country Library Service and the School Library Service. The Library School and the National Library Centre complete the four. The writer submits it formally, with the honour due official reports. Country service took books to rural districts by van and post.

Library reports sound dry until their reach becomes clear. A small nation was building reading access for every town. School services put books into children's hands nationwide. The divisions show a complete system, planned as one. Historians of libraries use reports like this as benchmarks. They record staff, stock, and ambition in plain figures.
22725-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, offers its issue of March 31, 1920, from volume 158. The catalog record names no editor. Parliamentary reporting gives this number its sample joke, from Question Time in the House of Commons, where Welsh place names tripped English tongues.

Trouble arose, Punch reports, over how to pronounce Bryngwran and Gwalchmai. One Welsh member present joked that he could have played those names, had he brought his harp. The gibe is gentle, and very Punch: politics softened into music-hall wit. Around the joke sit cartoons and verses of postwar life. The number catches the magazine in 1920, its war service done, settling back into the ancient trade of teasing the House.
alkhwarizmi-algebra-rosen-1831:
Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi wrote the founding text of algebra in ninth century Baghdad. Frederic Rosen translated the Arabic work into English in 1831 for the Oriental Translation Fund. The edition prints the English alongside the Arabic. Algebra takes its very name from the book's Arabic title word, al-jabr.

Al-Khwarizmi teaches how to solve equations by restoring and balancing both sides. He sorts problems into types and works each one with clear rules. Trade, inheritance, and land measure supply his practice cases. The book carried Hindu-Arabic methods toward Europe through later copies. Readers meet a science at its birth. The voice is calm and practical.
an-accursed-race-pg2531: Gaskell took up the cause of the Cagots, the shunned outcasts of the French Pyrenees. Her tale of their wrongs burns with anger at bigotry. A brave and moving plea for the despised. Her anger at injustice burns through every page.
arxiv-2511-20231:
Mason, Garrett, and Siemion count the silent stars hiding inside SETI telescope beams. Their 2025 paper simulates the stellar bycatch of radio surveys. A telescope aimed at one star captures many others too. Those background stars widen the true search sample. Gaia catalogs miss faint and crowded-region stars though.

The Besançon Galactic Model simulates the missing population. It fills beams with statistically realistic stars. The team reanalyzed Breakthrough Listen's Enriquez and Price survey. Over six million stars fell inside 1,229 pointings. The search volume reached out to twenty-five kiloparsecs. Limits tightened on strong, steady alien transmitters. Within 2.5 kiloparsecs, under a thousandth of a percent of systems host one. That bound assumes near-zero signal drift rates. A free calculator spreads the method to others. SETI limits now rest on fuller star counts. Surveys look less human-centered than often claimed.
arxiv-2511-20531:
Hossain fact-checks image captions by walking a knowledge graph step by step. Her 2025 paper addresses hallucination in vision-language models. Such models describe images fluently but invent entities confidently. Humans verify visual claims against background knowledge naturally. Models lack any structured mechanism for that checking.

The framework first recognizes visual entities in the image. It then traverses a structured knowledge graph across multiple hops. Facts found along the path refine the draft caption. Three knowledge formats were compared for effectiveness. Hierarchical, triple-based, and bullet-point representations all got tested. Factual accuracy improved by about thirty-one percent in trials. Hallucinated entities dropped by roughly 31.8 percent in the prototype. Test data mixed Google Landmarks, Conceptual Captions, and COCO. Failure modes and reasoning patterns were analyzed too. The knowledge graph was hand-curated for landmarks so far. Scaling to open domains remains future work.
arxiv-2511-20631:
Bradley and Morán Ledezma listen to a p-adic space and hear arithmetic in its spectrum. Their 2025 paper studies Laplacian operators on compact p-adic analytic manifolds. Like hearing a drum's shape, spectral data should reveal geometry. Their kernel-based Laplacian builds on an atlas of local charts. Wavelets diagonalize pieces of that operator.

One wavelet eigenvalue always matches the Serre invariant modulo q minus one. Here q counts the residue field's elements. Elliptic curves give the concrete proving ground for the claim. Counting rational points on the special fibre links to the spectrum. Earlier work recovered point counts for good reduction curves. For split multiplicative reduction the invariant vanishes modulo q minus one. Néron models supply the special fibre in that analysis. Diffusion on p-adic domains motivates the whole construction. Mumford curves showed spectra can rebuild underlying graphs. Arithmetic invariants now join the audible list.
arxiv-2511-20831:
Khuram Naveed and Naveed ur Rehman build in 2025 a fault-finding method for machines watched by many sensors at once. Their tool extends multifractal detrended fluctuation analysis, a way of reading how a signal wiggles at many scales, so it treats all channels jointly instead of one by one. A new fluctuation measure, weighted by how channels vary together, captures links between channels that older versions miss.

Before the analysis, a mode decomposition step strips out noise and keeps the parts of the vibration tied to faults. On wind turbine gearbox data, the method beat standard approaches at telling healthy machines from faulty ones. It kept that edge even when the signals were noisy. The authors pitch it as a practical monitor for rotating equipment, where early warning of gearbox damage saves costly breakdowns.
arxiv-2511-20931:
Biagio La Rosa and Leilani H. Gilpin free in 2025 a neuron-explanation technique from its dependence on hand-labelled data. Compositional explanations describe what a neuron detects as a logical formula over concepts, matched against where the neuron fires. Until now they needed datasets where humans had marked each concept's location, confining the method to fixed concept lists. The new framework swaps human masks for open-vocabulary segmentation models, which can outline any concept a user names.

The pipeline runs in three steps: name arbitrary concepts, generate their masks with an open-vocabulary segmenter, then derive the logical explanation from mask overlaps. The authors compare the output with classic human-annotation explanations on quantitative metrics and on human interpretability. They also study how explanations shift when model-made masks replace human ones. The result is a flexible probe: any neuron, any dataset, any concept vocabulary, with readable explanations.
arxiv-2511-21131:
Taejun Kim, Auejin Ham, Sunggeun Ahn, and Geehyuk Lee presented at CHI 2022 the Lattice Menu, a gaze interface that trades empty space for visual anchors. Marking menus let experts flick their eyes toward a memorised item, but unguided gaze gestures land sloppily, especially in multilevel menus. Lattice Menu overlays a lattice of dots along the gesture paths, giving the eyes targets to lock onto at each level. Users who know an item's location trace the anchors instead of aiming into the void.

In expert use, the menu held its error rate near 1 percent across 4 by 4 by 4 and 6 by 6 by 6 structures, with selection times of 1.3 to 1.6 seconds. Against a traditional gaze marking menu without targets, errors fell fivefold. All 12 study participants preferred the lattice version, and 8 of the 12 said the anchors made selections feel more stable with less eye fatigue. One study logged 300,000 saccade landings to map the technique's precision.
arxiv-2511-21431:
The AIH Training Team tackles a memory wall in training mixture-of-experts language models in 2025. These models route each token to a few specialist subnetworks, but the routing is lopsided: popular experts get flooded, and their graphics cards run out of memory mid-training. Standard fixes cap how many tokens an expert may take, which protects memory but costs accuracy and still fails on small-memory hardware.

Their framework, MemFine, refuses to cap routing. Instead it slices token distribution and expert computation into fine chunks and recomputes selected activations on the fly, with chunk sizes tuned by a theoretical memory model balancing memory against throughput. In experiments, MemFine cut activation memory by about 48 percent compared with full-recomputation baselines. Throughput also rose by roughly 4 percent, and large models trained stably on memory-limited GPUs that previously overflowed.
arxiv-2511-21731:
Diederik Aerts and six coauthors ran classic quantum cognition tests on large language models and found human-like quantum structure in their language, in 2025. Quantum cognition studies how concept combinations defy classical probability rules. The team used ChatGPT and Gemini as test subjects, mirroring experiments once done with people.

In the first test, the models' judgments on combined concepts significantly violated Bell's inequalities, bounds classical theory sets on linked outcomes. That violation signals entanglement-like structure in how the tested concepts combine. In the second test, word distributions across large texts followed Bose-Einstein statistics rather than the expected Maxwell-Boltzmann pattern. Both match earlier findings from human participants and large corpora. The authors read this as evolutionary convergence: meaning organized in vector spaces pushes human and artificial cognition toward the same quantum-shaped structure, theirs by slow biology, the models' by fast training.
arxiv-2512-00631:
Multivariate time series modeling is stuck between Gaussian models and one-off models built for single applications. Jonas Andersson and Dimitris Karlis develop maximum likelihood estimation for the VARTA model in 2025. The name promises a vector autoregressive model that can be transformed to anything.

VARTA rests on an underlying, unobserved Gaussian vector autoregression, transformed to match the data's actual distributions. One general approach could serve finance, environment, and industry data alike. Careful likelihood estimation is what turns that elegant construction into a tool practitioners can fit and trust. Transforming to anything means the margins can be counts, positives, or bounded scores. Maximum likelihood gives the estimates a standard theory of uncertainty. For folks who fit such data, the gain is one frame for many kinds of counts. It can bend to fit the shape at hand, yet stay a single tool.
arxiv-2512-00931:
Imane Jaaouine and Ross King run a pilot study on a failure mode of AI summaries in a 2025 paper. Large language models sometimes hallucinate, writing output that clashes with the user's prompt or source. In science writing, such context inconsistency can quietly distort findings.

Their project asks whether prompt engineering can cut these errors in zero-shot summarisation of scientific texts. Zero-shot means the model gets no examples and works from pretraining alone. If careful prompting helps, it would be a cheap defense for students and researchers who use AI to digest papers. The pilot design shows how such claims should be tested.
arxiv-2512-01131:
M Martí Massó Moreno, C Pérez-Alanis, and P Manoharan generalize a model for solar eruptions in a 2025 paper. Interplanetary coronal mass ejections are huge clouds of solar material that travel through space. Scientists model them as flux ropes, twisted bundles of magnetic field, to rebuild their shape and field from spacecraft data.

Their generalized elliptical-cylindrical flux rope model allows a nonzero poloidal component in the internal magnetic field, a part older models set aside. A two-step method separates the geometric fit from the magnetic field fit. That split should improve stability and consistency when fitting real events.
arxiv-2512-01531:
Cibran Lopez and co-authors ask why a new class of solar cells lags its promise. Pnictogen chalcohalides soak up light well. They are non-toxic and can be made at low heat. Yet top cells stay well below ten percent efficiency. Their ideal cap is far higher.

The team blames defects in the material. Defects trap charge and waste light energy as heat. They map which defects hurt most. That map tells makers what to fix first in growth. Fixing the worst defects could lift these green cells toward real use in roofs and farms.
arxiv-2512-02031:
Drug hunters often start from a molecule known to bind a target and search libraries for new ones with a similar binding pattern. Omar Mahmood and four co-authors present a 2025 method that learns these patterns, called pharmacophores, directly on three-dimensional voxel grids.

The classic search is brute force: compare the known binder against a huge library with some similarity metric, one candidate at a time. Learning on voxel grids lets a model absorb the spatial arrangement of chemical features that makes binding work. Better search tools mean promising, structurally fresh drug candidates can surface earlier in discovery.
arxiv-2512-02531:
Ming Li and three co-authors study how quantum devices are read out through a faint reflected signal. Dispersive readout is a workhorse of quantum technology, used to learn a qubit state without touching it directly. Here the probe field is a squeezed vacuum, sent in a time symmetric way.

The team builds a full counting statistics framework, which tracks the whole spread of outcomes, not just averages. They pair it with a generalized mean field method suited to open, lossy dynamics. The analysis shows how much measurement information such a readout can deliver, guiding future quantum hardware design. The full spread of counts tells more than a lone mean could ever say on its own.
arxiv-2512-02831:
Ali Alvandi and Mina Rezaei revisit the theory of contrastive learning when test classes differ from training ones. Contrastive methods pull similar samples together and push unlike ones apart in a learned space. That recipe powers much of modern self supervised representation learning.

Standard theory assumes downstream classes come from the same latent distribution as pretraining. Domain generalization breaks that assumption, since the target world shifts. The authors rebuild the analysis for shifted settings. Sounder theory tells practitioners when contrastive pretraining should transfer, and when it may quietly fail. A shift in the world is the rule in real use, so tests that own shift tell us far more than clean room scores.
arxiv-2512-03231:
Power spectra of galaxies encode the universe's history. F. Qin and a large team use them to measure cosmic growth in this 2025 work. The work is part of the DESI first data release peculiar velocity survey.

The team measures the auto and cross power spectra of galaxy density and momentum fields. From those spectra they estimate cosmological parameters. This route uses the full pattern of clustering, not just average motions. It offers an independent check on growth rates found by other DESI methods. Spectrum methods capture clustering shape, adding detail beyond average growth numbers.
arxiv-2512-03331:
A nearby red galaxy offers a rare radio detection. L. F. Rodriguez and I. F. Mirabel report it in this 2025 work. The Webb telescope found huge numbers of Little Red Dots in the early universe, compact red galaxies with odd traits.

One odd trait is that no radio signals had been seen from distant Little Red Dots. A local example that does emit radio waves gives a closer test case. Studying it may reveal what powers these objects. That could clarify whether they hide black holes or intense star birth. A local case can be studied in depth that distant, faint dots do not yet allow.
arxiv-2512-03431:
A rare decay of the neutral pion gets its best measure yet. S. Prakhov and a large team report the measurement in this 2025 work. The Dalitz decay turns a pion into an electron, a positron, and a gamma ray.

The team used the A2 tagged-photon facility at the Mainz Microtron. They measured the decay in a photon-proton reaction with the highest statistical accuracy so far. Precise Dalitz data test theory of how pions are built. They also help calibrate detectors used in other particle studies. Tagged photons give clean initial states, which is why the Mainz setup suits rare decays.
arxiv-2512-03531:
A supernova showed helium-rich material around it, a first of its kind. Xiang-Cun Meng and Philipp Podsiadlowski explain that case in this 2025 work. SN 2020eyj is the first type Ia supernova with a signature of compact helium-rich circumstellar material.

Such a large amount of material is hard to explain if the donor star was a helium star. The authors propose a helium common-envelope wind scenario. Their account reshapes how some type Ia explosions are understood. Those explosions are key distance markers for the universe. Helium-rich shells are rare, so each well-modeled case tests donor star theories hard.
arxiv-2512-03831:
Steady water waves rolling through a channel of layered, stratified fluid are a classic problem in mathematical physics. Vladimir Kozlov examines such Stokes waves in a 2025 analysis preprint, focusing on the spectral properties of their Frechet derivatives. Those derivatives govern how a wave responds to small disturbances, and their eigenvalues decide which neighbouring wave patterns can exist.

One headline result is negative in a useful way. Near a Stokes wave, there are no subharmonic waves. That means no waves repeating over a multiple of the basic period. The first eigenvalue always comes out negative. If the second turns positive, he proves, no multiple-period waves can live nearby. His main assumption is stated through these eigenvalues, among solutions sharing the basic period. The result sharpens the map of which steady wave families can branch from a basic Stokes wave.
arxiv-2512-03931:
An autonomous agent that always obeys every rule may fail exactly when breaking one would prevent a disaster. Vineel Tummala and Daniela Inclezan build a reasoning framework for that dilemma in a 2025 artificial intelligence preprint. Their agents can weigh a violation against its penalty and choose the lesser harm, rather than treating rules as absolute.

It extends an existing policy language for authorisations and obligations by adding penalties, and it reasons using answer set programming. Policies are guaranteed well formed, priorities among rules are respected, and violations are named explicitly with their consequences, which keeps decisions explainable. An automatic translator converts the extended language into the logic program, and planners rank non-compliant plans by the fines they incur. Experiments in two domains produced higher-quality plans avoiding harmful actions. The tool could also help policymakers simulate realistic human choices.
arxiv-2512-04031:
Gravitational wave astronomy has the opposite data problem from most of machine learning: signals are precious and few, and the noise is unruly. Yixuan Li and a large team ask whether large language models can help in a 2025 instrumentation preprint. They test fine-tuned language models on identifying real gravitational wave signals in LIGO data, where noise is neither Gaussian nor stationary.

Working from only about ninety recorded events, the fine-tuned models reached accuracy above ninety-seven percent. Adding more simulated samples, the usual trick for conventional networks, did not help further. Scaling studies showed predictable gains as model size and dataset size grew. The authors read this as evidence that language models can pull discriminative structure straight from observational data. They suggest the same strategy could serve other noisy, data-starved corners of astronomy.
arxiv-2512-04631:
Amadeusz Dydniański, Mateusz Raczyński, Aleksandra Łopion, and co-authors show that the metal painted on a semiconductor chip can flip its local charge type. Their test bed is a quantum well based on cadmium telluride, laced with manganese and born p-type, meaning holes carry its charge. Five metals were laid down as thin films: gold, silver, chromium, nickel, and titanium. Their 2025 arXiv paper watches the well's charge through magneto-spectroscopy.

Magnetic readings track shifts at singlet-triplet crossings, which betray the charge state below each metal patch. Most metals left the well p-type. Gold and nickel flipped their patches to n-type, where electrons rule. The team credits strong bonding of those two metals to the surface, which seals flaws and lets electrons pour in. Such contact effects matter for spintronic devices, where a flipped patch can make or break a junction.
arxiv-2512-04731:
Jian Tang, Pu Pang, Haowen Sun, and co-authors tackle the sim-to-real gap that haunts robot training: skills learned in a simulator often fail on real hardware. Lighting, textures, and physics differ across the two worlds. Common fixes, such as randomizing the simulator or endless calibration, need heavy tuning and still break on new scenes. Their 2025 arXiv paper bets on features that both worlds share.

The method, Semantic 2D Gaussian Splatting, builds multi-view semantic fields from camera views. It projects those fields into one unified, object-centered feature space. Policies train in simulation on these features alone. At deployment, the same features come from real cameras, so the policy sees a familiar world. Tests on manipulation tasks show transfer gains over older approaches. Object-centered, domain-blind features may be the sturdiest bridge between practice worlds and the real floor.
arxiv-2512-04831:
Pedro Menezes de Araujo, Isobel Claire Gormley, and Thomas Brendan Murphy review how researchers cluster countries by their mortality patterns. Death rates shape demography, public health, and pension science. Grouping countries with similar mortality curves can reveal convergence, inequality, and clues for forecasting. Yet no review had covered clustering of country-level, all-cause mortality. Their 2025 arXiv paper surveys the recent literature and asks why clustering is used, which data and methods dominate, and what findings recur.

Most studies draw on the Human Mortality Database and cover developed countries. K-means and hierarchical methods lead the toolbox. Forecasting and the study of convergence and inequality motivate most work. The authors replicate selected approaches on database records to show how choices steer groupings. The review gives newcomers a map of a growing field and warns where habits, such as rich-country bias, narrow its lessons.
arxiv-2512-04931:
Rishika Agrawal, Thomas Bloom, and Giorgis Petridis push the sum-product problem forward for sets of integers built from few primes. The sum-product phenomenon says a finite set of numbers cannot stay small under both addition and multiplication at once; one of the two derived sets must swell. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies sets where every member is divisible by only a bounded number of primes, a smooth, structured family where growth is hardest to force.

For such sets, they prove the larger of the sum set and the product set grows by a strong power of the set's size. They extend the bound to repeated sums and products taken any number of times. A third result covers rational sets with few prime factors in numerator and denominator, where sums of products swell nearly to the square of the size. Each bound sharpens how arithmetic structure limits growth.
arxiv-2512-05031:
Rajneil Baruah, Subhadeep Mondal, Sunando Kumar Patra, and Satyajit Roy look for a cheaper way to sort the jets that spray out of particle collisions. At colliders, telling a jet born from a top quark apart from ordinary jets is a basic task. The best classifiers — transformers and graph networks — do it well but demand heavy computing. The team asks whether a lean image-based network can keep up.

Their answer builds on a slimmed-down version of EfficientNet, a family of networks designed to trade size for speed wisely. It feeds the network both the jet's image and a handful of whole-jet measurements. The result tags top-quark jets competitively at a fraction of the cost. The study also shows that the whole-jet measurements carry much of the signal, which hints that the added complexity of bigger networks may be partly redundant for this job.
arxiv-2512-05231:
Gili Goldin, Ella Rabinovich, and Shuly Wintner measure political polarization by tone rather than by ideology. Affective polarization — how warmly or coldly political camps speak — can climb even when policy positions barely move, and it corrodes public discourse worldwide. The authors quantify it from the emotional style of speech, scoring transcripts on valence, arousal, and dominance: how pleasant, how intense, and how powerful the language feels.

They apply the method to a large corpus of proceedings from the Knesset, Israel's parliament, written in Hebrew. Two findings stand out. Government members and opposition members speak in measurably different emotional styles. And the gap between those styles — the affective polarization of the chamber — is growing significantly over time. The method offers a language-based instrument for tracking a kind of division that opinion polls and voting records can miss.
arxiv-2512-05331:
Sadat Shahriar and four co-authors expose the linguistic fingerprints of pink slime journalism. These are auto-generated articles dressed up as local news, a deception aimed at the tens of millions of Americans who rely on local reporting. The authors conduct a study of what sets this content apart in wording, style, and vocabulary, and build detection strategies on the patterns they find.

The study raises a new alarm: consumer-grade language models can rewrite pink slime well enough to undermine detectors, cutting their accuracy scores steeply. In response, the authors introduce a learning framework designed to resist such model-based tampering and to keep pace as the fakes evolve. It recovers a large share of the lost performance. The work matters for platform moderation and media literacy alike: the arms race over fake local news now runs through the same tools anyone can open in a browser.
arxiv-2512-05631:
John Bourke writes on category theory, the branch of math that studies structures and the maps between them in very general terms. His subject is pseudomonads on two dimensional categories, and one special kind called lax-idempotent. The trouble is that telling whether a given pseudomonad has this property can be hard work. The 2025 paper gives a simple test that makes recognition easy.

The test looks at a certain construction from pairs of arrows, a comma object formed with loose, colax limits. If that construction behaves in the stated way, the pseudomonad is lax-idempotent. Bourke shows the test is easy to check in real examples. Building on it, he obtains a fresh characterization of these pseudomonads on any two category that has the needed limits. For category theorists, a hard property becomes quick to spot in new examples.
arxiv-2512-05731:
Najla Abassi, Lea Schwarz, Edoardo Filippi, and Federico Marini introduce DeeDeeExperiment, a software tool for the R and Bioconductor world. Modern omics studies test many conditions at once. Each run produces piles of results: which genes changed, and which biological functions those changes point to. No standard container existed to store all of this together with its context. Results ended up scattered and hard to share.

DeeDeeExperiment fills the gap with a new data class. It extends the widely used SingleCellExperiment object with dedicated slots for two kinds of results: differential expression and functional enrichment. Many comparisons, each with its metadata, live inside one object. Users can store, organize, and pull back exactly the result they need. The package is free on Bioconductor under the MIT license. By giving omics results a common home, it makes large studies easier to interpret, audit, and build upon.
arxiv-2512-06331:
Marcus Volp and five co authors ask how event driven real time systems can survive a flood of signals from a hostile world. Such systems, found in cars and planes, are designed for a safe range of conditions. Outside that range, a storm of interrupts can swamp the processor and risk safe action. Time driven designs have often been claimed to be immune to this threat by their very nature.

The authors test that claim and look for defenses event driven systems can use. They add a new notion, importance, kept apart from priority and critical rank, to say which tasks must still run when design assumptions fail. They draw links to mixed criticality scheduling, where tasks of unlike rank share one machine. Their account shows how an event driven system can shed the flood and guard its key work when the world breaks its design rules.
arxiv-2512-06731:
Tianjun Gan and a large team take a fresh look at the atmosphere of HAT-P-70b, an ultra hot Jupiter circling a young star. Such planets are bloated and scorching, which makes their air easy to study as they cross their stars. Using the CARMENES instrument on a telescope in Spain, the team recorded the planet's transmission spectrum at high resolution, reading which atoms soak up starlight in its upper air.

They confirm earlier sightings of hydrogen, sodium, and ionized calcium, add a tentative first sighting of potassium, and cap how much helium could be present. A second method finds calcium and iron vapor, both blown toward the night side by a day to night wind. No molecules showed in the near infrared. Set among its peers, this planet supports two patterns: young systems show hydrogen more often, and calcium and iron tend to appear together.
arxiv-2512-07331:
Kanishk Awadhiya examines a curious habit of vision transformers: although nothing in their design forces it. They often squeeze their internal picture of an image in the middle layers, then expand it again for the final answer. That U-shaped profile of information, which he calls an inductive bottleneck, might be a mere quirk of the architecture. His tests argue it is instead a response to the data itself.

He measures each layer's effective encoding dimension in self-supervised transformers across three data sets of differing compositional demand. The bottleneck's depth tracks the semantic abstraction the task requires. Texture-heavy collections keep their representations wide and high-rank through every layer. Object-centered ones drive the network to damp the high-frequency detail mid-journey, isolating the semantic features that matter.
arxiv-2512-07631:
Shahar Lutati wrote this 2025 paper on a basic question for autonomous agents. Before an agent spends time and money on a task, it should judge whether success is even possible. Guessing by habit or past feel gives weak guidance for that call.

Lutati frames the problem as gathering information. Every task hides a solution that takes a certain number of bits to identify. Each action the agent takes buys some bits at some cost. Dividing and combining those values yields a predicted total cost before any search begins. He proves this value sets a floor on the expected cost of solving the task. Tight probability bounds cap the cost from above as well. In experiments, the predictions track real agent performance closely. The method beats greedy and random strategies on efficiency. It also applies across language-model agents and wider automated workflows.
arxiv-2512-07831:
Jiehui Huang and nine co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on video generation with real world sense. Today's generators make lovely clips but learn from one kind of signal at a time. That single-modality diet limits how well they grasp the physical world.

Their framework, UnityVideo, learns from many modalities and tasks jointly. Segmentation masks, human skeletons, dense pose, optical flow, and depth maps all enter training. Two components make that union work inside one model. Dynamic noising unifies the very different training styles those modalities need. A modality switcher with an in-context learner handles processing through modular parameters. The team contributes a large shared dataset to feed the system. Joint optimization speeds convergence compared with separate training runs. Zero-shot generalization to unseen data improves markedly as well. Output videos gain quality, consistency, and respect for physical constraints. One model, many senses, is the paper's guiding bet.
arxiv-2512-08231:
Zong kai Peng, He Gao, and Xian Fei Zhang, astrophysicists in China, posted a simulation study on arXiv in December 2025. They compute what happens when a neutron star flies straight into a white dwarf, a rare but violent kind of stellar collision. Depending on the dwarf mass and makeup, the smash could light a thermonuclear explosion or leave the neutron star trapped in the wreckage.

The team models collisions with helium, carbon oxygen, and oxygen neon white dwarfs separately. An explosion needs two things: the impact must heat material past its ignition point, and the burning matter must stay degenerate. For some ranges of each type, both hold, so collisions can trigger unusual Type Ia supernovae or other exotic flashes. The trapped outcome, a Thorne Zytkow like object, needs strong drag without an explosion, and proved possible for low mass carbon oxygen and oxygen neon dwarfs, given enough viscosity.
arxiv-2512-08531:
Sangeetha Kizhakkekalam, Gopal Bhatta, Navaneeth P K, and Tek P Adhikari, astronomers, posted an observational study on arXiv in December 2025. Their target is Markarian 421, a nearby blazar whose jet points almost straight at Earth, shining from radio waves to very high energy gamma rays. They present the first detailed look at it from the NICER X ray telescope, using forty five observations gathered across two years.

The source varied strongly, on both daily and long timescales, with its X ray output swinging nearly thirty fold at the extremes. A curved log parabola fit the spectra best. The spectrum hardened as the source brightened, a classic blazar pattern, and its peak energy rose with flux. The fast flickering implies the X rays come from a compact region near the central engine. The patterns fit energy dependent particle acceleration inside the jet, shaped by turbulence and strong magnetic fields.
arxiv-2512-08731:
Qipan Wang and coauthors present a chip system design for serving large language models at scale, built around stacked memory technology. Such serving needs high throughput and low energy use. Stacked dynamic memory offers high bandwidth for the decode phase, but balancing compute for the prompt phase with bandwidth and capacity for decode remains an open design problem.

Their design, LaMoSys, places mixed chiplets on an interposer, with compute rich parts for prompt work and bandwidth rich parts for decode work. Hardware and software are designed together, covering data flow, parallel mapping, and scheduling, with a thermal aware search over design choices. Across models and workloads, the system improves throughput per watt over a leading server baseline and cuts end to end latency versus prior stacked designs. Design guidelines for this class of chips are also drawn out.
arxiv-2512-09431:
Quanyou Wang leads the ARTEMIS team in describing the system that won the RoboCup 2024 adult-sized humanoid soccer competition. RoboCup pits fully autonomous humanoid robots against each other at soccer, with a long-term goal of facing human players by 2050. Athletic humanoids demand advances in actuation, sensing, and control all at once.

On the hardware side, their robot pairs lightweight structures with high-torque quasi-direct-drive actuators and a special foot that can kick hard during the walking gait without losing balance. The software stacks stereo vision, object detection, and landmark-based fusion to track the ball, goals, teammates, and opponents. A navigation layer plans collision-aware paths, while a central behavior manager picks roles and times kicks from the game state. The paper lays out the design principles, architecture, and match results behind the championship.
arxiv-2512-09731:
Stanislav Fedotov and Evgeny Feigin state conjectures about a family of quiver Grassmannians, geometric spaces built from representations of Dynkin quivers. A quiver is a graph, they assign vector spaces and maps to its nodes and arrows, and a quiver Grassmannian collects the subrepresentations of a dimension inside a representation. These spaces connect representation theory with geometry.

Their setting is narrow. Start with projective and injective representations of the same quiver. Look at subrepresentations whose dimension equals that of the projective one, inside representations whose dimension is the sum of the two. The authors call Grassmannians of this shape principal. Based on computer experiments rather than completed proofs, they propose conjectures about the algebro-geometric properties of these spaces, such as their structure. The paper is an invitation to the community, supported by evidence, to prove or refine the patterns.
arxiv-2512-10331:
Marcilio Ferreira dos Santos builds an epidemic model where the geometry of the contact network shapes how disease spreads. The setting is the classic SIR model, susceptible, infectious, recovered, running on a network, but spread is modulated by a curvature weighted contact matrix. The setup covers both direct adjacency spread and Markovian mixing. The epidemic threshold takes a clean spectral form: the basic reproduction number is the ratio of spread to recovery rates times the largest eigenvalue of the weighted spread operator.

Using Perron-Frobenius theory and Lyapunov functionals, the author proves the expected threshold picture with full rigor. Below the threshold, the disease free state is globally stable: every outbreak dies out. Above it, a unique endemic equilibrium exists and attracts all solutions. Curvature acts as a geometric regularizer, lowering spectral radii and thereby raising the effective threshold a pathogen must cross.
arxiv-2512-10931:
George Yakushev and co-authors teach a reasoning model to think and talk at the same time. Today's best language models think before answering, which sharpens their reasoning but freezes interaction: new input cannot be absorbed until the thought finishes. Voice assistants and embodied agents cannot work that way. Humans listen, think, and speak asynchronously, and the authors retrofit that ability onto sequential models without any retraining.

Their method exploits properties of positional embeddings. Those are the signals that tell a model where each token sits. With them, a model built for step-by-step generation can keep thinking while new input arrives. It can also keep thinking while output is already flowing. On maths, commonsense, and safety reasoning tasks, models produced accurate, thought-enriched answers while the wait for the first spoken token fell from minutes to a few seconds. And total delays dropped by up to twelvefold.
arxiv-2601-06931:
Haodong Chen and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers measuring social bias in Vision-Language models with Face-Only counterfactuals from real photos. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed in socially consequential settings, raising concerns about social bias driven by demographic cues.

A central challenge in measuring such social bias is attribution under visual confounding: real-world images entangle race and gender with correlated factors such. As background and clothing, obscuring attribution. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07031:
Research by Yossef Zenati and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with structure of poloidal fields embedded in thin disks. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Many accreting systems are modeled as geometrically thin disks. Simulations of accretion disks cannot, at present, be extended to this regime.

Although local models can address the behavior of narrow annuli within the disk. A global model needs to account for the interactions between a large scale poloidal field, accreted from the environment, and the disk. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07131:
Sungwoo Kang and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with limits of complexity. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. The application of machine learning to financial prediction has accelerated dramatically, yet the conditions under which complex models outperform simple alternatives remain poorly understood. The work investigates whether advanced signal processing and deep learning techniques can extract predictive value.

From investor order flows beyond what simple feature engineering achieves. Using a comprehensive dataset of 2. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07331:
Yuanhe Zhang and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with SEE. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) have been widely applied in real-time scenarios, such as in-car assistants and online meeting comprehension.

In practice, audio inputs are often corrupted by device and environmental noise, leading to performance degradation. However, existing LALM studies on noise lack quantitative analysis and rely mainly on intuition and empirical observation, thus failing to understand practical robustness. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07631:
Marija Šakota and a team from the Wikipedia community report a pilot that put machine-written summaries inside the Wikipedia Android app. Short descriptions help readers judge an article at a glance, but coverage is uneven across languages and topics. The summaries came from Descartes, a multilingual model the team introduced in earlier work. Their 2026 preprint describes the deployment.

A pilot deployment tests more than accuracy: it tests how real readers and editors react. Machine-generated text inside Wikipedia raises questions of trust, editing workload, and quality control. Running the system in the live app gives answers that lab tests cannot. The report should interest anyone adding generated content to large public knowledge platforms. It documents both the model and its reception in practice.
arxiv-2601-07831:
A Cosmoglobe team models starlight in infrared sky data using two modern star catalogs. They build the model for the Diffuse Infrared Background Explorer, DIRBE, across 1.25 to 25 micrometers. Star positions and brightness come from Gaia and WISE measurements. Two classes of compact objects enter the model. Bright stars get individual spectral energy distributions measured by Gaia. Their 2026 preprint is part four of the Cosmoglobe DR2 series.

The second class is a diffuse background of dim point sources combined together. Separating starlight matters because it contaminates maps of galactic dust and the cosmic background. Gaia's precise star data make a cleaner subtraction possible. The model feeds the larger Cosmoglobe reanalysis of microwave and infrared skies. Cosmologists removing foregrounds are the main readers. Starlight, usually the signal, here plays the role of noise to model carefully.
arxiv-2601-07931:
Iván Garibay, Christian Ecker, and Luciano Rezzolla survey general traits of neutron stars across many possible interiors. They study curvature invariants for a large ensemble of neutron stars. The stars are built from equations of state that satisfy nuclear theory and perturbative QCD constraints. Measurements of masses, radii, and gravitational waves from mergers also constrain the set. Their 2026 preprint adds binding energy and the trace anomaly to the study.

Looking for general properties means finding patterns that hold regardless of the unknown interior. Such patterns let observers infer star properties with less model dependence. Curvature invariants describe spacetime bending in a coordinate-free way. The trace anomaly measures how matter breaks scale symmetry at high density. The paper serves gravitational wave and nuclear astrophysicists. It searches for universals in a famously uncertain system.
arxiv-2601-08231: L. Kleess wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on slow flows whose thickness varies from place to place. The flow is oscillatory, driven back and forth at one fixed rate. It can not be squeezed, so its volume stays the same. The thickness field is complex, with a size and a phase at each point. The phase, read as the argument of the field, forms a texture across the space. The work stresses three traits: non-normality with no drift, flaws at corners, and mode coupling in three dimensions.
arxiv-2601-08331:
Daniil Gurgurov and co-authors release CLaS-Bench, a benchmark for cross-lingual alignment and steering. Their 2026 arXiv paper addresses how to control language model behavior in multilingual settings. Steering changes internal representations during inference, offering a more efficient and interpretable route than prompting or fine-tuning.

A benchmark is needed because steering claims are hard to compare across languages. CLaS-Bench gives shared tasks for alignment and steering tests. Builders of multilingual systems can check whether a steering method works beyond English. The work supports safer control of models that serve users in many languages at once.
arxiv-2601-08731:
Yuanlin Duan and three co-authors work on robots that learn by watching a skilled user. Pure copy work breaks down on long tasks. One small slip can grow, and the robot soon drifts far from the shown path. The team wants a way to learn that can bend when the task is long.

Their method is called Cago. It picks goals that fit what the robot can do now, not just goals from the demo. The robot aims for those goals and learns from each try. In this way it is less tied to one fixed path. A reader who trains robots gets a plan that may hold up on long jobs where plain copy work fails.
arxiv-2601-08831:
Yang-Che Sun and a team from Taiwan and NVIDIA work on how to mark objects in video. Top tools can mark an object in each frame by use of past frames. But when the view shifts a lot, looks change and marks drift. Old 3D tools fix drift, yet they need much prep work and site data.

Their tool is called 3AM. It adds 3D aware traits from a model named MUSt3R to a top video tool named SAM2. The add on is used at train time, so run time stays light. A reader who marks video gets a path to firm marks through big view shifts. It needs no depth maps or pose data at run time.
arxiv-2601-08931:
Ori Fox and a large team report new star bursts found deep in space with the Webb scope. Bursts at great range show stars as they were long ago. Most scopes can not take the light print of such far bursts. The Webb scope can, and a wide survey named COSMOS-Web gave it much sky to watch in its first two years.

The team lists wide area finds of bursts at high range from that survey. Each find helps trace how star groups grew and changed over vast time. Far bursts also test counts of how oft stars die at each era. A reader in space work gets an early yield of a key survey. It shows the far burst field is rich, not bare.
arxiv-2601-09031:
Xuetao Li and three co-authors work on human shaped robots that must grasp and move things. Such a robot needs high thought, to know what a task asks. It needs low skill too, to move arms with care. Two hard parts block it. It needs a true read of a 3D scene. It also must learn from few human demos, not vast sets.

The team adds a shape based prior that holds across scenes. Prior here means built in shape sense the robot can reuse. They add a spiking learn part that fires in bursts, like nerve cells. It aims to learn fast from few demos. A reader in robot work gets a plan for robots that can shift to new rooms and tasks.
arxiv-2601-09431:
Matteo Bordin proposes a way to prepare strange quantum states of a tiny mechanical oscillator. His 2026 arXiv paper uses cavity optomechanics, where light trapped in a cavity pushes on a moving mirror. The target states are non-Gaussian and spread out, delocalized across the oscillator.

The protocol is measurement-based: it waits for a detector to click on the light leaving the cavity. That click heralds that the mechanical state has been projected into the desired form. Bordin works out when the coupling creates enough entanglement for the state's Wigner function to go negative. Such states are prized for quantum sensing and for tests of quantum physics at large scales.
arxiv-2601-09531:
Yue Yao, Ruining Yang, and Tom Gedeon address a common bind in computer vision. The target setting is known, but labeling data there is not feasible. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds a substitute training set from a large data server. The goal is a model that performs well on the target domain anyway.

Target domains usually split into distinct modes, or clusters of similar scenes. The authors match those modes to material on the server using bipartite matching. Pulling the right mix matters more than pulling lots of data. A well-matched training set can stand in for costly on-site annotation in tasks like inspection and monitoring.
arxiv-2601-09631:
Stergios Chatzikyriakidis and Anastasia Natsina test whether language models can hear rhyme in Greek verse. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds a hybrid system for rhyme detection and generation. Language models are strong at many language tasks but weak at sound-based skills like rhyme.

The gap widens in lower-resource languages such as Modern Greek. The authors pair the model with deterministic phonological algorithms that track sounds exactly. The hybrid aims at accurate rhyme finding and rhyme making. It shows a pattern for other sound-driven tasks: let the model propose, and let rules check.
arxiv-2601-10131:
Yizhan Li and co authors build new molecules to order. A drug hunt may need a molecule with set values on many traits at once. Traits can span how it binds, melts, or moves in the body. Language models are free in form but weak at exact counts.

The team made a two stage plan named M4olGen. It works at the level of chunks of a molecule. It fetches like chunks from a store to guide the build. Each stage takes feed back on the trait counts. The aim is a molecule that hits all the set values at once.
arxiv-2601-10231:
Rupert McCallum proves that a vast set idea clashes with the base rules of sets. The idea is a Reinhardt cardinal. It says a set can map into itself in a rich way. The map must be non plain but keep all set facts. Such a claim sat open for years.

McCallum shows the claim fails in ZF, the base rule set. His case rests on a map at a set rank plus three. Parts one and two sort past work on the theme. One past work holds the key force step. The proof closes a long open ask in set theory.
arxiv-2601-10631:
Andrés F. Izquierdo and co-authors report a possible circumplanetary disk inside the disk of the star HD 163296. Data from the ALMA telescope array suggest that unseen young planets are shaping this disk. Rings and gaps in its gas and dust match what planet-disk models predict. One spot now draws special attention.

The team traces that spot by localized emission from simple organic molecules. A circumplanetary disk is the small disk around a forming planet where moons may later form. Finding one would give direct proof of a planet still in the making. The result speaks to how moons, as well as planets, get their start.
arxiv-2601-10731:
L. G. P. Caramês and co-authors revisit the Lévy flight foraging hypothesis, a claim about how animals search. The claim says natural selection tuned many species to search in Lévy walks, bursts of short steps mixed with rare long jumps. Inverse square Lévy walks are widely held to be the best pattern for non-destructive foraging, where food can be revisited.

Yet a rigorous proof for two or more dimensions is still missing. The authors study Lévy walkers inside spherical shells with absorbing walls. Boundaries change the search game in ways open space does not. Their results push toward settling which Lévy strategy truly wins, a question that spans ecology, physics, and search theory.
arxiv-2601-10931:
David Szczecina and co-authors segment tree canopies in aerial images with very little training data. Canopy maps serve environmental monitoring, urban planning, and ecosystem studies. The Solafune competition they use mimics real annotation scarcity: only 150 labeled images, and an imbalanced set at that. Deep models trained on so few images tend to overfit badly.

The team fine-tunes leading pretrained models on this tiny set. Starting from models that already see well is the key defense against overfitting. Their results show what transfer can salvage when labels are scarce. Land managers and city foresters often face exactly this constraint: many images, almost no labels.
arxiv-2601-11231:
Savvas Papaioannou, Panayiotis Kolios, Christos Panayiotou, and Marios Polycarpou track wildfire fronts. Their 2026 preprint uses a mobile agent, such as a drone. Where the drone flies sets where sensor data comes from. That choice shapes how well the fire's spread can be guessed.

A wildfire front moves in a random, hard-to-know way. Good tracking must join sensing, guessing, and control in one loop. Past work often split those three jobs into parts. The team's control seeks data on purpose as it flies. It steers toward the spots that cut doubt the most. The aim is a sharper map of the front in real time.
arxiv-2601-11631:
Yurun Song and coauthors compress coordinates for multi-turn GUI agents. Their 2026 preprint is called Compress to Focus, on policy optimization. GUI agents finish complex tasks through sequential decisions. Each turn adds screenshots and actions to the history.

Accumulated history inflates context severely over long tasks. Truncation sacrifices long-term context that agents may need. Token pruning compromises the spatial structure of screens. The team compresses coordinates to focus the policy instead. Compact coordinates keep where things are on screen. Policy optimization then learns from leaner, structured states. The work comes from UC Irvine and partner labs.
arxiv-2601-12131:
Santosh Chapagain, MohammadReza EskandariNasab, Onur Vural, and their co-authors tune a language model for teaching on space weather. Solar flares, mass ejections, and geomagnetic storms can harm satellites, flights, power grids, and space work. Big events can cause vast loss with brief warning.

Their model, named SolarGPT-QA in the work, is adapted to heliophysics terms and facts. It answers student questions in that domain. A domain-tuned tutor could spread early warning skill more widely. The work tests its answers on space weather topics.  Space weather is a niche where plain chat tools fail most.
arxiv-2601-12231:
Kaichuan Kong, Dongjie Liu, Xiaobo Jin, Shijie Xu, and Guanggang Geng spot insider threats in user logs with wavelet tools. Logs hold rich behaviour data in many channels. They shift over time, and true threats are rare, which makes spotting hard.

Their frame joins wavelet-aware modulation, wavelet splits at many scales, and attention that adapts to scale. Wavelets track both fast bursts and slow drifts in acts. A robust spotter helps firms catch misuse early. The work tests it on multi-channel logs.  Rare threats need tools that miss few true cases.
arxiv-2601-12731:
Stefano Civelli, Pietro Bernardelle, Nicolo Brunello, and Gianluca Demartini study how language models represent problem difficulty. Predicting difficulty means estimating how hard a task is for the model itself. A common method trains linear probes on internal representations of the model. The team ask whether that difficulty signal has the same shape across languages.

They train probes on a benchmark subset translated into twenty one languages. The set comes from the AMC portion of the Easy2Hard benchmark. If a shared geometry of difficulty exists, one probe structure fits many tongues. That would suggest models judge hardness in a language neutral way. The finding would matter for multilingual evaluation and training.
arxiv-2601-13431:
Sandra Robles, Rosa Dominguez-Tenreiro, and Susana Pedrosa track how mass clumps around the birth sites of galaxies in a big sim. The sim is the EAGLE50 box, a large volume run of galaxy growth. The team starts with round lumps of matter at very high redshift, set at redshift fifteen.

Each lump is centred on a spot where a galaxy will form. They track how each lump is stretched by tides as time runs. A shrunk inertia tool reads that stretch. They track dark matter and cold baryons apart, to see where the two part. Such stretch sets the spin and shape a galaxy is born with.
arxiv-2601-13831:
Redamy Perez-Ramos, Stefan Kluth, and Wolfgang Ochs review the dead cone effect in heavy-quark jets in 2026. In QCD, a heavy quark sheds radiation as it flies. The dead cone is a zone near its path where radiation is suppressed. The team gives a unified study across charm, bottom, and top quarks.

They use precision data from LEP at 91.2 GeV collision energy. The data show strong momentum-space suppression in charm and bottom jets. Monte Carlo simulations with Pythia 8 support the readings. They give a quantitative account in the Modified Leading Logarithmic Approximation of perturbative QCD.
arxiv-2601-13931:
A study of music search models tackles how they handle the word not in 2026. Joint audio-text models are widely used for music retrieval. A user might ask for a track with vocals, or without vocals. Negation is fundamental for telling the absence of an element from its presence.

Current systems fail to represent negation reliably, the team reports. That failure can flip a search result to its exact opposite. The work targets effective negation modeling in these joint models. Music tools that grasp not would serve listeners and catalog teams far better.
arxiv-2601-14031:
Stefano Damato, Nicoló Rubattu, Dario Azzimonti, and Giorgio Corani forecast demand series full of zeros in 2026. Intermittent time series have a significant amount of zeros by nature. They make up a large percentage of inventory items in supply chains. Probabilistic forecasts are needed to plan inventory levels well.

A good predictive distribution covers non-negative values only. It should have a mass at zero and a long upper tail. The team compares local models, fit per item, with global models fit across items. The better style could cut both stockouts and wasteful overstock.
arxiv-2601-14131:
Amila Indika, Rick Kazman, and Anthony Peruma survey how app builders handle accessibility in practice in 2026. Mobile apps are now ubiquitous in everyday life. Developers must prioritize accessibility for users with diverse abilities. Past research found widespread accessibility issues in apps.

A lack of cross-platform, globally representative insights remains on practitioner views. Past work raised awareness of developer challenges but not this broad picture. Their study asks practitioners about practices and challenges directly. Knowing real habits helps target training, tools, and rules that improve access. The views come from a wide set of lands and app types. That breadth makes the gaps they name hard to wave away.
arxiv-2601-14231:
Alessandro Cucinotta, Mattia Magnabosco, and Daniele Semola prove new shape limits in this 2026 math paper. They work on complete Riemannian manifolds, curved spaces with no edge. The key rule is nonnegative Ricci curvature, a mild bound on how the space bends. They also treat RCD spaces, a wider class built for rough settings.

One main result is a rigidity theorem on Betti numbers, counts that track holes in a space. It answers a question open since work by M.-T. Anderson in 1990. A second result is a vanishing theorem for simplicial volume. That result widens a known theorem by another author, whose name is cut off in the abstract.
arxiv-2601-14631:
Jinyang Liao and Ziyang Lyu present a learning framework in this 2026 paper. It is semi-supervised learning for Gaussian mixture modelling under a Missing at Random mechanism. Semi-supervised means some data points carry labels and many do not. Missing at Random describes how the labels come to be missing. Their method explicitly parameterizes the missing-label mechanism.

They model the probability of missingness as a function of classification uncertainty. To quantify that uncertainty, they introduce margin confidence. They also incorporate the Aranda-Ordaz link function, which flexibly captures asymmetric relationships between uncertainty and missing probability. The fix is neat. Doubt is not a flaw in the data here; it is a clue the model can use. Readers get a mixture model that learns from its own doubtful cases instead of ignoring them.
arxiv-2601-14831:
J. McKean, L. Munteanu, and S. Abe benchmark neutrino scattering models in this 2026 paper. They examine three exclusive nuclear ground state shell models implemented in the NEUT neutrino event generator. They benchmark them against the recent JSNS2 measurement of missing energy, made with a monoenergetic neutrino source. A single-energy beam makes the test unusually clean.

The nature of the measurement allows a detailed investigation of nuclear ground-state modeling using a neutrino source. It gives access to a direct measurement of the neutron spectral function in a carbon-12 nucleus. Readers get a rare, sharp check on the nuclear models inside a major neutrino simulation tool.
arxiv-2601-14931:
Nouhoum Coulibaly, Ousmane Ly, Michael Leventhal, and Ousmane Goro study generative AI in Mali. Their 2026 arXiv paper asks if such tools can help build peace stories. It also asks if they can help revive the country's musical heritage.

The study sits in a hard setting. Tensions between groups and deep social splits shape daily life there. Those splits drive a search for new shared frames that can aid reconciliation. The authors test in depth what AI-made music and story work can add to that search for common ground and trust.
arxiv-2601-15131:
Ayan Maity and Sudeshna Sarkar plan delivery routes against the clock. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the vehicle routing problem under a finite time horizon. The goal is to serve as many customer requests as possible before time runs out.

The authors use deep reinforcement learning for the task. Their key piece is a new routing network embedding module. It builds local vectors for each node in the route graph. It also builds a global view of the graph that knows the context. Those two views guide the agent's choices.
arxiv-2601-15231:
Hanchen Wang, Junfeng Hu, and a large team report the first direct sighting of antimagnons. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with spin waves in magnetic materials. An antimagnon is a spin wave with negative energy, marked by a dispersion curve that runs the wrong way round in momentum space.

The team used Brillouin light scattering spectroscopy to catch that signature. Their sample is an ultrathin BiYIG film. Its perpendicular anisotropy just cancels the demagnetizing field. In that tuned state, the inverted dispersion shows up clearly, giving direct spectroscopic proof of antimagnons.
arxiv-2601-15331:
Rishit Chugh probes language models with hostile prompts, and counts the cost of doing so. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with jailbreaking: prompt tricks that push a model to produce outputs it should refuse. Wide deployment has raised the security stakes.

Models out of the box often lack robust guardrails. Manual exploits take time and effort to craft. Chugh presents RECAP, a resource-efficient method for adversarial prompting. It aims to test a model's defenses at scale without the heavy cost of hand-built attacks crafted fresh by hand on each new system.
arxiv-2601-15531:
Felipe Atenas, Minh N. Dao, and Matthew K. Tam build optimization methods in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their topic is structured monotone inclusion problems. These are problems of finding a point where a sum of operators vanishes. Distributed forward-backward splitting is a standard way to attack them. The team's version allows variable stepsizes. Step sizes can change as the method runs.

The framework rests on relocated fixed-point iterations. It extends an approach from a 2025 paper they cite. The extension covers conically averaged operators. That widens the class of methods the theory supports, including graph-based forward-backward schemes. Variable stepsizes can speed convergence in practice. A theory that certifies them helps users trust the faster runs.
arxiv-2601-15631:
Xingzhou Chen and a large team report an optical effect in a layered material in a 2026 arXiv paper. Atomically thin transition-metal dichalcogenides carry a valley degree of freedom. It works like a binary index, fit for storing information. Bare valley excitons live briefly and move poorly, which limits their use. Coupling them with light forms exciton-polaritons. These hybrids offer a route past those limits.

The team reports an anomalous optical valley Hall effect. Their system is a monolayer of WS2 in the polariton regime. A Hall effect here means valley types drift apart under a drive. Anomalous behavior hints at physics beyond the plain version. Valley-based devices remain a research goal. Effects that steer valleys with light are steps toward that goal.
arxiv-2601-15731:
Linyong Zou and a large team improve a brain-imaging method in a 2026 arXiv paper. The method is electrophysiological source imaging, or ESI. It locates brain activity from scalp signals. ESI is an essential technique for diagnosing brain disorders. Model-based and deep learning methods have made promising progress. Precise imaging still hinges on choosing and refining features well. That step remains a central challenge, the authors say.

Their method is FAIR-ESI. The name expands to feature adaptive importance refinement. It adapts which features matter as imaging proceeds. Better feature handling should sharpen the source maps clinicians read. For epilepsy and other disorders, a sharper map can change care. The paper targets that refinement step directly.
arxiv-2601-15831:
Faruk Pasic and five co-authors analyze beamforming with cheap converters in a 2026 arXiv paper. Future wireless systems will use MIMO beamforming at millimeter-wave bands. Those bands deliver high data rates. Fully digital beamforming gives flexible spatial processing. It suits latency-critical applications well. It also depends on accurate channel estimation. Every antenna path needs its own data converters in a digital design.

High-resolution converters are costly and power-hungry at these speeds. The paper studies low-resolution DACs and ADCs instead. Coarser conversion saves power but adds error. The question is how much performance survives the savings. For network gear makers, that trade-off decides real products. The analysis speaks to 6G hardware planning.
arxiv-2601-16031:
Galen Bergsten and seven coauthors ask how hidden partner stars skew counts of small planets. Their 2026 preprint uses data from the Kepler space craft. A close star that is not seen on its own can make a planet look too small. It can also make the planet look more easy to find than it is. Both flaws bend the rate at which small worlds seem to occur.

To size the second flaw, the team picked 198 Kepler stars. Each star could show an Earth like world if it stood alone. The team then took sharp views of those stars with ground optics. The views test how often a hidden mate was in fact there. The work helps clean up planet counts for small worlds.
arxiv-2601-16231:
Aafiya Hussain and four coauthors test sound only attacks on models that join three modes. Their 2026 preprint deals with models that take sound, pics and words. Such models score well on thought and build tasks. Their strength when sound is bent with ill will is less known. The team bends sound in ways a hearer may not note.

Bent sound aims to throw the joint model off its true pick. The attack needs no change to pics or words at all. If sound alone breaks the model, guards must watch sound most. The study maps that risk in a set, step by step way. It warns build teams of a blind spot.
arxiv-2601-16431:
Ruonan Zheng and three coauthors set test plans for Kriging models of costly runs. Their 2026 preprint deals with stand in models for hard lab runs. Comp runs now stand in for real tests in much build work. A Kriging model then stands in for the comp run. Good test points cut the gap of the stand in across the whole space.

Step by step plans add points where the gap is most large. Each new run then trims the worst flaw in the model. Trim plans save runs while they lift trust in the stand in. The work sorts plans by how fast they close the gap. It serves teams with tight run counts.
arxiv-2601-16831:
Shangjie Tian, Qi Wang, and a team of co-authors squeeze a crystal to make it lossless. The crystal Ge2Bi2Te5 blocks current flow in a rare, twist-tied way. Such twist traits make it a topological insulator. Their 2026 preprint tracks the crystal's flow traits under huge force. They also swap in manganese atoms to add magnetism.

Force can flip such crystals into superconductors. The swap of atoms shifts that flip in clear ways. The team maps how the flip point moves with the swap. States that mix pairing and twist could host new quantum bits. High-force maps guide the hunt for those states.
arxiv-2601-16931:
Mauro D'Onofrio, Francesco Brevi, Cesare Chiosi, and Paola Marziani draw a wide view of galaxy scale links. Galaxies of unlike shapes still share tight links. Size, mass, and spin tie in set ways. Their 2026 preprint pulls those links from two big sky surveys. WINGS and MANGA give the base facts for the work.

The team sorts galaxies by shape in the link planes. Each zone of a plane gets a share count. Model data from Illustris joins the view as a check. Shared links test how galaxies grew and aged. Shape-wise gaps can flag where growth tales fall short.
arxiv-2601-17131:
Ondřej Kubíček, Viliam Lisý, and Tuomas Sandholm sharpen game play by use of fine tie rules. Big games are played from a pre-set plan, then tuned live. In hid-fact games, the live tune must weigh unseen states. It must also weigh the foe's past plan. Their 2026 preprint adds equilibrium refinements to that tune step. Such refinements pick the best of tied best replies.

Fine picks can lift the tune past the base plan. They curb plays that a smart foe could exploit. Games here span cards, bids, and guard work. Sharp subgame tools push AI skill in all three.
arxiv-2601-17331:
Fabian Vazquez and seven co-authors work on finding polyps in colonoscopy images. Polyps can grow into colorectal cancer, so early finds save lives. Computer tools help doctors spot them in scans. U-Net style models, in CNN, Transformer, and Mamba forms, already score well. They still miss shape and structure cues. Low contrast and clutter make those cues hard to read.

The team adds geometric priors to guide the models. Priors tell the network what shapes to expect. That help should sharpen borders in messy scenes. Sharper maps mean fewer missed polyps. The work serves computer-aided diagnosis in real clinics. It aims at the cases where current tools are weakest.
arxiv-2601-17431:
H. Kemal İlter audits how AI help can decay the facts in survey papers. Language models make writing faster. They can also add informational entropy, a slow blur of truth. İlter ran a forensic audit of 50 recent AI survey papers. The set held 5,514 citations from late 2024 to early 2026. He tracked how valid citation chains degrade.

The title names a 17 percent gap. That figure sums up the decay he found. Hallucinated papers are a known flaw; broken chains are quieter. They let false claims look sourced and sound. The audit gives editors a scale for the harm. It argues for citation checks as a core step, not an extra.
arxiv-2601-17531:
José Manuel Casas, Emzar Khmaladze, and Manuel Ladra study Leibniz n-algebras. These algebras generalize Leibniz algebras to higher arity. The authors analyze forgetful functors and the Daletskii-Takhtajan functor. They focus on perfect objects and crossed modules in this setting. Functors move results between categories in algebra.

They then apply the work to homology and universal central extensions. Central extensions are a core tool to classify algebras. Homology reads the deep shape of such structures. Clear functor behavior makes those tools safe to move. The paper serves pure algebra. It firms up a young field where base results are still being set. Each firm base saves later work.
arxiv-2601-17831:
Zehao Liu, Xiyan Peng, Zhenghong Tang, Zhaoxiang Qi, Shilong Liao, and Yong Yu rework an old sky survey to find stars it missed. Their 2026 preprint describes a software pipeline for 2MASS, the Two Micron All Sky Survey. The pipeline re-runs detection on the survey's J-band images. It tunes the search settings and adds a screening step that weighs signal strength and image sharpness together.

That joint screen helps pick out faint point sources that the first pass left behind. A first paper in a series, it sets up the method and its gains. Faint objects matter for maps of the Galaxy and for counts of cool, dim stars. Old survey data can still yield new finds when read with fresh tools.
arxiv-2601-18331:
Junmo Jeon and Shiro Sakai extend the idea of hyperuniformity from classical matter into quantum electron systems. Their 2026 preprint builds a framework on that extension. Hyperuniform systems hide their disorder: density fluctuations shrink at large scales. The quantum version adds the intrinsic fluctuations of many-body ground states. The team studies long-wavelength fluctuations through the charge-density structure factor. A quantity called the quantum weight enters, tied to the system's gap structure.

The framework can flag quantum phase transitions. It also reveals gaps that other probes may miss. A new lens on ground states serves the study of quantum materials. The work joins two fields that grew up apart.
arxiv-2601-18431:
S. Kumano turns to a second spin topic: how the core of an atom shifts the traits of the parts inside it. Work on that shift goes back to a shock find in the early eighties, when tests showed that quarks in a heavy core do not act like quarks in a lone proton. Most past work charted one curve that sums over all spin states.

Kumano looks at a finer split, the gap between two curves tied to how the beam and the target line up. The deuteron, with one proton and one neutron, is the best test bed for that split. Small shifts there can tell us how the strong force bends when parts sit close in a core. The note maps what is known and what new tests could pin down.
arxiv-2601-18631:
Mingyang Song and six colleagues give sight-and-text models a way to call on tools as they think. A person who hits a hard task picks up a tool: a lens, a map, a count aid. A model can do the same if it knows which tool to pick, when to call it, and how to chain calls over steps. That skill is hard when the tool or the task is new.

Their tool, daReasoner, learns to run that chain on the fly. It picks a tool, reads what comes back, and picks the next step from the gain. A good chain could lift scores on tasks that mix sight, facts, and steps. It could also make the model's path clear for staff to check. Tool use of this kind is a key step toward agents that work in the real world.
arxiv-2601-18931:
Frederick Tsz-Ho Fong and Hung Tran follow a flow that slowly reshapes curved spaces. Ricci flow deforms a shape's metric over time, much as heat evens out warmth. The pair study it on bundles built over products of special curved spaces called Kähler-Einstein manifolds.

Their starting metric comes from a known ansatz, a structured guess used in past work. They prove the flow keeps that structure as it runs, which tames a hard equation into parts that can be tracked. Keeping the ansatz lets them say how the shape evolves and what it may settle toward in the long run.
arxiv-2601-19231:
Yangyang Guo and four co-authors show that safety training in language models can wash out with harmless data. Aligned models refuse unsafe asks, and those refusals tend to start with a fixed few words, like an apology. That sameness, the team finds, is a crack in the armor.

Fine tuning on a small set of purely benign samples can undo the refusal habit. The study is a warning, not a how-to celebration: guards that rest on surface patterns are fragile. Builders who ship fine tuning to users need defenses that survive contact with ordinary data.
arxiv-2601-19331:
Giovanni Valvassori Bolgè characterizes the corner points of a class of monotone functions, then puts them to work on contests. Extreme points are the shapes that cannot be built by blending others, so knowing them maps a whole family. The family here is multi dimensional and monotone, growing in every direction at once.

He applies the result to large contests, where many players vie for prizes under set rules. The corner point view gives a handy form for the best prize allocation rules across a broad range of tastes about risk and fairness. Contest design, from sales races to grants, rests on such rules.
arxiv-2601-19431:
Markus Seidel, for the CMS Collaboration, reviews the building blocks of particle events in the LHC's third run. CMS is one of the two great detectors at the Large Hadron Collider, now colliding at higher energy in Run 3. Its physics objects are the reconstructed leptons, photons, jets, and missing momentum that every analysis starts from.

Their performance and calibration decide the quality of all CMS science. Run 3 piles many collisions into each crossing, so the algorithms must stay sharp in a crowd. Seidel's review tells analysts exactly how these objects behave and where their limits sit.
arxiv-2601-19531:
Alex Mauch-Soriano and nine colleagues ask how many Jupiter-like planets should circle white dwarfs. White dwarfs are the dense embers left when stars like the Sun die. Giant planets are common around living stars, and some are known around evolved stars. Yet only a handful have been found near white dwarfs, despite careful imaging surveys.

The team predicts how often such planets should occur if they survive the star's death. Their forecast can be compared with what surveys actually see. A gap between the two would point to planets being destroyed or thrown out as the star ages. A match would mean the planets mostly endure. Either way, the count tells us how planetary systems end. The work guides future searches around dead stars.
arxiv-2601-19731:
