Massimiliano Di Penta and a large group of colleagues write on behalf of SIGSOFT, the software engineering research community's main society. Their subject is the future of the field itself. Conferences keep growing, and with size come rising costs and stale formats. Those barriers shut out many researchers, especially from poorer regions.

That exclusion threatens the inclusivity and global diversity behind the field's success. The authors set out the society's perspective on what must change. The piece is a position statement rather than a research result. It aims to steer community debate about venues, formats, and access. Anyone planning the next decade of software engineering meetings is its intended reader.
arxiv-2601-19831:
Michael Y. Hu, Jane Pan, Ayush Rajesh Jhaveri, Nicholas Lourie, and Kyunghyun Cho study how language models improve with scale. Neural scaling laws predict that overall performance rises smoothly with compute. Validation loss follows tidy power-law curves. But single downstream tasks behave far less tidily: some improve steadily, others plateau, and some get worse with scale.

The authors call their study neural neural scaling laws, a play on modelling the models themselves. Understanding per-task curves matters for anyone deciding how big a model to train. Aggregate laws can hide tasks that matter to real users. Task-level prediction would make compute budgets smarter. The work urges the field to look beneath the smooth averages.
arxiv-2601-19931:
Sebastien Kawada and Dylan Holyoak describe a system entered in a shared task on story similarity. SemEval-2026 Task 4 asks systems to judge how similar two narratives are. Their entry, CascadeMind, mixes neural and symbolic methods in a cascade. The neural part uses a language model that votes many times in parallel, a technique called self-consistency voting.

A supermajority threshold settles confident cases at once. Uncertain cases escalate to more voting rounds. A symbolic ensemble that analyses narrative structure at several scales acts as tiebreaker. Cascades spend heavy computation only where doubt remains. The design reflects a wider pattern in applied AI: fast neural judgement, checked by slower structured analysis.
arxiv-2601-20131:
Deep Shah, Sanket Badhe, and Nehal Kathrotia map out the design choices behind embedding retrieval systems. These tools find matching text or images by meaning. Their paper walks down the full design stack, layer by layer. At the top sits the representation layer, where loss functions and model shapes define what counts as a good match.

The authors contrast bi-encoders, which encode query and item apart, with cross-encoders, which read both together. Each choice trades speed against accuracy in a different way. Their taxonomy names the common pitfalls in these choices, and it gives builders a clear map for weighing cost against quality.
arxiv-2601-20531:
Saurabh Verma and Shivam Dubey prove weaker quantization dimension results for self-similar measures. Quantization asks how well a probability measure can be approximated by finitely many points, and its dimension describes how the error shrinks. The authors study measures whose generating system does not satisfy the usual separation condition.

They use the fact that a subsystem at some level does separate. They also study approximation of the space of Borel probability measures under geometric mean error. Results of this kind extend quantization theory to overlapping fractals, which arise often in practice. These are quiet proofs, but they let the rest of the field build with trust.
arxiv-2601-20631:
Gianluca Allinson and a large team review Rydberg-atom receivers and their potential for space applications. These sensors convert radio, microwave, and terahertz fields into optical signals. They offer calibration traceable to fundamental constants, high sensitivity, and broad tunability.

The review compares five receiver architectures, from Autler-Townes and AC-Stark schemes to superheterodyne and fluorescence designs, against the needs of space missions. Rydberg receivers could give satellites a single sensor for many bands. The assessment helps mission planners judge where the technology is ready and where it is not. One sensor for many bands would cut weight, and weight is cost on any launch to space. The team weighs each design on that scale.
arxiv-2601-20831:
Vishnu Sashank Dorbala and Dinesh Manocha give embodied agents a memory that a model actively runs. Their 2026 paper presents MemCtrl. Foundation models personalize their choices through in-context learning. But the context window is small, so memory must be compressed and fetched. Systems like RAG treat memory as a large offline store. That view fits embodied agents poorly.

An embodied agent, such as a robot, works online under tight limits. It has strict memory and compute budgets. MemCtrl uses a multimodal model as an active memory controller instead. The model decides what to keep, drop, and fetch as events unfold. The paper argues this active style suits agents that act in the world. It points toward robots that remember what matters and forget the rest.
arxiv-2601-21331:
Filippo Portera proposes a new loss function for support vector machines and neural networks. Loss functions steer training by scoring how wrong a model is. A convex loss is prized because it avoids bad local traps during the search.

The author derives the paired dual problems for both sorting and regression tasks. Tests run on several small datasets, since support vector methods scale poorly to large ones. The new loss aims to keep the good math of classic methods while behaving better in practice. Small, careful tests show where the trade-offs land.
arxiv-2601-21631:
Nicolas Pope and Matti Tedre turn language model training from a black box into a classroom sandbox. Most lessons on generative AI only let students prompt a finished model. The data and mechanics that shape the model stay hidden, which feeds both hype and fear.

The authors built a browser tool where students train a small transformer on their own device. Every step of training is visible and touchable. Students can swap the training text and watch behavior change. Seeing a model learn from data they chose gives a grounded sense of what these systems are and are not.
arxiv-2601-21731:
Kaustubh Sharma, Srijan Tiwari, Ojasva Nema, and Parikshit Pareek extract readable kernels from networks fitted on synthetic data. Such prior-data fitted networks do fast, learned inference, but their priors and kernels stay hidden inside. That opacity blocks uses like surrogate optimization, which need an explicit covariance model.

The authors build a framework that recovers the spectral story of the learned kernel. A decoupled attention design helps separate the pieces. Making the kernel visible turns a black-box predictor into a tool other methods can build on. It also lets users check whether the learned prior matches the problem at hand.
arxiv-2601-21831:
Daniel Gonzalez-Alvarado, Jonas Cassel, Stefania Petra, and Christoph Schnörr work on generating discrete data, such as categories and counts. Generative models usually learn in smooth spaces, which fits awkwardly with data that come in separate bins. Their 2026 preprint builds the learning space from the geometry of categorical distributions themselves.

The authors place a low-dimensional latent space inside the parameter space of product manifolds of categorical distributions. That latent space captures how the variables depend on each other while dropping redundant degrees of freedom. A well-shaped latent space lets a model generate new discrete samples that respect the patterns in the real data. Which matters for survey data, genetics, and other fields built on categories.
arxiv-2601-21931:
Karel Devriendt, Ignacio Echave-Sustaeta Rodríguez, and Frank Röttger work on the statistics of extremes. Hüsler-Reiss distributions are a parametric family used to model multivariate Pareto data, the joint behavior of several variables when all are large at once. A key question is when extremes in some variables tell nothing about extremes in others.

That property is extremal conditional independence. The authors introduce two set functions, which assign values to a distribution and to each of its marginals. They show that independence statements of this kind can be characterized through those functions, using modular structure. Their 2026 preprint gives risk modelers a cleaner test for dependence among rare events, such as joint floods or simultaneous market crashes.
arxiv-2601-22031:
Junhao Ruan and co-authors merge two rival ways of generating text. Autoregressive models write one token at a time, which trains efficiently but decodes slowly. Diffusion language models generate in parallel and run fast, but their training is less direct.

Their 2026 preprint proposes Causal Autoregressive Diffusion, or CARD. It reshapes the diffusion process inside a strictly causal attention mask, so every token still only sees what came before. That design enables dense, per-token supervision in a single forward pass, combining autoregressive training efficiency with diffusion-style throughput at inference. Faster text generation at the same quality would cut serving costs across every product built on language models.
arxiv-2601-22131:
Leonard Papenmeier and Petru Tighineanu speed up optimization problems that pull in opposite directions. Multi-objective optimization balances competing goals with only black-box access to the system and a limited budget of measurements. Many teams hold historical data from related past tasks, which meta-learning could exploit.

Their 2026 preprint presents SMOG, a scalable meta-learning method for multi-objective Bayesian optimization. By learning from earlier tasks, the optimizer starts new problems already knowing where good trade-offs tend to live. That head start matters in drug design, engineering, and materials work. Where each measurement can cost days or thousands of dollars and budgets never stretch as far as the questions do.
arxiv-2601-22331:
Aditya Narayan Ravi, Snehal Vadvalkar, Abhishek Pandey, and Ilan Shomorony fix a flaw in cell imaging that can hide real drug effects. Cell Painting stains cells so a microscope can read their shape and state in fine detail. Their 2026 preprint notes that lab, tool, and protocol shifts add batch effects that swamp the true signal.

Their fix uses kernels that shift with each batch, plus smart sampling to keep the cost low. Clean data let teams spot how a drug changes cells. The method aims to scale to huge screens. It serves the hunt for new medicines.
arxiv-2601-22531:
Jiayi Dai and Randy Goebel train networks that show their reasons as they decide. Their 2026 preprint works on rationale extraction: one network picks the key input parts, a second decides from those parts alone. The design makes the logic open to view by construction.

A teacher model, the rationalist of the title, guides the learner with step-wise, readable reasons. Such guidance aims for reasons that are both true to the model and clear to people. The need is sharpest in high-stakes fields like health and law. The work seeks trust through shown work.
arxiv-2601-22631:
En Fu, Yanyan Hu, Changhua Hu, Zengwang Jin, and Kaixiang Peng predict how much useful life a machine has left, from little data. Such forecasts guide repairs, yet they have long needed heaps of past wear data from twin machines. Their 2026 preprint, PEFT-MuTS, takes a leaner path.

Their frame fine-tunes only a small part of a model, across many signals at once. Small-data forecasts could serve rare or new gear, where twins do not exist. The work cuts the data bill for a key factory task. It also aims to keep accuracy high. Less data, same warning time, is the goal.
arxiv-2601-23131:
Christiaan P. Opperman, Anna S. Bosman, and Katherine M. Malan survey methods that help neural networks generalize. Networks ace many tasks, yet they can stumble on data they have not seen. A large family of tricks, called regularisation, has grown up over the years to fight that weakness.

The authors review those approaches and test them empirically side by side. A clear map of what works, and at what cost, saves practitioners from folklore. Generalization is the difference between a demo and a tool people can rely on. The empirical analysis keeps the survey honest, testing whether celebrated techniques still earn their place in current practice.
arxiv-2601-23231:
George Webber, Alexander Denker, Riccardo Barbano, and Andrew J Reader solve inverse problems with flow-based models under model predictive control. Flow models provide strong priors for rebuilding hidden images from measurements. Guiding them toward a specific measurement, though, is computationally heavy.

Casting guidance as optimal control is elegant but demands costly differentiation through the flow. Their predictive control scheme seeks the same guidance at lower memory and compute cost. Cheaper conditional generation helps medical imaging and other reconstruction tasks. Model predictive control sidesteps repeated differentiation through the flow dynamics, the cost that made control-based guidance heavy.
arxiv-2603-01931:
Megan Harris, John Little, and Amro Farid model watershed systems as linked networks of natural and human parts. Their 2026 work spans hydrology, land-use choices, estuary ecology, and overlapping governance areas. Regional tools give good nutrient estimates, yet their opaque routing blocks wider systems analysis.

The team first builds a region-independent reference architecture for any watershed system. They then adapt a hetero-functional graph state estimator with weighted least squares to infer nutrient flows. The estimator extends a graph theory built for systems whose parts do unlike jobs. A shared ontology in a standard systems language ties the natural and institutional pieces together. The Chesapeake Bay watershed serves as the case study, using its known assessment tool for nutrient estimates.
arxiv-2603-02031:
Atreya Vedantam and Radha Krishna Ganti characterize blind recovery of a code rate from a received signal. Their 2026 work sits in noncooperative decoding, where the receiver does not know the error-correcting code settings. Forward error correction guards nearly every modern communication link against noise.

They present a metric for the quality of rate recovery that works with any rank-based estimation method. A closed-form expression ties that metric to algorithm settings and channel conditions at once. Low metric values signal good recovery, giving designers a target to aim for. In high noise, the metric yields a better rate estimate than existing formulas. Simulations with a low-density parity-check code validate the metric and the gain, and they pin down optimal algorithm parameters.
arxiv-2603-02431:
Fanjun Xu derives a direct measure of quantum fluctuations in clean magnets in this 2026 paper. Quantum effects shrink the ordered moment of a magnet below its full value. Measuring that shrinkage usually needs indirect modeling of scattering data. Xu starts from a sum rule that fixes the total magnetic moment in neutron scattering.

He links moment reduction to the long-time limit of a scattering function. Neutron spin-echo spectroscopy can read that limit directly in an experiment. The long-time value equals the ratio of ordered to total moment, squared over plain. Spin-wave calculations for two lattice types confirm the link. Both quantum effects and geometric frustration lower the plateau as predicted. The method works on powder samples, widening its reach for bulk magnets.
arxiv-2603-02531:
Kwanyoung Kim links diffusion guidance to a classic acceleration trick in this 2026 paper. Guidance improves diffusion image quality by pushing apart two model outputs. It costs extra passes at run time and fails for distilled, single-step models. Attention-space methods are cheaper, but their theory was murky.

Kim models attention dynamics as fixed-point steps inside modern Hopfield networks. Attention extrapolation then becomes a special case of Anderson acceleration on those dynamics. A weak contraction property of the dynamics supports that reading. His method splits attention updates into parts along and across the guidance direction. That split stabilizes the speedup and squeezes the most from guidance. The plug-and-play method fits existing frameworks and improves generation quality a lot.
arxiv-2603-02931:
Cristian Di Pietrantonio, Marcin Sokolowski, Christopher Harris, and colleagues fix a bottleneck in hunting flashes from deep space. Radio signals smear across frequencies as they cross ionized gas, and undoing that smear, called dedispersion, is vital for spotting pulsars and fast radio bursts. Image-based searches made the standard cleanup far too memory-hungry.

Their algorithm, STRIDE, builds dedispersed time series pixel by pixel straight from telescope images, without costly data reshuffling. It is the first to split the smear correction across time as well as frequency, so only a slice of images must sit in memory at once. In their test case, memory needs fell by nearly ninety-eight percent. The authors argue STRIDE is the practical route for low-frequency sky surveys.
arxiv-2603-03331:
Hung Manh Pham and eight colleagues introduce PulseLM, a dataset linking pulse signals to language. The signals come from photoplethysmography, the light-based sensing used in clinic monitors and smartwatches to track the heart and body. Older datasets label such signals with numbers or task tags, which limits training models to reason about health in words.

PulseLM gathers recordings from fifteen public sources and restates their varied labels as twelve shared question-answering tasks about physiology. It holds more than a million standardized ten-second signal segments and over three million question-answer pairs. The team also fixes shared rules for cleaning, supervision, and scoring, then benchmarks multimodal language models on the data. Everything is public, giving the field one standard foundation for pulse-based language research.
arxiv-2603-03531:
Yiming Sun and eight others predict ecosystem carbon fluxes by giving every input a role. Land ecosystems trade carbon dioxide and methane with the air, and forecasting those fluxes is central to carbon accounting. Flux responses are ruled by slow regime settings, yet wiggled by fast daily drivers. Most learning models dump all inputs into one undifferentiated pile, assuming one global response, and generalize badly.

Their 2026 approach, Role-Aware Conditional Inference, separates the roles explicitly. Hierarchical time encoding disentangles slow conditioners from fast drivers. Spatial retrieval then supplies context that is both nearby and functionally similar, matched per role. Tested across wetlands and farm systems, three carbon fluxes, and both simulated and observed data, the method beat strong baselines everywhere. Accuracy and spatial generalization both improved under strong environmental diversity.
arxiv-2603-03631:
Vernon Barger finds the pattern of particle masses written in ninths, and traces it to a gauge symmetry that also creates the axion. Quark and lepton mass hierarchies follow rational powers of one small parameter, counted in units of one ninth. His 2026 paper argues this flavor-in-ninths structure points to a discrete eighteen-fold gauge symmetry behind the Froggatt-Nielsen mechanism, with a nine-fold subgroup running the flavor pattern.

Identifying the flavon field with the Peccei-Quinn field makes the same symmetry do double duty. It stabilizes the QCD axion, forces the safe domain-wall number, and predicts the axion's coupling to photons. Harmful Planck-suppressed corrections are pushed to very high dimension, solving the axion quality problem naturally. For a decay constant in the favored range, the axion accounts for dark matter and sits within reach of near-term haloscope searches.
arxiv-2603-03931:
Rafal Bartoszewicz and others report how pressure and temperature reshape light emission from a two-dimensional tin halide perovskite. These layered materials are tunable platforms for exciton-phonon coupling because their lattice is intrinsically soft. The team studied photoluminescence of the bromide compound across temperatures and under hydrostatic pressure, comparing it with its iodide analogue.

At room temperature the emission is dominated by near-band-edge excitons, which shift steadily to lower energy under pressure up to about three gigapascals, with no sign of a phase transition. Cooling reveals a broad, strongly shifted self-trapped exciton emission, showing a crossover from delocalized to self-localized states. Unusually, that trapped emission shifts to higher energy under pressure, while the iodide analogue shows no trapped emission at all, pointing to lattice rigidity and screening as the deciding factors.

audubon-ornithological-biography-vol1-18:
John James Audubon painted the birds of America, and his Ornithological Biography supplies their written lives. Volume one appeared in 1831 as the text companion to his great picture work. Audubon writes species accounts from years of field watching. Habits, nests, song, and range fill each account with fresh detail.

Frontier tales run between the science, drawn from his travels in wild America. He shot, drew, and watched birds from Labrador to the Gulf shores. The mix of story and study made the volumes famous on two continents. Volume one opens a five volume companion set. Readers who know the prints meet their author here. His energy fills every page.
cia-0000008631:
September 1972 brought a report of two downed American pilots sighted in Hoa Binh province, North Vietnam. Hoa Binh, southwest of Hanoi, saw heavy fighting and bombing across the war years. The sighting entered the files while the air war over the north was still intense.

Reports of downed pilots triggered checks against loss lists, unit records, and earlier sightings. A confirmed place could narrow a search or confirm a capture. Most sightings stayed fragments, useful only beside many others. Together they built the case files behind the POW and MIA accounting that outlasted the war itself.
cia-0000009531:
An American pilot beaten to death by North Vietnamese militiamen is recorded in a January 1972 CIA report. The heading adds that the death was attributed to a source the title cuts off. Pilots who parachuted into villages faced crowds before guards arrived.

Reports of killings after capture were logged as possible war crimes as well as losses. Each needed names, places, and witnesses solid enough to stand later. Many never reached that standard, yet the record was kept. The file preserves one brutal allegation in official form, part of the accounting of how captured men died.
cia-0000011831:
Across southern Africa in 1967, armed movements were rising against white minority rule, and a CIA paper that October surveys them country by country. Portugal still held Angola and Mozambique, Rhodesia's white government had defied Britain, and South Africa ruled itself and Namibia. Guerrilla groups in each territory were taking up arms with outside backing.

The survey weighs each movement's strength, its leaders, and its ties to communist states. It also judges their chances of winning power in the near term. The paper captures the start of bush wars that would reshape the whole region over the next two decades.
cia-0000012431:
A redacted person had dinner with Fedorenko on the evening of May 27, and a CIA note from April 1963 records the fact. Fedorenko moved in the Soviet diplomatic world the file watched. Dinner tables were working ground in Cold War diplomacy. Guest lists, seating, and table talk all carried intelligence value, and officers filed them as carefully as any cipher traffic.

The note preserves the social texture of that world in one line. Even suppers were intelligence, and the files treated them accordingly. For readers, the fragment shows how completely the watchers watched: down to who ate with whom.
cia-0000012831:
The communist bloc's aid programs, economic and military, are surveyed in a CIA paper from January 1963. Moscow and its allies were spending money and sending arms across Asia, Africa, and Latin America. Their checkbook was a weapon in the contest for the new nations, and Washington tracked the spending the way it tracked fleets and divisions.

The paper totals the bloc's generosity and maps its reach. It weighs credits, weapons, and technicians as moves in one game. For readers, it shows the Cold War fought with rubles as well as rockets, counted by the other side.
cia-0000013931: American prisoners of war were sighted in Quang Binh, Kontum, and Haiphong, in a CIA note dated January 3, 1968. The three places span North Vietnam's coast, the southern highlands, and the great port. A single note tying them together shows the sweep of the search. Each sighting pinned a prisoner report to one more point on the map.
cia-0000014631: Espionage charges against Alfred Sarant and Bruce Dayton anchor a CIA file dated January 5, 1951. The file concerns the probe of Sarant and his flight from questioning. Sarant had known Julius Rosenberg in college and in left wing circles. When agents closed in, Sarant slipped away, and the file follows that thread of the spy hunt.
cia-0000014731: The Seborer family is profiled in a CIA file dated January 1, 1961. The file gives highlights on Abraham Seborer and Jennie Scheine, born Chanover. Family sketches were a basic tool of the security files, mapping kin and ties. This one kept a family's record open a full decade after the great spy trials.
cia-0000015331: A letter to Lawrence Tacker from Philip Strong fills a CIA file dated January 2, 1961. Strong thanks Tacker for sending on his material, per the clipped title. The Tacker thread had run since 1958 in these files. A new year brought the same calm thanks and the same firm close. The Tacker letter is now held in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015431: Release of CIA material on unidentified flying objects was the subject of an Air Force request logged August 4, 1966. The Air Force wanted agency material opened, and the file tracks that push. Such requests forced officials to weigh public curiosity against secret sources and methods. Coming in 1966, the request landed just as a new official study of saucers was taking shape.
cia-0000022331: Moscow claimed Powers flew for money and criticized his father, a CIA record dated in 1960 reports. The money charge aimed to strip the pilot of any sense of duty. Attacking his father widened the blow to the whole family. Such items show the trial being fought in print as much as in court during those weeks.
cia-0000027631: Probable political developments in West Germany during 1952 are forecast in a CIA paper dated in 1952. A forecast for 1952 judged whether that young state would hold its course or swing toward neutral ground.
cia-0000044431:

Inside, his account and judgment of the murders are preserved. The rebels blamed the army's death squads for the killings. Their version accused the state in the strongest terms they had. The file holds that version beside the government's, which is how the archive serves readers best: both stories present, and the weighing left to them.

A September 1956 CIA report describes Hungarian public demonstrations growing into a political crisis. Street protests that autumn were swelling beyond anything the regime had faced. Within weeks they would grow into the full revolution of October.

The report tracks the crisis from its first public signs: crowds, demands, and a government losing control of the streets. Demonstration reports mattered because they measured pressure that official statements hid. For readers, this paper stands near the head of the Hungary file of 1956. It marks the point where private discontent became public action. The agency began reporting a revolution in the making rather than mere unrest.
cia-0000124331: A January 1957 CIA document weighs the possible release of American prisoners by the Chinese Communists. Years after the Korean armistice, a small number of Americans were still held in China. The paper judges whether Beijing was ready to let those men go. Release questions lingered because a handful of held men had become bargaining counters, and papers like this one tracked Beijing's price and mood over time.

cia-0000132431:
Cuban-Soviet relations are examined in a CIA document dated January 3, 1960. Havana and Moscow were still feeling each other out at that point. Analysts watched every meeting and public statement for signs of a firmer commitment between the two governments.

Within months the careful courtship turned into a working alliance of trade, arms, and advisers. The document tracks its early steps, before either side had promised much in public. For readers, it captures the opening of a partnership that would shape the Cold War in the Americas. Few relationships of the era carried heavier consequences for Washington or lasted so long.

europmc-pmc10161731:
Ruze and colleagues review the links between obesity and type 2 diabetes in a 2023 paper, covering spread, causes, and treatment. Both conditions have grown steadily more common across the world. They share genetic and lifestyle roots, and excess weight strongly raises the chance that diabetes will develop.

The review explains how stored fat, especially around inner organs, disrupts sugar control. It surveys treatments that address both conditions at once, from lifestyle change to surgery. The authors make the case for treating the pair as one problem. They argue that joint care gives better results.
europmc-pmc10172131:
Schneider, Lee, and Mathis present a method for analyzing animal behavior and brain activity together, in a 2023 study. Linking what an animal does to what its neurons do is a core goal of neuroscience. As recordings grow larger, scientists need models that can find shared patterns across both kinds of data.

Their method learns compact embeddings, or summaries, that capture behavior and neural signals in one frame. It can then relate movements to brain states in fine detail. The tool, called CEBRA, opens new ways to study how brains produce adaptive behavior.
europmc-pmc10439131:
Arora and colleagues mapped two zones of mouth tumours in 2023 and linked them to patient outcomes. The cancer is oral squamous cell carcinoma not tied to the HPV virus. The team read gene activity in single cells and in tissue, keeping each cell's place. They set the tumour core against its leading edge, the rim that pushes outward.

Each zone had its own gene profile and its own mix of nearby cells. The edge profile was much the same across many cancer types, while the core was tissue-specific. Arora found that a strong edge mark tied to worse survival in many cancers. The core mark tied to better outcomes. A model of cell growth in place also foretold drug response.
europmc-pmc10635831:
Blanco-Míguez and co-authors released MetaPhlAn 4 in 2023, a tool to name microbes in a sample. The tool reads DNA from a whole community at once, a method called metagenomics. Past versions could name only species in a fixed catalogue. Many real species have never been grown or named.

The new version draws on 1.01 million microbe genomes, from lab strains and sample builds. Blanco-Míguez defines marker genes for 26,970 species-level groups. Of those, 4,992 have no species name yet. The tool explains about 20% more of the DNA in human gut samples than before. In farm animal guts the gain passed 40%. It can even track single strains of unnamed species.
europmc-pmc10700131:
Merchant and co-authors scaled deep learning in 2023 to find new stable materials. New crystals drive gains from chips to batteries, yet trial-and-error hunts are slow and costly. The team trained graph networks, AI that learns from atom links, on a far larger scale than past work. Their base held 48,000 known stable crystals.

The models flagged 2.2 million new structures as stable, an order-of-magnitude leap. Merchant reports that 736 of them had in fact been made in labs on their own. Top finds will be shared for screening toward uses such as layered materials and battery electrolytes. The same scale yielded atom force models of high accuracy for later studies.
europmc-pmc1084331:
Hippenmeyer and co-authors probe timing in nerve growth in this 2005 mouse study. Dorsal root ganglion neurons are nerve cells that carry touch and body signals to the spine. Two gene switches, called ETS factors, switch on late in their growth under signals from their targets. These switches guide late steps such as reaching the target and branching.

The team forced the switches on too early in young nerve cells. Early switching warped the wires' paths and blocked the cells from gaining their final traits, they found. It also changed how much the cells leaned on growth support factors. The authors conclude that nerve cells pass through a timed switch in how they answer these signals. Getting the timing right, they say, is part of normal nerve wiring.
europmc-pmc11446831:
Schlegel and a large team annotate every neuron class in the fruit fly brain in this 2024 paper. The FlyWire project had mapped the wiring of about 140,000 neurons in the fly brain. Wiring alone does not say what each cell is. The team added a systematic annotation, in a hierarchy, of cell types, neuronal classes, and developmental lineages.

The count came to 8,453 cell types. Of these, 3,643 matched types proposed in an earlier partial map, they report. Another 4,581 are new, mostly from regions the earlier map lacked. About one third of the earlier types could not be reliably reidentified, despite matching cell shapes. The authors therefore propose a new definition: a cell type must be more similar across two brains than to any other cell within the same brain. They validate it by jointly analysing both connectomes.
europmc-pmc1183531:
Hansen and colleagues screened the roundworm C. elegans for long life genes in 2005. Most aging knowledge came from mutants found for other reasons. That history could bias what scientists think aging is. A full genome screen offered a fairer test.

The screen found 23 new genes that extend worm lifespan. They touch signals, stress defense, gene control, and metabolism. Eating less seemed to work by quieting certain key genes. Hansen also flags a hormone path tied to a known aging switch. Nearly all new genes fit known paths, which supports past work.
europmc-pmc1280331:
Delfino, Sioutas, and Malik weighed ultrafine particles in heart harm from air pollution in 2005. Daily studies link particle mass to heart admissions and deaths. Panel studies add links to ischemia, blood pressure, and rhythm changes. The exact causal component stayed unidentified.

Ultrafine particles under 0.1 micrometers dominate particle counts and surface area. That surface can carry large loads of toxic pollutants. Combustion products show up in the indirect evidence so far. The authors argue reactive cargo in ultrafines reaches heart targets. Fossil fuel combustion sits at the center of their case. Panel data back the time trend data well.
europmc-pmc1464831:
Even mice with the same genes gain weight in unlike ways on a rich diet. Koza and co-authors used that spread in 2006 to hunt for non-gene drivers of obesity. Male mice on a high-fat diet showed a four-fold spread in body fat. High and low gainers could be told apart at six weeks, before the rich diet began.

Fat samples taken at seven weeks showed gene activity gaps that foretold later fat gain. Genes in the Wnt signal path and tissue reshaping stood out. Koza points to one Wnt blocker, SFRP5, among others. The team proposes that fat tissue holds marks that set obesity risk.
europmc-pmc1750931:
HIV builds its new particles at the cell's outer skin, not in inner compartments. Jouvenet and co-authors settled that debate in 2006. Prevailing models held that assembly starts on late endosomes, inner membrane sacs, and rides outward.

Blocking endosome movement did not stop the viral protein Gag reaching the surface or virions being released. Targeting assembly to the surface worked; targeting it to endosomes did not. Gag first gathered at the surface, and the share later seen inside had been swallowed back. Jouvenet concludes assembly begins and completes at the plasma membrane.
europmc-pmc1808431:
Han and Boyden added in 2007 a second color of light control over brain cells. Their earlier tool, channelrhodopsin-2, lets blue light switch targeted neurons on. A matching off switch, driven by a different color, would let researchers shape exact firing patterns in living circuits.

They used Halo, a light-driven chloride pump from the salt microbe Natronomas pharaonis, tuned for use in animal cells. Yellow light pulses silenced neurons carrying Halo reliably and reversibly, within milliseconds. Cells carrying both tools could be driven through precise sequences of firing and silence by alternating blue and yellow pulses. That allowed the team to break up synchronized firing without changing overall spike rates. No added chemicals were needed for either switch.
europmc-pmc1969431:
Simon and Altman wrote in 1994 a guidance editorial on the statistics of prognostic factor studies in cancer. Such studies ask which traits, from tumor size to molecular markers, predict a patient's outcome. They fill much of the oncology literature and can reveal disease mechanisms or guide hard treatment choices.

A sound prognostic study can flag patients at high enough risk of recurrence to justify a toxic or costly therapy. Major prognostic determinants also sharpen the design of later clinical trials, make trials comparable with each other, and ground the counseling of patients. As leaders at a national cancer institute and a major statistics laboratory, the authors set out the statistical standards these studies should meet. Their editorial anchors a special series on statistics in cancer research in the journal.
europmc-pmc2002031:
Wu, Paganini-Hill, Ross and Henderson tracked colorectal cancer risk in 1987 in a retirement community. Their prospective study followed 11,888 residents for four and a half years. During that time 58 men and 68 women developed colorectal cancer. The team examined alcohol, body weight, activity and several nutrients as possible causes.

Daily alcohol drinkers had nearly twice the risk of others. Higher body mass, measured by Quetelet index, also raised risk. Leisure physical activity lowered it. These patterns held for both sexes but reached significance only in men. Most nutrients showed no link. People with three or more children had a markedly lower risk, with a relative risk of 0.45, and confidence limits excluding no effect.
europmc-pmc2048531:
Morschhäuser and colleagues found in 2007 the switch behind drug resistance in the yeast Candida albicans. This fungus often resists fluconazole, a common antifungal drug, by overproducing a pump called MDR1. The pump ejects toxic compounds from the cell. Why the pump gene stays switched on in resistant clinical strains was unknown. The team compared gene activity across resistant and sensitive isolates.

A regulator gene, MRR1, rose together with MDR1 in resistant strains. Deleting MRR1 in two resistant isolates abolished both pump production and resistance. Resistant strains carried single-letter changes in MRR1, at positions 683 and 997. Adding those changed versions to a sensitive strain switched the pump on permanently. Many MRR1 target genes make oxidoreductases, enzymes that may limit drug damage.
europmc-pmc2125231: A medical paper on the experimental production of necrosis of the liver in the guinea pig. The dead guinea pig liver. This article preserves that pathology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2125331: A medical paper on the nature of anaphylatoxin in immunity studies. The shock substance. This article preserves that immunology. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2130931: A medical paper with experiments on cultivating the active agent of tobacco mosaic disease. The plant virus, grown. This article preserves that virology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2131231: A medical paper with studies on d'Herelle's bacteriophage, the mechanism of lysis. The bursting germs. This article preserves that virology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2131431: A medical paper with studies on immunological relationships among the pneumococci, a comparison. The germs' kinship. This article preserves that immunology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2140631: A biology paper on the kinetics of senescence. The mathematics of aging. This article preserves that gerontology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2360431:
Frattini and colleagues looked for markers that predict who benefits from cetuximab in spread colon cancer in 2007. Cetuximab blocks EGFR, a growth receptor on tumor cells. The team checked three parts of that signal path in 27 treated patients: EGFR itself, the K-Ras gene, and a brake protein called PTEN.

Ten patients had their tumors shrink on the drug. Every patient whose tumor had lost PTEN gained nothing, a pattern the statistics flagged as strong. All 16 patients with normal PTEN included the 10 responders. Extra copies of the EGFR gene also marked likely responders, with six of eight such patients shrinking. A mutated K-Ras gene pointed the other way, with only one responder among 10 cases. The authors presented PTEN loss as a new warning sign of non-response.
europmc-pmc2483731:
Novaes and colleagues produced the first broad gene survey of the eucalyptus tree Eucalyptus grandis in 2008. This species is the world's most planted hardwood, yet its genome was uncharacterised. The team sequenced expressed genes, the stretches of DNA actually read in cells, using fast 454 pyrosequencing.

They generated 148 million bases of sequence from mixed tissues and tree varieties, finding matches to almost half of all known genes in the model plant Arabidopsis. Comparing reads across varieties exposed 23,742 single-letter variants, called SNPs, and lab checks confirmed 83% of a tested sample as real. Diversity in protein-changing positions ran about four times lower than in silent positions, the fingerprint of purifying selection weeding out harmful changes. The catalogue fed the United States Department of Energy's effort to sequence the full eucalyptus genome.
europmc-pmc2567431:
Ku and colleagues mapped in 2008 how two silencing machines, the Polycomb complexes PRC1 and PRC2, sit on DNA in embryonic stem cells. Stem cell genes for development are often held in a poised state called bivalent, carrying both activating and repressing chemical marks. The team charted these marks and both complexes across the genomes of human and mouse stem cells.

Bivalent regions split into two classes: those bound by both complexes and those bound by PRC2 alone. The doubly bound class kept its repressive mark more stubbornly when cells specialised, and it covered nearly all the key developmental regulator genes. Computer analysis showed the complexes' landing spots could largely be predicted from CpG islands, stretches of DNA rich in particular letters. Large islands lacking activating signals seemed to recruit the full silencing set.
europmc-pmc2605931:
Teixeira, Ferreira, and Ashburner reported in 2008 that a common insect bacterium, Wolbachia, protects fruit flies against RNA viruses. Wolbachia live inside cells, pass from mother to offspring, and are famous for manipulating host reproduction. In the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster no strong effect had been found, so discovering protection was unexpected.

Flies carrying Wolbachia resisted Drosophila C virus and carried lower virus loads than uninfected flies. The protection extended to two other RNA viruses, Nora virus and Flock House virus. It did not extend to a DNA virus tested. This is the first strong beneficial effect of Wolbachia reported in this fly. The authors argue that shielding hosts from natural viruses may explain why Wolbachia is so widespread in wild insect populations.
europmc-pmc2630331:
Meyer, Lafitte, and Bontempi released a software package called minet in 2008 for reconstructing gene networks from microarray data. The package works in R and Bioconductor and builds networks where genes are nodes and edges represent statistical dependence between their activity levels. Dependence is measured by mutual information, a quantity capturing how much knowing one gene's activity tells you about another's.

Minet offers four ways to estimate that information from data, from a simple empirical estimator to a shrinkage estimator. On top of these it implements four network inference methods: relevance networks, ARACNE, CLR, and MRNET, which differ in how they prune indirect links. The package also integrates accuracy tools. These include F-scores and ROC and precision-recall curves. They compare an inferred network against a trusted reference. It is freely available.
europmc-pmc2671031:
Garrido and colleagues reviewed in 2009 the mismatch negativity, a brain wave that fires when a sound breaks an expected pattern. Play a stream of identical tones with one odd note slipped in, and the brain produces this wave even if the listener pays no attention. It measures how well the brain learns sound rules and notices change.

Two explanations had long competed. One says nerve cells simply tire of the repeated tone, and fresh cells answer the odd one. The other says the brain builds a model of the pattern and flags a mismatch against it. The review weighs the proof for each and offers a unifying frame called predictive coding. In that view, the brain constantly predicts incoming sound and passes surprises upward. Tiring and model updating then become two sides of one process, not rivals.
europmc-pmc2687931:
Samuels and Szabadi reviewed in 2008 the locus coeruleus, a tiny blue-tinted cluster of brain cells that supplies most of the brain's noradrenaline, a wakefulness chemical. Despite its size, this nucleus sends fibers almost everywhere. It sits at the crossing of two jobs. One is keeping us aroused. The other is steering the body's automatic systems, such as heart and gut.

Part two of their review covers what pushes the nucleus up or down in living people. Pain, threat, and temperature extremes fire it up, as do stimulant drugs and medicines that block noradrenaline recycling. Sedatives and drugs that press its own brake receptors quiet it, bringing drowsiness and a shift toward the rest-and-digest mode. The nucleus also fails early in aging, Parkinson disease, and Alzheimer disease, which may explain some of those illnesses' sleep and mood symptoms.
europmc-pmc2697331:
Reimann and colleagues studied single gut L cells in 2008. These cells release GLP-1. That hormone boosts insulin and helps control blood sugar in type 2 diabetes. Drugs mimicking GLP-1 already treat diabetes, but coaxing the body to release more of its own supply needs basic knowledge of how these scattered cells sense glucose.

The team bred mice whose L cells glow, fished them out pure, and probed them with electrodes and calcium imaging. Single L cells fired electrically and answered glucose directly. Their behavior pointed to two sensors: a sodium-glucose transporter that hauls sugar in, and potassium channels that close when energy is plentiful, the same design the pancreas uses. Gene readings confirmed both parts run high in these cells. Each identified pathway, the authors note, is a possible handle for future diabetes drugs.
europmc-pmc2697631:
Banks reviewed in 2009 what lets a compound cross the blood-brain barrier, the sealed vessel lining that guards the brain. Most brain drugs are small, fat-loving molecules that slip through cell membranes by diffusion, a route that never fills up. But that is only one of several doors, and the others decide the fate of modern large-molecule drugs.

Transport systems ferry chosen cargo across and boost uptake roughly tenfold, but they can be saturated, and illness changes their settings. Pumps also push many compounds back out, an exit system that silently defeats drugs. Blood flow, protein binding in plasma, and enzymes at the barrier further trim what arrives. Banks details two newer delivery hopes: short DNA-like drugs and replacement enzymes, both with newly found transporters. The review doubles as a design brief for getting medicines into the brain.
europmc-pmc2698831:
Verstraelen and co-authors followed 100 pregnant women in 2009 to learn which vaginal bacteria keep the vaginal community stable. A healthy vagina is dominated by lactobacilli, friendly bacteria that hold rivals down. In some women the balance flips mid-pregnancy toward abnormal flora, a state tied to early birth risk. Swabs were taken three times across pregnancy.

Seventy-seven women started with normal flora. Thirteen of them flipped to abnormal by the second or third visit. The starting species mix predicted the flip strikingly. Women whose flora lacked the species Lactobacillus crispatus were about ten times more likely to flip. Flora built on L. gasseri or L. iners carried the same raised risk, while crispatus-based flora was fivefold protected. Not all lactobacilli guard equally, the authors conclude; identity matters, not just presence.
europmc-pmc2702831:
Cani and colleagues tested in 2009 whether changing gut microbes, the tiny living things in the bowel, can calm swelling in obese mice. Obese mice often have a leaky gut wall, so bits of bacteria pass into blood and drive low-level swelling. The team focused on a gut hormone called GLP-2 that helps keep the gut wall strong.

Mice fed prebiotics, foods that feed good gut microbes, had lower blood markers of swelling and a tighter gut wall. Blocking GLP-2 wiped out most of that gain, while giving GLP-2 alone copied it. The work ties microbe shifts to better gut barrier health through GLP-2 in these mice.
europmc-pmc2736831:
Loupakis and co-authors tested in 2009 whether extra mutations in KRAS and BRAF genes predict resistance to two drugs in metastatic colorectal cancer. Those drugs are cetuximab plus irinotecan. The cancer is of the large bowel and has spread. Mutations in KRAS codons twelve and thirteen, gene positions, were already known to block benefit from anti-EGFR antibody drugs. Other KRAS positions and BRAF were less certain.

Among eighty-seven patients lacking the known mutations, eight carried KRAS changes at codons sixty-one or one hundred forty-six, and none of them responded. None of thirteen patients with the BRAF mutation responded either, while about a third of mutation-free patients did. Mutation carriers also progressed sooner, which supports wider gene testing before treatment.
europmc-pmc2746531:
Antoniou and co-authors built in 2002 a comprehensive model of familial breast cancer that includes BRCA1, BRCA2, and other genes, for use in genetic counselling. Carrier probability calculations must allow that other susceptibility genes may exist beyond the two known ones. They fitted models to a population series of cases and to high-risk families in the United Kingdom with known mutation status.

BRCA1 and BRCA2 alone could not explain all family clustering seen. A polygenic effect, many small-effect genes acting together, fit the remaining familial risk best, though a single recessive gene fit almost as well. Other genes also significantly modified risk in BRCA1 and BRCA2 carriers. Estimated breast cancer risk by age seventy averaged about one third for BRCA1 carriers and about one half for BRCA2 carriers.
europmc-pmc2793031:
Li and co-authors showed in 2010 how a tiny RNA called miR-30 helps control when cells die. MicroRNAs are short RNA pieces that dial down gene activity. The team focused on fission, the splitting of mitochondria, the cell's energy units, which helps trigger apoptosis, a form of planned cell death.

Members of the miR-30 family blocked fission and slowed cell death in the experiments. They did so by holding down p53, a protein that switches on a splitting protein named Drp1. When death signals arrived, miR-30 levels fell and p53 rose, freeing Drp1 to split mitochondria. The chain gives a clear new route by which small RNAs steer cell death.
europmc-pmc2829031:
Mercer and colleagues tracked long noncoding RNAs during brain cell development in 2010. These long RNA strands never become proteins, yet they help steer which genes switch on. The team followed mouse neural stem cells as they split into neurons and oligodendrocytes, the cells that wrap nerve fibers in insulation.

Many noncoding RNAs rose and fell at set stages of each fate path, including the insulation-building stages. They clustered near key development genes and matched those genes' timing, and some sat in known control regions or nuclear landmarks. A drug that blocks insulation-cell maturation by reshaping chromatin, the DNA packaging, also shifted the RNA patterns. The work links these RNAs directly to fate decisions and rewiring in stem cells.
europmc-pmc2831931:
Clark and colleagues asked in 2010 whether breathing polluted air before birth and in the first year of life helps cause asthma, rather than just triggering attacks. Their study followed every child born in 1999 and 2000 across southwestern British Columbia, over thirty-seven thousand children, checking health records for asthma diagnoses by age three or four.

About nine percent of the children developed asthma. Risk climbed with early exposure to carbon monoxide, nitric oxide, nitrogen dioxide, coarse particles, sulfur dioxide, and black carbon, and with living near pollution sources. Traffic-related pollutants carried the highest risks of all. The authors read the pattern as support for a role of early-life air pollution in causing the disease.
europmc-pmc2865531:
Eckerle and co-authors disabled the proofreading tool of the SARS coronavirus in 2010 and watched its copying accuracy collapse. Most RNA viruses copy with many errors, but coronaviruses carry an enzyme, in a protein called nsp14, that can snip out mistakes. The team engineered viruses lacking that snipping activity and read their full genomes after growth in culture.

The mutant viruses grew with stable defects and made about twenty-one times as many copying errors as the normal virus. Mutations piled up across the genome during passage, far beyond what the intact virus allows. The result proves the enzyme guards the large coronavirus genome. It also shows how much error the virus can bear before fitness fades. Drug designers hope to push the virus past that limit.
europmc-pmc2913331:
Cassano and co-authors built in 2010 computer models that predict whether a chemical can harm a developing baby, for Europe's REACH chemical safety law. REACH demands assessment of thousands of market chemicals, and developmental toxicity testing is among the slowest, costliest, and most animal-heavy. Their CAESAR project trained quantitative structure-activity models, which infer toxicity from molecular structure, on curated experimental data.

Two models using different mathematics, a random forest and a fuzzy partitioning method, both classified chemicals well. The designers deliberately tuned them to minimize false negatives, the dangerous error of clearing a harmful chemical, even at the price of extra false alarms. The random forest model was placed in a free online application, so industry chemists and regulators can screen a structure in seconds before any animal test.
europmc-pmc2948931:
Rakhshandehroo and co-authors reviewed the target genes of PPAR-alpha, a fat-sensing switch protein, in a 2010 article. The switch responds to fatty acids and to fibrate drugs used to lower blood fats, and it reshapes gene activity across many pathways.

Because the switch works by turning target genes up or down, its roles in burning fat, handling energy, and calming inflammation all trace back to those genes. The review organises the known and likely targets gene by gene, with emphasis on the liver where the switch is busiest. Readers get a map for judging new drugs and diet effects.
europmc-pmc2953531:
Collins and colleagues hunted signalling peptides in the flatworm Schmidtea mediterranea in a 2010 genome and peptide study. Planarians can switch between sexual and non-sexual reproduction and rebuild reproductive organs, hinting at flexible chemical control.

Combining genome scans with direct peptide measures, they logged more than two hundred candidate nerve peptides. One conserved peptide proved necessary for the reproductive system to mature and stay functional. Because related parasites also reshape breeding in response to conditions, the worm's peptide set offers leads. It may help explain flatworm breeding control. It could even help break parasite life cycles.
europmc-pmc2987831:
Katzourakis and Gifford screened animal genomes for viral fossils, DNA copied from viruses into the germ line and inherited like ordinary genes, in a 2010 study. Retroviruses were famous for this trick, while other virus families were thought to rarely leave such traces.

Computer screening turned up elements from ten non-retroviral families, including first examples for several major virus kinds and the first DNA virus fossils in mammal genomes. Family trees of the fossils revealed fresh detail on virus origins. Some elements still hold intact genes or are switched on, and one primate element shows strong signs of being put to host use.
europmc-pmc2998531:
Wang and colleagues built prediction tools for how strongly small protein pieces bind the immune display molecules HLA DR, DP, and DQ in a 2010 study. Such predictions shortlist candidate targets from germs, allergens, and tumours, but DP and DQ had been neglected.

They measured binding for tens of thousands of peptide and molecule pairs, more than doubling the data for the neglected types. Learning methods trained on the enlarged set predicted binding for all three families about equally well, with accuracy up over earlier reports thanks to the bigger training pool. They warn that near-duplicate peptides in tests inflate scores.
europmc-pmc3048531:
Greaves and the IMAGE study group reviewed in 2011 what makes diet and activity programs work for people at risk of type 2 diabetes. Rather than reviewing single trials, they reviewed thirty existing reviews covering a decade of work, and extracted well over a hundred analyses that tied program features to results. Programs on average produced modest weight loss and a real rise in weekly activity.

Features tied to better results included enlisting social support and targeting food and movement together. Programs worked better with more frequent contact and with a cluster of self control techniques such as setting goals and tracking one's own behavior. Setting, delivery style, and who delivered the program showed no clear effect. The authors note that keeping new habits going needs more attention, and they advise program funders to require the proven ingredients.
europmc-pmc3130631:
Teresa Hart and colleagues worked out how many days of activity tracking older adults need in a 2011 paper. Studies link daily movement and sitting time to health, but guessing habits from a single day misleads. Fifty-two adults around age seventy wore two motion devices and kept activity logs for three straight weeks.

Three days of one motion sensor and four days of a step counter or written log captured usual activity levels well. Judging sitting time took longer, needing five days of sensor data. Differences between weekdays were small but not zero, so very short tracking windows still carry risk. The paper gives designers of aging studies a clear, tested minimum for believable activity estimates.
europmc-pmc3131731:
Stefano Ferrari and colleagues reviewed an inherited eye disease group in a 2011 paper in Current Genomics. The condition slowly destroys the light-sensing cells of the retina, starting with night vision and side vision, and often ends in blindness by middle age. It strikes roughly one person in several thousand and can pass through families in three different patterns.

More than forty genes have been tied to the disease, most of them working in the light sensors or their supporting layer. Different faults in the same gene can cause different diseases, which tangles efforts to match a patient's genes to their outlook. The review maps the known genes and fault mechanisms, arguing that better gene-to-symptom matching will guide future treatment choices.
europmc-pmc3148231:
Dwi Karolina and colleagues fingered a tiny RNA as a driver of insulin failure in type two diabetes in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Small RNAs that tune gene activity drift out of balance in many diseases. The team profiled them across tissues and blood in diabetic rats, then checked blood from men with early and full diabetes.

Eight small RNAs formed a signature separating healthy, pre-diabetic, and diabetic samples. One stood out as sharply raised in blood, and its level matched falling levels of a key insulin-signalling protein in target tissues. Direct tests confirmed the small RNA switches that protein off. The work suggests blood small RNAs can flag metabolic trouble early and points to one culprit worth blocking.
europmc-pmc3150331:
Kira Makarova and colleagues unified the protein families of a bacterial immune system in a 2011 paper in Biology Direct. Most archaea and many bacteria carry this system, which stores snippets of invader DNA and uses RNA copies of them to destroy matching viruses. Its proteins are numerous, diverse, and fast-changing, which had tangled classification.

Comparing sequences and shapes across species revealed hidden kinships. A major protein clan split neatly into three large groups. The big subunits of most systems proved related to one family, with an active copying domain in some types and a silenced one in others. Since many parts share a common RNA-gripping core, the authors propose the system began in heat-loving archaea and spread sideways between microbes.
europmc-pmc3230631:
Giuseppe Esposito and colleagues tested how cannabidiol, a cannabis compound without mind-altering effects, protects rat brains from amyloid damage, in this 2011 study in PLoS ONE. The compound had shown promise in Alzheimer's models, but its mechanism was unclear. The team focused on a receptor called PPAR-gamma, recently suggested as cannabidiol's binding partner.

In rats given beta-amyloid, cannabidiol reduced the inflammatory reaction in brain support cells and the neuronal damage that followed. When the researchers blocked PPAR-gamma with antagonists, those protective effects were largely blunted, showing the receptor is required. Through the same receptor, cannabidiol also stimulated the birth of new neurons in the hippocampus, the brain's memory center. The findings pin the compound's benefits to this pathway.
europmc-pmc3257631:
James Lattimer and Mark Haub reviewed dietary fiber and metabolic health in this 2010 article in Nutrients. Fiber and whole grains carry a distinctive mix of resistant starches, vitamins, minerals, and plant chemicals. Population and clinical studies consistently tie higher fiber intake to lower rates of obesity, type 2 diabetes, cancer, and cardiovascular disease, and the authors examine the evidence component by component.

Even defining fiber turns out to depend on whether the lens is nutritional or analytical. The review separates fiber into fractions such as arabinoxylan, inulin, pectin, bran, cellulose, beta-glucan, and resistant starch, and asks what each contributes. Proposed mechanisms include thicker gut contents, slower nutrient absorption, faster transit, and the short-chain fatty acids and gut hormones fiber produces. The authors note where studies disagree and where the case is firmest.
europmc-pmc3291531:
Liu and a large team studied a gene tied to inherited Parkinson disease, publishing their findings in 2012. Changes in the gene, called PINK1, cause some early onset cases, and earlier work linked it to the health of mitochondria, the cell's power plants. What remained unclear was how its roles fit together, so the team tested it in fruit flies and in human cells grown in the lab.

They found that PINK1 also controls how mitochondria move along nerve fibers. In flies, lowering a transport protein called Miro rescued many defects caused by faulty PINK1, while extra Miro alone killed dopamine producing nerve cells. In human cells, PINK1 worked with a second disease gene to tag Miro for removal, linking movement control to the cleanup of damaged mitochondria.
europmc-pmc3406031:
Gauffin Cano, Santacruz, Moya, and Sanz tested in 2012 whether a gut bacterium could undo the damage of a fatty diet in mice. Obesity is tied to shrunken numbers of Bacteroidetes bacteria in the gut, but cause and effect were unproven. Obese mice on a high-fat diet received the strain Bacteroides uniformis CECT 7771 daily for seven weeks.

Treated mice gained less weight, stored less fat and cholesterol in the liver, and showed smaller fat cells. Blood sugar, insulin, and cholesterol readings all improved, and the mice absorbed less dietary fat. Immune defenses dulled by obesity recovered as well. The strain also partly restored the gut community the diet had disturbed.
europmc-pmc3470931:
Jackson, Riley, and White weighed the promise of multivariate meta-analysis in Statistics in Medicine in 2011. Standard meta-analysis pools one outcome at a time, but medical studies often measure several linked outcomes, such as survival with and without disease return. Pooling them jointly can sharpen estimates, at the cost of more assumptions about how the outcomes relate.

The paper grew out of a one-day meeting where statisticians aired hopes and doubts about the approach. Four examples show where joint pooling helps and where it can mislead. Jackson's team concludes the methods hold real potential and can give estimates with better properties. Still, they urge even more care than with ordinary meta-analysis, since wrong assumptions undo the gains.
europmc-pmc3472231:
Williamson and colleagues laid out the issues in building core outcome sets for clinical trials, in Trials in 2012. Trials in the same field often measure different outcomes, which blocks fair comparison and lets authors report only flattering results. A core outcome set is an agreed minimum list that every trial in an area should measure and report.

The authors cover how to set the scope of such a set and whose voices must be heard, including patients and the public. They also discuss how to run the agreement process and judge when agreement is real. Williamson's team stresses that core sets add a floor, not a ceiling, and that trials remain free to measure more. Wider use would raise the value of each trial.
europmc-pmc3492331: Doctors got an anti-fat bias study. This 2012 paper measures hidden anti-fat bias among doctors. The authors reveal the bias. Their work guides medical training. Sabin's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It made headlines. It is a classic.
europmc-pmc3558331: Realist reviews got RAMESES standards. This 2013 paper sets publication standards for realist reviews. The authors reveal the standards. Their work guides researchers. Wong's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. Journals adopted the standards.
europmc-pmc3650931: Homebound seniors got an internet study. This 2013 paper studies internet use in low-income homebound seniors. The authors reveal the patterns. Their work guides policy. Choi's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped digital inclusion.
europmc-pmc3710231: Frailty got a measures overview. This 2013 paper surveys frailty measures in studies. The authors map the measures. Their review guides geriatrics. Bouillon's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped geriatric care. The review is widely taught. The study shaped aging research.

fort-lo-1931:
Things fall, move, and appear where they should not in Fort's third book, Lo, of 1931. Teleportation is his word and his theme: matter shifted by a force no law yet names. Poltergeists, falls from clear skies, and wild shifts of place fill the file.

Fort piles case on case from the news of the world, each with its date and source. His tone is drier and his aim surer than in the first books. Lo is the damned data at its strangest and most pure. Few books make the world feel so thin at the seams.
frankenstein-1831:
Mary Shelley took her famed novel in hand once more and made this new form in 1831. It is the text most readers have known since that year. She added a long new start, in which she tells how the tale came to her in 1816.

The frame of the tale is reworked, and Victor's fate bears a more dark and fixed cast. The being he made stands in a more grave light, and the blame shifts in tone. This is Frankenstein as Shelley at last chose to leave it to the world.
frus-1861-d131:
On 17 June 1861, William H. Seward wrote to William Dayton in a settled, watchful tone. The letter is document 131 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Mid June letters from Seward have a settled feel: the lines are set, the work is watch and ward. His note to Dayton keeps Paris inside the same firm frame as London. The two posts, read together, formed the Union's wall in Europe. London and Paris, held in one frame, left the South no great door into Europe. No great door left open meant no great hope left alive for the South in Europe.
frus-1861-d231:
Orders from Washington reached James Shepherd Pike in a State Department letter dated 16 May 1861. It stands as Document 231 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. By then, in the opening months of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d31:
On 30 July 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Henry Sanford, his envoy in Belgium. The letter is document 31 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The Union defeat at Bull Run on 21 July shook faith at home and abroad. Seward now had to hold foreign courts steady while the army rebuilt. A letter to Brussels nine days after the battle belongs to that work of repair and resolve. After Bull Run, Seward's aim was to show a Union shaken but far from beaten. Resolve, repeated in plain words, was the coin Seward paid out all that autumn.
frus-1862-d131:
The home office spoke to Charles Francis Adams on 18 August 1862, through a letter from Seward. It stands as Document 131 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d231:
The second Stuart letter of 2 September 1862 stands as Document 231 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William Stuart, acting head of the British legation, sent both letters to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

Two letters in a day from the legation suggest several live matters at once, each kept on its own sheet by custom. Early September 1862 gave the legation plenty to handle: invasion news, shaken markets, and fresh instructions to seek from London. Paired letters like these show formal business keeping its order in a disordered week. Cases under such notes were often small: one ship, one prisoner, one point of form.
frus-1862-d31:
Orders from Washington reached Charles Francis Adams in a State Department letter dated 11 March 1862. It stands as Document 31 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It was written in the winter of the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d331:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 6 October 1862 in a letter printed as Document 331 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

By the time Dayton wrote, the Emancipation Proclamation's text was known in Paris and French opinion was stirring. Working-class sympathy for the Union grew harder for the emperor to ignore. Dayton's report that week fed Washington's sense that the proclamation was doing diplomatic work no envoy could have done alone. Paris and London consulted each other often before either acted on the American war. Dayton's French was limited, and he leaned on his staff and on careful written notes.
frus-1862-d431:
On 16 July 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this reply to Gabriel García Tassara, the Spanish minister in Washington. It stands as Document 431 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Mid-July 1862 was a low point for Union arms, with McClellan driven back from Richmond. Foreign ministers in Washington watched for signs that the government might bend, and Seward's notes had to show no bend at all. His exchange with Tassara kept Spain at formal arm's length on the war while handling the standing business between the two countries. The letter is a sample of Seward's desk diplomacy in the war's hardest summer.
frus-1862-d531:
On 7 June 1862, the same day the Dutch minister's two notes were dated, Secretary of State William H. Seward answered Roest van Limburg. The reply is Document 531 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Same-day answers were Seward's specialty when a matter was warm, and the Dutch file in June 1862 was warm indeed. His reply kept the exchange moving without conceding the Union's reading of its belligerent rights at sea. The Netherlands, whose trade the blockade touched daily, pressed its points through Van Limburg with equal energy. Read in sequence from Document 527, the June letters form a compact case study in how wartime questions between friendly governments were actually worked through.
frus-1862-d631:
On 6 May 1862 Edward Joy Morris sent this report from Constantinople to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is Document 631 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the President's annual message.

Morris's May report came from the far end of the Department's world in a season of Union advance. At the Ottoman court the American war was by then a settled topic: a great republic was fighting its rebels, and the powers watched. His dispatch kept the record of American business at the Porte complete for the spring. Read with the instructions Seward sent him, it shows a mature posting running itself, with Washington informed at intervals and local judgment trusted in between.
frus-1863p1-d131:
On 26 March 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 131 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The mate to a dispatch often held what the first had no room for. Adams's pair of 26 March closed the legation's mail for a crowded week. This letter is its second half. With the Seward sheet of the same date set just before the pair in the volume, the cluster shows the sea mail at its busiest. Two pens worked one war, an ocean apart.
frus-1863p1-d231:
Writing from London on 10 July 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. The dispatch is document 231 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Public meetings across Britain, many of them backing the Union and emancipation, formed part of the picture Adams reported. He tracked opinion as carefully as he tracked ministers. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d31:
On 16 January 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams in London. The letter is document 31 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. Seward's January mail to the legation runs thick in this part of the volume.

The secretary wrote to keep Adams's hand strong in talks with Lord Russell. Each letter restated the Union's claims and fed the envoy the facts he needed from home. This one falls between Adams's reports of mid-January, a sign of how tight the loop had grown. It is a plain working sheet, and its worth is in the chain it holds together.
frus-1863p1-d331:
The American answer to London on 3 December 1862 took the form of this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 331 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Lyons was the man Seward had to persuade, warn, or answer in person in Washington. Notes to him carried the American side of each dispute between the two governments. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d431:
The letter printed as document 431 was written on 28 March 1863 by William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page.
frus-1863p1-d531:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State wrote this official letter to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington on 23 May 1862. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.
