It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d631:
Dated 16 October 1863, document 631 is a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d131: Secretary Hull wrote to Minister Kirk in Cairo on November 16, 1943, six days before the Cairo Conference opened in Kirk's city. The letter is Document 131 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Washington-to-host messages in the final week tended to the practical, though this record names no subject. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series, among the papers of the president's voyage and arrival.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d231:
Paper C.C.S. 300/2, issued by the United States Chiefs of Staff aboard the Iowa on 18 November 1943, estimates the enemy situation in the Pacific and Far East for 1944. A long appendix carries the detail, with separate notes on what the Soviets and the Chinese might do.

The estimate expects Japan to stay on the strategic defensive through 1944, striking locally where needed. Tokyo would fight hardest to stop Allied air bases rising in China and to hold Burma, while watching the Soviet border with care. War with the Soviet Union is judged likely only if Japan became convinced that Moscow meant to attack her, or to hand Siberian air bases to the other Allies.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d31: One day after Stalin's reply, Roosevelt wrote to him again, on September 9, 1943. The letter is Document 31 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Back-and-forth at this speed shows the summit planning gathering pace as autumn began. The record gives sender, receiver, and date, and no subject line. Readers will find the message in the Foreign Relations volume, in the sequence that runs from Quebec toward Moscow, Cairo, and Tehran.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d331:
General Patrick Hurley sent President Roosevelt a second telegram from Tehran on 26 November 1943, following his wire of earlier that day about the Soviet invitation. He had since toured the offered quarters with General Connolly, Secret Service agent Rowley, and Soviet security officers.

The suite sits inside the Russian Embassy compound, in the building Reilly had inspected. It holds six rooms to the left of the entrance, a large reception room, bedrooms, and a dining room. A kitchen below serves the President's staff. It is steam heated, has a private entrance, and stands on the same floor as, and adjoining, the large conference room. Only bathtubs and toilets, removed earlier, need putting back. Hurley judges the quarters far better than the American legation for convenience, communications, and security, while repeating that he told the Russians the legation decision was definite.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d431: President Roosevelt wrote a short letter of welcome to President Ismet Inönü of Turkey from Cairo on 3 December 1943, as Inönü set out for the second Cairo Conference. The letter was carried to Adana by the President's son-in-law, Major John Boettiger. He rode aboard the plane sent to collect the Turkish party. The plane was in the command of Major Otis Bryan. Roosevelt hopes Inönü will have a smooth trip, and says he looks forward with great pleasure to seeing him on Saturday afternoon.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d531:
Lord Halifax, the British ambassador in Washington, wrote to President Roosevelt on December 24, 1943. A Christmas Eve letter from an ambassador to a president was unusual paper, crossing the line between formal business and personal regard. The State Department printed it in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Halifax, a former foreign secretary and viceroy of India, brought great weight to the Washington embassy. His access to Roosevelt was part of the alliance's daily machinery in the capital. For readers, the message shows the British mission working its most important relationship at the highest level, even on a holiday, as the conference season closed.
frus-1944-quebec-d131:
London's chiefs of staff cabled General Eisenhower on September 10, 1944, with an urgent request about Warsaw. The British ambassador in Moscow had reported the Soviet position. Moscow was willing to cooperate in supply drops if the aid followed a prearranged plan, and His Majesty's Government wanted no chance of helping the Poles to be missed.

The chiefs asked Eisenhower to consider mounting a supply-drop operation at the earliest possible date. British representatives in Moscow had been told of the Russian decision and asked to make the needed arrangements. Eisenhower was to inform General Deane, the American mission chief in Moscow, of his decision and his requirements from the Russians.
frus-1944-quebec-d231:
The secretaries of the Combined Chiefs drafted the implementing messages on September 12, 1944, as C.C.S. 618/4. Identical letters, adjusted for the recipient, were proposed for Generals Burrows and Deane, the British and American mission chiefs in Moscow. Each man was to propose the tripartite Military Committee to the Soviet General Staff at once.

The message to Deane stresses the limits: the committee would be purely consultative, unable to decide anything without reference home. It must not impinge on the European Advisory Commission's work. A cardinal point was that the Russian member be a senior General Staff officer. With the three armies approaching each other, Deane was told to act immediately so the committee could function soon.
frus-1944-quebec-d31:
Harry Hopkins wrote to Prime Minister Churchill on August 28, 1944, the first of three messages from him to Churchill bearing that date. The State Department printed them in the Quebec 1944 volume.

Three messages in a day from the President's aide suggest detailed work being finished: the Quebec Conference was a fortnight away, and its arrangements and agenda ran through Hopkins. He wrote as Roosevelt's agent, free to arrange what the President would later approve. For readers, the cluster shows a summit being built piece by piece in late August, in the alliance's most trusted staff channel.
frus-1945-50-intel-d131:
Russell, assistant secretary of state for administration, sent an instruction to Alling, the American minister in Tangier, on 3 January 1947. Instructions from the department direct a post's conduct. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Tangier appears in both volumes of this slice of history: a Potsdam question in 1945, and a post receiving department instructions in 1947. The paper belongs to the volume's State thread, where intelligence business touched ordinary diplomacy in small ports. Readers can take it as a sign of the system's settling. The secret work of the postwar world now ran through channels as plain as an administration chief's instruction to a minister in North Africa.
frus-1945-50-intel-d231:
The General Counsel of the Central Intelligence Agency (Houston) addressed a memorandum to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter on 7 April 1948. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 231 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The young CIA was still defining its job, while the Council weighed how far secret action abroad should go.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d31:
Donald Russell, assistant secretary of state for administration, wrote to McCormack, the special assistant for research and intelligence, on 22 October 1945. Both men served in the State Department. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Russell ran the department's housekeeping: people, money, and space. McCormack's new intelligence office needed all three at once, having just absorbed the OSS analysts. An inside paper from the administration chief to the intelligence chief shows the unglamorous work of housing a new function. Readers often skip such papers, yet they decide whether bright plans live or die. This one shows the State Department's intelligence office being built from the inside.
frus-1945-50-intel-d331:
A memorandum dated 20 November 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Armstrong). The reader was Acting Secretary of State Lovett. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 331 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The old board and its group were gone, replaced that fall by the CIA under the new National Security Council.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d431:
On 6 January 1950 the National Security Council issued Intelligence Directive No. 12. The text is document 431 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Two directives on one day point to a full agenda at the start of 1950. The Council used the numbered series to keep every agency inside one frame. Read beside Directive No. 11, this order shows the steady, formal way the early Cold War state managed its secret work. Issued as a pair, the two January orders divided fresh duties between the same set of agencies. The pair shows the Council at its most brisk, settling two points in a single day.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d131:
Writing from Warm Springs, Georgia, on 4 December 1944, President Roosevelt gave the State Department three points to keep in the linings of their hats. His short memorandum to Secretary Stettinius is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It answers the summary of British views sent on 29 November.

Germany, he says, should be let back industrially far enough to meet her own needs. But she should do no exporting for some time, until we see how things work out. Second, “we are against reparations.” Third, “we do want restitution of looted property of all kinds.” The one-page note cut across months of staff argument in the President's plainest style.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d231:
Stettinius told Harriman on 30 October 1944 to put the Soviet government straight on Iran. His secret cable, number 2566, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Soviet press articles and statements by Mr. Kavtaradze had shown Moscow's annoyance at Iran's freeze on oil talks.

Harriman is to say that Washington noticed the annoyance. He is also to lay out what the American embassy in Tehran was told to convey. The American firms chasing a concession in southern Iran were disappointed, but Washington expressed confidence in Iran's good faith. When talks resume, American firms expect treatment no worse than any other foreigner's. The policy, the cable begins to explain, rests on respect for the sovereign right of an independent nation.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d31: From Moscow on 26 December 1944, Harriman sent Roosevelt a report the day after Christmas. It is document 31 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences, published by the Department of State. His holiday-week reporting kept Washington current on Soviet attitudes at a moment when the president was weighing what could realistically be achieved at Yalta in February.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d331:
Dinner talk at Yalta on February 4, 1945, turned serious in its last half hour, and Bohlen's minutes preserve it. Most of the evening was general and personal. Stalin, Roosevelt, and Churchill stayed in very good humor. Then the talk drifted to the rights of small powers in the peace body planned for after the war.

Stalin made his view plain more than once. The three great powers had borne the brunt of the war. They had freed the small states from German rule. So, he argued, they should hold the right to keep the peace. No lesser state, he implied, could have an equal say. The minutes catch a core Yalta dispute surfacing over dinner.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d431:
Article by article, officials took apart the prisoner-of-war draft on February 9, 1945, and this memorandum records the examination. The preamble drew no comment. Neither did Article I. Then the Soviet negotiator, Novikov, began asking for changes in wording.

In Article II, one phrase should be replaced so each side would take the necessary steps to implement the agreement. Elsewhere, transfers should be effected as a rule by agreement, or only after notice to the competent authorities. For Article III, Novikov preferred the Soviet draft's text. The record is dry, clause by clause. It is also where the repatriation bargain took its final legal shape.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d131:
Acting Secretary Grew noted a British hope for early talks in a memorandum dated July 7, 1945. The memo is document 131 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. John Balfour of the British Embassy had called that morning about the coming meeting of heads of government in Berlin.

Balfour said his government very much hoped one or more Americans bound for Berlin might pass through London first. That way, the two sides could talk over matters coming up at the main meeting. He knew Washington would not want the Russians to think the two were ganging up on them, but thought lower-level experts could come quietly. Grew replied that feeling in the American group ran against such early talks, though he would look into it at once. Nothing in the record shows the visit happening.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d231:
Ambassador Winant handed the foreign ministers proposal to Anthony Eden in a letter dated July 8, 1945. The letter is document 231 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It transmits the draft the President planned to present to Churchill and Stalin early in their talks.

The same document was being shared in advance with the British and Soviet governments, Winant explains, in the belief that they might wish to think it over before the meeting. Harriman delivered the same paper to Molotov in Moscow the same day. The enclosed text matches the State Department's proposal for a Council of Foreign Ministers. Sharing the draft early was a deliberate American choice: the machinery question headed Truman's agenda, and he wanted no ally surprised by it.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d31:
Truman sent a second envoy in this telegram to Churchill of May 22, 1945. He was asking Joseph E. Davies to come to London ahead of the pending three-power conference. A number of matters needed exploring with Churchill, which Truman preferred not to handle by cable. Davies would be in London probably on the twenty-fifth.

He asked Churchill to see Davies at his convenience. The wire, sent by Navy channels, ran in parallel with the Hopkins mission to Moscow. Together the two journeys — Davies west-facing, Hopkins east-facing — prepared the ground for Potsdam by personal talk rather than paper.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d331:
Partition of Germany is the question a briefing book paper of June 29, 1945, answers with a clear no. Its recommendation: the United States should oppose splitting Germany into two or more separate states. Border changes and cessions, it says, are a different matter from partition itself.

The discussion traces how the idea rose and fell in Washington. Roosevelt at Tehran was ready to see five German states, but by the Crimea conference he had changed his mind. He then opposed taking up partition before the fighting ended and conditions could be studied. The paper carries that later, cooler judgment into the Potsdam briefing book.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d431:
Washington's concern over Clay's Berlin deals comes in General Marshall's top secret message of July 10, 1945. The interim commitment to provide food and coal for Berlin, outlined in Clay's message of July 9, causes concern, Marshall writes. The wish for three-power control and government of Berlin is appreciated, but the agreement must not prejudice America's basic principles in Germany.

He lists disturbing questions. The State Department advises, first, that this government cannot accept the Soviet position that Silesia has been turned over to Poland. The reply, Marshall notes, had been agreed by representatives of the State and War Departments, and the State Department would advise Murphy.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d531:
Air communications with Moscow are discussed in a memorandum of conversation by Edward Page, first secretary of the Moscow embassy, dated June 29, 1945. Ambassador Harriman inquired whether there had been any developments in opening new routes to Moscow. Vyshinsky replied that he had been too busy with the Czechs, the Poles, and the Berlin conference to give the question any time.

Planes, though, were flying back and forth to Berlin, and communications were much better than previously. Events had overtaken themselves, Vyshinsky indicated, and the Moscow-Berlin service would be open to American passengers. Harriman expressed the hope that the United States-Soviet line could be opened shortly. Vyshinski said he favored the Berlin route and saw no reason it should not open once technical details were worked out.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d631:
Ambassador Wallace Murray reported from Tehran on June 19, 1945, on pulling U.S. troops out of Iran. His secret wire is document 631 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Washington had asked about speeding the withdrawal up.

Murray doubts a fast, full exit is possible for anyone. The British, he says, are even keener than the Americans to see foreign troops go, so they need no prodding. Yet British forces must guard the oil fields and the Abadan refinery in the southwest, both vital to the war on Japan. Some 1,500 U.S. men must likewise stay at Abadan airfield while war planes pass through. Murray adds a sly warning about Moscow. The Russians might pull all their troops out overnight and claim the credit for it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1031: Ambassador John Winant cabled the Secretary of State from London on July 24, 1945. Only an extract of the message is printed here. Winant reports that the European Advisory Commission met the night before to finish two outstanding documents. One was the agreement amending the zones of occupation in Germany. The British told the Americans they lacked full authority to accept the Soviet draft of the final paragraph. That paragraph belonged to the report covering the agreement. The extract ends there, with the wording still unsettled.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1131:
On 21 July 1945 the three heads of government approved this text at Potsdam. It stands in the volume beside the draft they had weighed. Approval turned working words into a summit decision, one the three powers were bound to honor.

Agreed texts of this kind went into the summit's official record. They were the points on which the talks had closed, at least for that week. Set beside the draft version, the approved words show which lines survived the leaders' review. The gap between draft and final text is where the bargaining lives. This entry preserves the finished side of that exchange.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1231:
Sato answered Tokyo on 21 July 1945, the same day as the minister's twin cables. The Moscow envoy's reports formed a steady answer to Togo's hopes: polite Soviet phrases, no firm word, no date for an envoy's hearing. Time favored Moscow, not Tokyo.

Sato read the delay rightly as a kind of answer. His cables grew blunter as the week wore on, urging Tokyo to face facts. This dispatch sits in that sequence. It is part of the hidden record at Potsdam. The Allied leaders read this enemy traffic each morning, while they set the terms Japan would soon receive.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1331:
Assistant Secretary Dunn wrote to the Secretary of State on 23 July 1945. Dunn was among the most seasoned career envoys on the American team. His notes carried staff judgment to the chief in the middle of the talks.

A message from Dunn at Potsdam joined two layers: the working staff and the man who bargained for the United States. It could fix a stand, report a talk, or ready the chief's next move. This one dates from the second week's start. It shows the professional core of the team at work, in the plain channel of a note to the secretary.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1431:
The Soviet delegation submitted another text on 29 July 1945, the third of that date in the volume's closing pages. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Three texts in a day from one delegation is a drafting offensive. As Potsdam wound down, the Soviet side worked to lock its gains into the conference's papers before the leaders left Germany. Readers can follow the effort across this cluster and into the protocol. The texts also show the limits of paper power. Some Soviet wording was taken, some was fought to a draw. The difference between the two is the summit's true result.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-131:
Cohen's notes continue with the Potsdam session of July 28, 1945. Benjamin Cohen recorded the talks as Attlee replaced Churchill at the British seat. His notes appear in the second Potsdam volume among the layered American records. Each set from Cohen adds a lawyer's check on the words exchanged.

Readers who compare Cohen with the formal minutes gain depth. He tends to catch qualifications and asides that summaries drop. Those small words later mattered in disputes over the settlement. The notes show the care with which the American side guarded its record, day after day, session after session.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-31:
Philip Mosely, a U.S. political adviser at Babelsberg, sent word to Ambassador Winant in London on July 20, 1945. The extract is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. It concerns the agreement on additional requirements to be imposed on Germany.

Mosely reports that Vyshinsky told him the day before of Moscow's stance. The Soviet government had approved the agreement, save for its new title and new first paragraph. He expected those last points to be cleared shortly. A note adds color from a private Mosely letter of July 24. The title and preamble, he learned, had to be referred to Stalin himself before the Soviet signer could be instructed to sign. The full text of Mosely's message is printed later in the volume as document 1036.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d731:
The United States delegation put forward this proposal on July 30, 1945, two days before Potsdam closed. Document 731 belongs to the endgame. Late texts were drafted with the finish in view. Each line was weighed for what the other sides might still accept. The proposal joined the second Potsdam volume.

Endgame proposals repay study. They show what a side still hoped to win when time ran short. Readers can compare the text with the protocol signed on August 1. The distance between them maps the last concessions. The document catches the conference at its most practical: aims trimmed to the size of the possible.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d831:
A second Barnes letter from Bulgaria is dated July 31, 1945, as document 831. Two reports on the conference's last full day close his run in this volume. The representative in Sofia wrote to the Acting Secretary of State. This one joined the second Potsdam volume beside its pair.

Closing pairs of letters show a post tidying its account. Barnes left his record complete as the summit ended. Readers gain a double exposure of Bulgaria at the hinge. The document ends the Bulgaria thread of this run on a fitting note: a watcher still watching, as the lights of the conference went out.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d931:
American staff compiled this undated manuscript working paper of German asset figures during the Potsdam talks. It uses 1936 data. The tables compare the eastern zone, Berlin excluded, with the land east of the Oder-Neisse line. Sums are in billions of Reichsmarks, with shares of the Reich beside them.

Factory assets in the east came to 5.3 billion, near 29 percent of the Reich. Total assets were 20.1 billion in the east and 7.1 billion east of the Oder-Neisse. The paper also lists movable assets, livestock, and farm machinery. Population in the east was 24.6 million in 1939, about 35 percent of the Reich.
frus-1952-54v10-d131: Another 1952-1954 FRUS editorial note on Iran from volume ten. The crisis deepened through 1953. This note preserves that context. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
frus-1964-1968-south-central-america-mex:
Volume thirty-one of Foreign Relations of the United States for 1964 to 1968 covers South and Central America and Mexico in the Johnson years. The Office of the Historian publishes the series from declassified files. After the Cuban revolution, Washington's watchword in the region was counterinsurgency.

The papers record military aid, police training, and support for anti-communist governments across the continent. The Alliance for Progress, Kennedy's aid program, runs through them as it fades under Johnson. Mexico gets its own careful diplomacy, as a neighbor too large to pressure openly. The volume shows the Cold War's southern front in daily cables rather than crises.
gao-gaoreports-b-298831: AllWorld Language Consultants took its December 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Language deals get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-298931: ViroMed Laboratories took its December 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Lab deals get the same full hearing as the rest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299931: A 2007 GAO ruling on two linked contract fights from GlassLock, Inc. The container maker said the agency's award was off; the ruling tests each claim and calls the winner. For firms that sell to the government, the published call is part of the playbook — a look at how GAO scores fair bidding, case by case.
gao-gaoreports-b-310031: The FitNet Purchasing Alliance was back before GAO in 2007 with another contract fight, and this ruling is the outcome. The group challenged a federal buying setup; the call parses the legal arguments to a finish. Repeat players like FitNet helped write the protest case law one filing at a time.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-131: Loan commitment pricing and accounting got a GAO review in 2005, and the report covers the issues. The review reads the loan books line by line. The bankers' promises were studied. The study was thorough. The issues were covered. The books were read.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-231: Emerging cyber threats loomed over federal systems in 2005, and GAO's report says new cybersecurity issues threatened the networks. The findings sound the alarm. The report warns that the digital homeland deserved protection. The issues had to be faced. The digital homeland deserved protection.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-331: FAA air traffic control acquisitions were progressing in 2005, and GAO's report says the agency advanced, though challenges in major buys remained. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the skies deserved modern gear. The challenges had to be faced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-731: USAID's Egypt cash transfers got a GAO review in 2005, and the report says the program supported economic reform, though factors complicated. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the aid dollars deserved watching. The factors had to be faced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1031: The terror watch list was snagging innocents in 2006, and GAO's report examines efforts to reduce the adverse effects on the public. The findings target the false hits. The report warns that the security net should not strangle the innocent. The list needed cleaning.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-231: China trade duties could drop for some firms in 2006, and GAO's report says eliminating the nonmarket methodology would lower antidumping duties. The findings do the math. The report warns that the trade remedy needed honest calculation. The duties had to be fair.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-31: The Defense Logistics Agency's security program needed full implementation in 2005, and GAO's report says the agency had to finish the job. The findings demand the completion. The report warns that the supply chain's data deserved protection. The program had to be implemented.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-331: Haiti's blue-helmet bills got weighed in 2006, and GAO's report pits the UN's real costs against a what-if U.S. run. The findings do the math. The report warns that the peace bills deserved honest numbers. The peacekeeping bills deserved honest comparison.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-431: National park funding trends got a GAO review in 2006, and the report examines major operations funding and park responses. The findings do the math. The report warns that the crown jewels' budgets needed watching. The trends had to be faced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-831: Enterprise architecture needed leadership in 2006, and GAO's report says leadership remained key to building and leveraging the architectures. The findings demand the direction. The report warns that the blueprints needed bosses behind them. The leadership had to lead. The blueprints needed bosses behind them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1131: A 2007 Government Accountability Office report on the fees international air passengers pay for inspection services — the charges funding customs and immigration processing at airports. GAO argues key aspects of the fee structure should be addressed whether or not the fees are consolidated. The report digs into the economics of who pays for keeping the nation's airports secure and orderly.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-231: Long-term care policies with a Medicaid twist got a GAO look in 2007 — the report says the partnership plans shielded buyers and likely cost little. The findings bless the experiment. The report's take: private insurance plus public backstop can share the elder-care load.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-31: The UN's headquarters renovation needed watching in 2007, and GAO's report says the planning followed industry practice, though procurement and oversight could falter. The findings balance credit and caution. The report warns that the world body's facelift needed honest contracting. The renovation had to be clean.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-331: Disability rulings were a legal patchwork in 2007 — GAO's report says the Social Security agency had wrestled with conflicting court decisions but still managed its data poorly. The findings demand better records. The report's plea: the disabled deserve decisions built on data, not guesswork.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-531: The special counsels' spending got audited in 2007 — GAO's report grades the independent and special counsel outlays for the half-year period in full. The findings deliver the formal audit opinion. The report shows that even the investigators get investigated in turn.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-631: The Pentagon's upkeep bills kept climbing in 2007 — GAO's report tracks operations and maintenance costs plus the service-contracting surge in detail. The findings follow the money trail year over year. The report asks whether the war machine's maintenance was eating its modernization alive.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-831: Military medicine's overhaul needed a watchdog's blueprint in 2007 — GAO's report says a full oversight framework was missing for the health-system rebuild. The findings demand the guardrails before the construction. The report's warning: big reforms without big oversight invite big waste.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1031: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at stabilizing and Rebuilding Iraq: Iraqi Revenues, Expenditures, and Surplus. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-31: This 2007 Government Accountability Office investigation targets a troubling pattern: recipients of federal grants and direct assistance who abuse the federal tax system. Auditors traced cases where organizations receiving taxpayer-funded aid owed large unpaid tax debts of their own. The report documents the scale of the problem and asks whether agencies should screen recipients more carefully before handing out public money.
hermes-unveiled-1831: Hermes Unveiled, 1831. The unveiled Hermes. This book preserves that work. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Those who study the era will use it in their work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marmorek-oskar-:
Oskar Marmorek was an Austrian architect. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Skirta, in Galicia, on April 9, 1863. He studied at the polytechnic school in Vienna and took a course in Paris. He settled in Vienna in 1889 and built his practice there.

Among his works, the entry names the illuminated fountain for the Forestry Exposition of 1890. It also names the music hall for the Vienna Musical Exposition of 1892. A third work was his plan for the villa district of Assee. Like his brother Alexander, he was an active Zionist. He sat on the Actions Committee from the first Zionist Congress on and joined the Arish Expedition of 1902.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-b-judah:
Menahem ben Judah, a Roman halakist of the twelfth century, is sketched in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Isidore Singer, H. Brody, and Gotthold Weil. Almost nothing is dated in his life: Benjamin of Tudela mentions him, he knew Joseph ibn Plat of southern France, and in 1166 he directed the Talmudic academy at Rome. His father Judah, a younger contemporary of the great Nathan, filled the Roman prayer-book with liturgical poems; the son, by contrast, wrote nothing and confined himself to the Halakah.

What survives of him is a single responsum, on the benedictions at a circumcision, given when Ibn Plat visited Rome. The entry toys with two further identifications, that he answered a famous question addressed to "the wise men of Rome," and that Abraham ibn Ezra praised him in verse, but proves neither. He left one son, Moses, through whom his line of scholars continued.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-miles-of-marsei:
Miles of Marseilles was born Samuel ben Judah ben Meshullam in 1294. He was a Provençal physician and philosopher who carried Arabic learning into Hebrew. Richard Gottheil and Isaac Broydé wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. In some manuscripts he is Bongodos, Provençal for Ben Judah. From early youth he gave himself to science and philosophy. He studied astronomy at Salon.

In 1322 Miles sat in prison with other Jews in the tower of Rodorte at Beaucaire. He kept translating there. Averroes on Aristotle's Ethics and on Plato's Republic both date from his Beaucaire years. The article lists his dated translations one by one. They run from the Organon questions finished in 1320 to a compendium completed at Tarascon. Later he drifted through Murcia, Aix, and Montélimar.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-molina-isaac-10:
Isaac Molina was a Venetian-born Egyptian rabbi of the sixteenth century. He survives in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 chiefly as an opponent of Joseph Caro. The notice is by the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn. The two men disputed Rabbi Gershom's ordinances. Caro's Abḳat Rokel prints Molina's responsum, with Caro's answer immediately following.

His larger work was editorial. He gathered all the responsa of Asher ben Jehiel into a single volume. Some responsa by other rabbis went in too. He called the volume Besamim Rosh, adding his own notes and a preface. It was printed at Berlin in 1793. In that preface he claims responsa and novellae of his own. They cover the Talmud and Maimonides' code, works the entry cannot show in print.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morteira-morter:
Saul Levi Morteira was a Dutch rabbi of Portuguese descent who led Amsterdam's Sephardic community in the sixteen hundreds. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Venice about 1596, he came to Amsterdam in 1616 with the body of the physician Elijah Montalto. The congregation Bet Ya'akov chose him as its hakam that year.

Morteira founded the school Keter Torah and taught Talmud and Jewish philosophy to its top class. His pupils included Baruch Spinoza, yet in 1656 he sat on the court that excommunicated the young philosopher. His pupils later printed fifty of his five hundred sermons as Gibe'at Sha'ul. He also wrote a Spanish defense of Judaism, the Tractado de la Verdad de la Ley, still in manuscript in his day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nasi-joseph-duk:
Joseph Nasi rose from a refugee banker to a duke under Ottoman rule. His entry was written by Isidore Singer and Max Schloessinger for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Portugal early in the sixteenth century, he fled forced Christian practice with his family. He settled first in Antwerp, then reached Constantinople in 1553. There he openly returned to Judaism and married Reyna Nasi.

The article follows his rise at the court of Sultan Sulaiman. Nasi backed Salim in a fight for the throne and won great favor. The sultan gave him Tiberias for a new Jewish settlement. He rebuilt its walls and urged persecuted Jews to move there. In 1566 Salim made him Duke of Naxos and nearby islands. He ruled them through an agent and set light taxes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neighboring-lan:
Neighboring landowners in Jewish law must not harm each other. Wilhelm Bacher and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Mishnah sets restraints on the use of one's own land. Its rule matches the Latin maxim on harming another. Distance is the chief tool in these laws.

A cistern must stand three palms from a neighbor's wall. Dung, lime, ovens, and mills keep set distances too. No bakery or stable may open under a neighbor's store room. Windows and ladders must not spy or endanger doves. Trees stand twenty-five cubits from a walled town. Tanneries and graves keep fifty cubits away from towns. Maimonides later reshaped many of these rulings. The entry also treats the abutter's right of first purchase.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-niebla-original:
Niebla ranks among Spain's oldest towns of all. Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stands twelve miles west of Seville. Jews lived there already under the Visigoths. It was one of Spain's earliest Jewish settlements.

Alfonso VI took Niebla from the Moors in time. He left the town in the care of its Jews. Alfonso X of Castile conquered it in 1257. He generously gave the rebel emir part of the Juderia taxes. Jews stayed in Niebla and Mogüer until the expulsion. About fifty families formed the congregation there. Its medieval slave market was a noted one. The old synagogue is now a church, still standing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nunez-vaes-jaco:
Jacob Nuñez-Vaes was a rabbi and editor at Leghorn, in Italy. He died there about 1815. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the son of Isaac Joseph Nuñez-Vaes. He was also a pupil of Isaac Nuñez Belmonte.

Jacob put out the second part of his father's book Siah Yizhak. He also edited a twofold note on the five books of Moses. That work, Da'at Zekenim, came out in 1783. It drew on the Tosafists and on Judah ben Eliezer. He edited the Sefer ha-Makria of Isaiah di Trani too. A poem in his honor was written after his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppenheim-herma:
Hermann Oppenheim was a German doctor of the nerves. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Berlin on January 1, 1858. He read drugs and cures at Göttingen and Bonn. He took his degree in the year 1881.

Hermann settled in Berlin to work in his field. In 1883 he joined the staff of a nerve hospital. He kept that post till the year 1891. He joined the medical school staff in 1886. In 1893 he gained the honor title of professor. From 1891 he ran his own clinic and work room. His books treat nerve ills brought on by wounds. They treat growths of the brain and ills of its core. His text book on nerve ills came out in 1894.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oxford-11831:
Oxford is the county town of Oxfordshire, in England. Joseph Jacobs wrote its long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews settled there soon after the Norman Conquest. So Anthony à Wood, a writer on the town, reports. They lived on Fish Street, by the Christ Church gate.

Their row of houses formed a Jewry in the town. A church, St. Edward's, stood in the midst of it. Some halls that birthed the university were owned by Jews. Moysey's Hall and Lombard's Hall were two such halls. In 1141 war tore the realm between two claimants. The Jews of Oxford were squeezed by both sides for funds. King Stephen burnt the house of Aaron son of Isaac. The first firm record is a tax paid in 1156.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-passau-11931:
Passau is a town in eastern Bavaria with a long Jewish history. Jews settled there near the end of the twelfth century. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The town's Jews lived under the rule of its bishop.

After Christians looted Jewish homes, the bishop granted money and relief in 1210. Later bishops promised a break from new taxes and forced loans. The article also records dark years of persecution. Jewish martyrs died there in 1337 and again in 1349. By 1904 only thirty-four Jews remained in the town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pergamenter-sol:
Solomon ben Shalom Pergamenter was an Austrian Hebraist and poet. He lived at Brünn in the early nineteenth century. Isidore Singer and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He wrote for Jews who spoke German.

His main book was Yesode ha-Lashon, the Foundations of the Language. It taught Hebrew to readers on their own. The book was written in Judaeo-German for that purpose. It came out at Vienna in 1813 and again in 1832. He also wrote Hebrew poems of high quality. Delitzsch ranked him among the best German school poets.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pichon-picho-jo:
Joseph Pichon was the chief tax farmer of Seville. Henry the Second of Castile appointed him in 1369. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The king prized his honesty and his cleverness.

Rich Jews at court accused Pichon and had him jailed. He bought his freedom with forty thousand doubloons. Restored, he struck back at his enemies in turn. After Henry died, his foes plotted at Burgos. They called him an informer who deserved death. The young king signed a nameless death order. The executioner beheaded Pichon at his own door in 1379.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-polacco-vittori: Vittorio Polacco was an Italian jurist of Polish descent, born at Padua on May 10, 1859. Isidore Singer and Rosa H. Knorr wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Since 1884 he taught civil law at the University of Padua. His books deal with family division of goods and with payment in law. He also wrote against divorce in Italy. His main work treats duties under Italian civil law. He wrote many shorter pieces for law journals as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-prayer-12331:
Prayer in Jewish life is the subject of a long article by Cyrus Adler, M. H. Harris, the Editorial Board, and Judah David Eisenstein. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. From the first ages in the Bible, deep pain found voice in prayer. Great joy found voice in prayer as well. Even the most simple worship shows a man asking or thanking God.

Apart from the Psalms, the Bible is full of prayers. The Pentateuch, the Prophets, and the Writings all hold them. At least one prayer is told of each great Bible figure. The line runs from Hannah to King Hezekiah. The article studies these lone prayers first. It then turns to the fixed prayers of the synagogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pucher-solomon-:
Solomon Pucher was a rabbi who served in the Baltic lands. Herman Rosenthal and J. Brennsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in 1829 in a Polish town. He died at Riga in 1899. He learned at yeshivot and at the rabbinical school of Wilna.

In 1859 Pucher was called to the rabbinate of Mitau. The state gave him silver and gold medals of merit. In the sixth decade of the century he spoke out with force. He fought the Christian mission to Jews in Courland. His speeches and writings caused a great stir. He worked with tact to win his people fair treatment.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ragoler-elijah-:
Elijah ben Jacob Ragoler was a Russian rabbi and cabalist. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in 1794 near Kovno. He died at Kalisz on November 5, 1849.

The article stresses that Ragoler taught himself Talmud without a yeshivah. He liked the plain sense of the text and Rashi's notes. He served as rabbi at Shat, Eiragola, and Viliampol-Slobodka. In 1840 he moved to Kalisz and stayed until his death. The entry also shows him defending Orthodox Judaism with a calm tone.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reed-12631:
Reed is an English word used for several Hebrew plant names. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Each Hebrew word points to a different water plant. The article sorts them out one by one.

The writers identify gome with the papyrus plant. Suf is tied to an Egyptian word for Nile reed. Ahu means a marsh grass used as fodder. Agmon is likely a kind of rush. Kaneh is the stout marsh reed of Palestine. That reed served as staff and measuring rod. Behemoth hides among its thick cover in Job. The entry helps Bible readers picture plants named in translation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ribkas-moses-be:
Moses Ribkas was a Russian Talmudist who died at Wilna in 1671 or 1672. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. His family came from Prague. He settled early at Wilna.

The article says war forced him to flee Wilna in 1655. He left all his property behind him. At Amsterdam, leading rabbis valued his Talmud knowledge. There he revised proofs of a new Shulhan Aruk edition. His marginal notes, Be'er ha-Golah, give sources for rulings. Those notes still print in Shulhan Aruk margins today. When peace returned, he went back to Wilna. At death he left much wealth to charity. The entry honors work that still guides daily readers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosello-ruscell:
Mordecai Raphael ben Jacob Rosello was a scholar and liturgical poet of the early sixteenth century. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was born in Barcelona, where his family held a leading place.

Forced out of Naples when its Jews were expelled in 1541, he moved on to Avignon. In Rome in 1549 he finished Sha'are Hayyim, a work on the Ten Sefirot. He also wrote an elegy on the martyrdom of the priest Eleazar. That poem later entered the ritual of Carpentras, in southern France.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saloman-nota-s-:
Nota S. Saloman was a Danish physician born at Tondern on March 21, 1823. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He took his medical degree at Copenhagen in 1850, then sailed in the merchant navy.

Saloman next assisted at Copenhagen's Frederiks Hospital for a time. In 1853 he joined the Danish army as an assistant surgeon. He served through the war of 1864 and rose steadily in rank. In 1873 he became surgeon-general of the Danish army at last. The entry credits him with greatly improving its hospital and ambulance services.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-b-moses-:
Samuel b. Moses Phinehas was a Polish rabbi who died at Posen on November 25, 1806. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He descended from R. Joshua, author of Maginne Shelomoh.

At twenty-three Samuel became rabbi of Bilguria, near Zamoscz in Poland. He later held pulpits at Przeworsk and at Tarnopol, where he lived in 1795. In 1801 he succeeded his brother Joseph as rabbi of Posen city. He held that post until his death five years later. His Bet Shemuel Aharon joins responsa with sermons on the weekly lessons.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saul-ben-joseph:
Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Saul ben Joseph of Monteux. He was a French poet who wrote prayers for the liturgy. Saul lived at Carpentras in the second half of the seventeenth century. The Avignon prayer rite preserves one of his poems. It marks a narrow escape for his town's Jews.

On the ninth of Nisan in 1682, a riot broke out at Carpentras. The Jews of the town survived the danger. Saul's piyyuṭ gives thanks for that deliverance. It opens with the words Shebaḥ yeḳar u-gedullah. He was probably the son of another prayer poet, Joseph ben Abraham. That Joseph copied an extract from Caro's Bet Yosef. The copy survives at the library of Avignon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schur-william-1:
Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on William Schur. He was an American author. Schur was born at Outian, near Vilkomir, in Russia, on October 27, 1844. He studied Talmud at home and at Kovno. He studied theology at Berlin's Lehranstalt from 1868 to 1870. He then taught Hebrew at Constantinople, Port Said, and Cairo.

From 1874 to 1879 Schur traveled the world. He crossed Africa, India, and China. He visited the Philippine Islands and the China Sea. Settling at Vienna, he wrote for Smolenskin's Ha-Shaḥar and other Hebrew papers. In 1887 he went to America and lived in city after city. He has resided at Chicago since 1897. His two travel books tell of his journeys. He also wrote novels and a work on Israel's endurance.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sepphoris-greek:
Sepphoris was a city in Palestine perched like a bird on a high hill. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Josephus first names it during the reign of Alexander Jannaeus. Rome later placed one of its five councils there.

Under Rome, Sepphoris ranked as the chief city of Galilee. It backed one Jewish king, then fell to Herod. After Herod died, rebels held it, and Roman troops burned it. Its people were sold into slavery. Yet the city rose again into a new phase. The entry follows a hill town pulled again and again into wars over the land.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shehitah-13531:
Shehitah is the ritual slaughter of animals for food in Jewish law. Wilhelm Bacher and Julius H. Greenstone wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. The Bible condemns cutting a limb from a living animal. Yet it sets no definite method for slaughter itself.

For sacrifices, the verb used means simply that the animal is killed. Priests likely followed one steady method for that work. Rabbis later argued that law requires cutting the throat. They sought a scriptural base for that rule in word roots. Common opinion held that God gave Moses all shehitah laws directly. The entry shows a daily practice built from sparse verses, custom, and rabbinic reasoning about kindness to animals.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sichel-jules-13:
Jules Sichel was a French eye doctor born at Frankfurt-on-the-Main in 1802. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He earned his medical degree at Berlin in 1825. A postgraduate course at Paris followed his Berlin training.

Sichel settled in Paris and opened an eye clinic in 1836. It offered free consultations to patients there. He grew into one of Paris's most popular oculists. His books covered eye disease, cataract, and loss of sight. An illustrated eye atlas from him appeared in the 1850s. Late in life he studied Roman eye doctors' seal stones. He died at Paris in 1868. The entry honors a doctor who joined free care with exact scholarship.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sossnitz-joseph:
Joseph Judah Löb Sossnitz was a Russian-American Talmudic scholar and scientific author. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Birzhi on September 17, 1837. At age ten he prepared a calendar for the year 1847. At nineteen he went to Riga as a Hebrew teacher.

At Riga a professor gave him use of a fine library. There he studied German and the secular sciences in depth. In 1891 he went to New York and settled there. He founded a Talmud Torah in 104th street in 1893. His books covered astronomy, geometry, physics, and chess as well. He also wrote a perpetual calendar for three faiths.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stern-julius-14:
Julius Stern was a German musician born at Breslau on August 8, 1820. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He learned violin as a child and played concerts at age nine. His family moved to Berlin in 1832. He died at Berlin on February 27, 1883.

In 1847 Stern founded the Stern singing society in Berlin. Its first Elijah performance made his name as a conductor. The choir grew to cover Handel, Haydn, Bach, and newer composers. In 1850 he co-founded the Stern Conservatorium with Kullak and Marx. He later ran that school alone until his death. He also led the Berlin Symphony Orchestra for two years. The entry marks his deep effect on Berlin musical life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-susskind-alexan:
Alexander Süsskind was a wealthy Jew of Frankfort and Worms in the 1200s. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He lived in the second half of the thirteenth century. He died on the Day of Atonement in 1307. His tombstone survives almost intact today.

Süsskind spent nearly his whole fortune on one act. He ransomed the body of Meïr of Rothenburg for burial. That body had been denied burial for almost fourteen years. As his sole reward he asked to lie beside it. The brief entry rests on chronicles and grave records. It honors a man who traded wealth for a teacher's honor. Readers meet a stark example of medieval Jewish loyalty and charity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tanhum-b-hiyya-:
Tanhum ben Hiyya was a Palestinian amora of the third century. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. He came from Kefar Akko and lived at Tiberias. He studied under Simeon ben Pazzi. His sayings pass through both Talmuds by that link.

At Tiberias, Tanhum helped ransom captured Jewish women. Roman troops had likely brought them there. He sat on the commission that fixed calendar intercalations. Wealthy and generous, he gave freely to the poor. His mother doubled household meat purchases for the poor. Only three legal sayings of his survive. More of his sermonic sayings remain in the sources. One warns scholars who fail to prevent evil they could stop. The entry gathers a generous sage's scattered record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-teraphim-14331:
Teraphim, the household gods of early Semitic life, are examined here. John Dyneley Prince, Wilhelm Bacher, and M. Seligsohn wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Greek versions render the word as images, figures, or oracles.

The figures had human shape and stood fairly large. Michal placed one in David's bed to hide his escape. Rachel stole her father Laban's teraphim and sat on them. Laban called them his gods when he chased Jacob. Micah kept teraphim in a house of gods with its own priest. The article traces how this old cult faded over time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tithe-10231:
The tithe, a tenth given as tax or offering, is traced from the patriarchs onward. Joseph Jacobs, M. Seligsohn, and Wilhelm Bacher wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Abraham gave Melchizedek a tenth of all he had. Jacob vowed God a tenth if he returned home safely.

Moses later made the tithe a binding law. Produce of land and trees belonged to God. Cattle were counted one by one under the rod. Every tenth beast became holy and could not be swapped. Numbers gives all tithes to the landless Levites. Levites in turn gave priests a tenth of that. Deuteronomy instead has families eat the tithe at the Temple city. Every third year it fed widows and strangers at home.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-valerio-samuel-:
Samuel ben Judah Valerio was a doctor and writer in the Greek islands. He lived in the second half of the sixteenth century. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. Valerio is known for two Bible commentaries, both printed at Venice in 1586.

His first book explains the Book of Esther. He finished it at Corfu in February 1579. His second book is a thoughtful commentary on the Book of Daniel. He finished that work a year later, near Patras in Greece. Parts of it were later quoted in a large rabbinical Bible from Amsterdam. Three more of his works survive only in handwriting.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-volterra-aaron-:
Aaron Hai Volterra was an Italian liturgical poet. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Volterra served as rabbi in Massa e Carrara. He wrote in the first half of the seventeen hundreds. His fame rests on one bold prayer.

That prayer is called Bakkashah, or Elef Shin. Every word in it begins with the letter shin. The title claims a thousand shin words. The true count is only seven hundred. Volterra admitted the strain in his preface. Artificial word forms were needed to keep the pattern. A commentary with a glossary accompanies the poem.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weil-tiah-jedid:
Tiah Weil, also called Jedidiah, was a German rabbi. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Gotthard Deutsch wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Prague on October 2, 1721. He died at Carlsruhe on October 10, 1805. His father was Nethaneel Weil, who taught him first.

Expulsion from Prague drove Tiah to Metz in 1745. There he studied under Jonathan Eybeschütz. He became rabbi of Wottitz in 1754. In 1770 he succeeded his father at Carlsruhe. Only his Haggadah commentary was ever printed. His legal answers appear in other rabbis' collections. His will shows deep piety and belief in Kabbalah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-willow-14931:
The willow is a tree of riverbanks in Palestine. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Löw wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Many willow and poplar species grow there. The white willow and Euphrates poplar occur most often. The crack willow and white poplar are also common. Some kinds grow only near the Jordan.

The Bible's willows were likely Euphrates poplars. Psalms picture exiles hanging harps on them. Leviticus requires willows of the brook for Tabernacles. Karaites and modern scholars link that rule to booth building. The Mishnah still reads the word as true willow. The entry sorts species, names, and ritual uses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yudghanites-151:
Yudghanites were the sect formed by Yudghan of Hamadan in Persia. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broyde wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Yudghan was a pupil of Abu Isa al-Isfahani. Abu Isa led a sect that fell in a fight at Rai.

That fall came early in the eighth century of this era. Yudghan then sought to form a new sect from the scraps. He was more wise than his master in one key way. He did not claim a call to free the Jews by force. He took the role of a seer and a teacher in peace. Men called him al-Rai, or the Shepherd, in that role. Sufi thought swayed him as it spread in that land. He set the deep sense of the Torah above its plain words.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zekor-berit-152:
Zekor Berit is a hymn by Gershom ben Judah of old fame. Isidore Singer and Francis L. Cohen wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Gershom lived from 960 to 1040 in the Rhineland. Men call him the Light of the Exile to this day.

North rite Jews sing his hymn in the pardon prayers. It stands at the core of the rite on New-Year eve. That day takes its pet name from the hymn in talk. Its plea rests on the worth of the sires of old. It asks God to free the last of Israel for their sake. Two more hymns with the same first words came in time. Both were bound in some rites of the north as well. In the Polish rite his hymn heads the New-Year close set. An old west air is used for that chant to this day.
kingsborough-mexico-vol-1-1831:
Lord Kingsborough gave his wealth and health to one vast work. The Antiquities of Mexico, Book One, came out in 1831. Edward King, Lord Kingsborough, held that the Jews were kin to the folk of old Mexico. The set runs to nine books of plates and text.

Book One gives fine copies of Mexican paintings and glyph texts. Kingsborough paid skilled hands to copy codices from stores all over Europe. Most of the source books have since been lost or harmed. The set is a chief store of the art of old Mexico.
kingsborough-mexico-vol-3-1831:
Book Three of Kingsborough's Antiquities of Mexico came out in 1831. Lord Kingsborough built the set in nine books in all. The work prints copies of the paintings and texts of old Mexico. Kingsborough spent his fortune on the grand scheme.

Plates of codices fill the book, with their gods, kings, and rites. The copies were made by fine hands from books held in Europe. Kingsborough adds text to back his claim of a link with the old East. The set is a key store of Mexican art from a lost age.
kingsborough-mexico-vol-4-1831:
Book Four of the Antiquities of Mexico came out in 1831. Lord Kingsborough's vast set runs to nine books in all. The work gives copies of the art and glyph texts of old Mexico. Book One of the set stands at the start of the run.

More codices pass in fine plates through this book. Gods, wars, and the rounds of the year crowd the old pages. Kingsborough's team copied books that have since been lost to fire and theft. The set kept a vast store of Mexican lore safe for all time.
kingsborough-mexico-vol-5-1831:
Book Five of Kingsborough's Antiquities of Mexico came out in 1831. The full set runs to nine books in all. Lord Kingsborough, Edward King, gave his life to the work. It prints the paintings and texts of old Mexico in fine copies.

The plates run on with the codices, book by book, glyph by glyph. Kingsborough held that the folk of Mexico had links to the lost tribes of Israel. That claim drove his vast spend on the work. The set is still a chief store for the study of the codices.
kingsborough-mexico-vol-6-1831:
Book Six of the Antiquities of Mexico came out in 1831. Lord Kingsborough's set runs to nine books in all. The work prints fine copies of the paintings and glyph books of old Mexico. Edward King, Lord Kingsborough, paid for the whole vast scheme.

Codices and plates of old towns fill this book as the set runs on. Kingsborough's claim was that the folk of Mexico had roots in the old East. Few back that claim now, but the plates keep their worth. Scores of the source books are lost, so the copies stand in their place.
kingsborough-mexico-vol-7-1831:
Book Seven of Kingsborough's Antiquities of Mexico came out in 1831. The set runs to nine books and nears its end here. Lord Kingsborough gave his fortune to print the art of old Mexico. The work copies codices held in stores all over Europe.

Glyph books and plates of gods, kings, and towns crowd the pages. Each plate was drawn by a skilled hand from a rare source book. Kingsborough adds text in aid of his claim of links with Israel. The set is a vast, flawed, and grand store of Mexican lore.
l-idee-parfaicte-de-la-philosophie-herma: Jean Collesson's 1631 French book promises a perfect idea of hermetic philosophy. Its subtitle calls it an abridgment of that theory. The sample pages survive only as garbled scan text. Even so, the title and date ground the work clearly. It belongs to the early modern French literature of alchemy. Such short guides summed up secret doctrine for new readers.
limborch-history-of-the-inquisition-vol-:
Philipp van Limborch, a Dutch Protestant scholar, published his Historia Inquisitionis in 1692, the classic early account of the tribunal. Samuel Chandler translated it into English in 1731, and this is the first volume. Limborch built his history on the archives of the Inquisition of Toulouse, which had come into his hands.

He traces the rise of persecution from the early church through the Albigensian wars to the standing tribunal. His tone is grave and fair for his age, and his documents do the accusing. Protestant Europe read Limborch as the standard proof of Rome's cruelty. The work shaped every history of the Inquisition written for two centuries.

The second volume of Samuel Chandler's 1731 English Limborch is the documentary heart of the work. Philipp van Limborch printed here the Book of Sentences of the Inquisition of Toulouse, the Liber Sententiarum, as his appendix of proof. The first volume told the history; this one shows the papers.

Sentence by sentence, the record names men and women of Languedoc, their alleged errors, and their punishments: penances, crosses worn on the coat, prison, the stake. The years covered run from 1307 to 1323, under the inquisitor Bernard Gui and his fellows. Few books bring the medieval tribunal so close. Limborch let the archive speak, and it still does.
london-in-1731:
Don Manoel Gonzales presents this account of London in 1731. Cassell's National Library reprinted it in 1888. The introduction warns that Gonzales is an assumed name. His Voyage to Great Britain first appeared in the Harleian Collection.

That collection, published in 1745 and 1746, drew on Harley's library. Pinkerton's voyages later reproduced the narrative for wider readers. The writer poses as Portuguese, praising Lisbon's extensive city. Yet he writes of London like one born to the city. Edward Harley continued his father's collecting industry after 1724. Pinkerton's seventeen quartos later carried the account worldwide. John Pinkerton's travel collection later carried the account around the world.
near-v-minnesota-1931:
Near v. Minnesota is a United States Supreme Court ruling from 1931 about freedom of the press. Minnesota law treated a paper printed often as a nuisance if officials called it malicious, scandalous, and defamatory. The state could then sue to shut it down and bar future issues.

The Court held that use of the law unconstitutional for papers charging officials with neglect and corruption. It said press liberty falls under the liberty guarded by the Fourteenth Amendment against state action. It also warned that a law is judged by what it does, not by its form. The ruling stands as a key bar on stopping a press before it prints.
observations-on-mental-derangement-being:
Andrew Combe published Observations on Mental Derangement in 1831, applying the principles of phrenology to insanity. The full title promises light on the causes, symptoms, nature, and treatment of the condition. The record notes bibliographical references and an index. Combe sought a system for a subject then dark to most doctors.

The sampled pages, in garbled type, report curious experiments from Italy on colour and the nerves. A hospital for the insane at Alessandria, they say, set rooms with red or blue glass. A violent patient brought into a blue room was left to that colour's effect. One maniac was cured in an hour, the report claims. Combe's own frame stays phrenology applied to the mind.
old-lady-number-31:
Louise Forsslund published this novel in the year 1909. She had written The Story of Sarah before it. Chapter titles point to a tea table and old letters. Other chapters name an anniversary and a winter butterfly. A prodigal departs, and apron strings are cut.

The number in the title hints at an old ladies' home. Samuel receives a welcome in a late chapter. Forsslund writes warmly about age, friendship, and change. Small events carry deep feeling for her characters. The book suits readers who enjoy gentle domestic fiction. Its tone stays kind, humorous, and hopeful throughout.
openalex-w1976685031:
Laurens Manning, Moses Laman, and co-authors studied severe malaria. Their paper is dated 2011 in the catalog record. Deaths from severe falciparum malaria seem low in Oceania. Vivax malaria is now seen as a cause of death too. Mixed-species infections were poorly described before this study.

The team detailed features of severe cases by species. Falciparum, vivax, and mixed infections were compared directly. Prognosis, meaning likely outcome, was tracked for each group. Such detail helps doctors triage sick children faster. It also guides treatment where several species circulate together. The study fills a gap in Oceania malaria care.
openalex-w2035901831:
Jill Cairns, Jon Hellin, Kai Sonder and colleagues reviewed how maize farming in Africa can adapt to climate change. Their paper appeared in Food Security in 2013. Maize is a staple crop across sub-Saharan Africa. Evidence of warming there is growing. Farmers need more resilient maize systems soon.

The authors reviewed outputs from nineteen climate models. By 2050, temperatures may rise across maize regions. Rainfall change varied a lot by location. Adaptation will likely need better seed varieties. Heat and drought tolerance are key traits needed. Better farm management practices also matter. New varieties take years to reach farmers. So breeding and policy work must start early.
openalex-w2059758031:
Ximena Rueda and Eric Lambin studied eco-certification among small coffee growers in Colombia. Their paper appeared in Ecology and Society in 2013. Certification pays farmers a premium for greener practices. Past studies focused mostly on money benefits. Those benefits swing with prices, so they explain only part of farmer choices.

The study compared certified and similar non-certified households. It covered eighty-six households in Santander. Certified farms showed clear environmental benefits. Farmer and community well-being also improved. Price premiums mattered most for joining the scheme. Other gains helped farmers stay and upgrade practices. The authors link certification to more resilient local systems.
openalex-w2079479731:
Vardan Khachatryan, Armen Sirunyan, Armen Tumasyan and colleagues in the CMS Collaboration pinned down the Higgs boson mass. Their paper appeared in 2015. The Higgs particle had been found near a known mass range. Precise mass and behaviour tests were still needed. The standard model makes clear predictions for both.

The team combined many production and decay measurements. Data came from proton collisions in 2011 and 2012. Two clean decay channels gave the sharpest mass value. The measured mass sat close to earlier estimates. Yields in each channel matched standard model expectations. Coupling strengths also agreed with predictions within errors. The result strengthened confidence in the standard model picture.
openalex-w2560556331:
Aracy Lopes da Silva reviewed Renato Rosaldo's book Culture and Truth for Revista de Antropologia in 1992. The review, written in Portuguese, introduces Brazilian readers to Rosaldo, a Stanford anthropologist. His earlier work combined anthropology and history in a study of Ilongot headhunting. In this 1989 book he proposes new paths for social analysis.

The book has three parts, Silva explains. The first attacks classical anthropology and the idea that neutrality guarantees objectivity. The later parts urge process-based analysis, room for subjectivity, and attention to the porous borders of cultures. Stories from Ilongot and Chicana narrators supply his working examples. Silva finds the critique sometimes naive and late for Brazilian anthropologists. Still, the review maps Rosaldo's challenge to positivist habits in American social science.
openalex-w2616775231:
Andreas Crivellin, Dario Müller, and Toshihiko Ota wrote this 2017 theory paper in the Journal of High Energy Physics. It tackles puzzling results in flavor physics, where B meson decays refuse to match Standard Model predictions. Two anomalies stand out: one in decays with tau leptons, another in decays to muon pairs. Each deviates at a level too large to ignore comfortably.

The authors show that two hypothetical particles, scalar leptoquarks, could explain both anomalies at once. Leptoquarks would link quarks and leptons, which the Standard Model keeps separate. Their setup ties the two particles' masses and couplings through a symmetry. It also predicts greatly boosted decays into tau pairs, within reach of LHCb and Belle II experiments. A third anomaly, in the muon's magnetism, cannot join the package. Any two of the three anomalies can be explained together, but never all three.
openalex-w2898393231:
Maria Camila Ariza-Tarazona, Juan Francisco Villarreal-Chiu, and Virginia Barbieri reported a light-based attack on microplastics in Ceramics International. The journal version came out in 2019; the hosted sample is the authors' accepted draft. Microplastics are now a growing marine pollutant of worldwide concern. Cutting inputs from land is essential, since the ocean cannot be filtered.

The team presents the first use of photocatalysis against polyethylene microplastics taken from a facial scrub. Their catalyst is nitrogen-doped titanium dioxide, a light-driven semiconductor. One version was green-synthesized using fluid from blue mussels. It broke down the plastics strongly in both solid and water settings. A standard sol-gel version also caused mass loss in water. Microscopy and spectra confirmed genuine breakdown. Careful control proved necessary to keep the reaction from stalling.
openalex-w3004876731:
Robert Ross, Ian Neeland, Shizuya Yamashita, and colleagues issued this consensus statement in Nature Reviews Endocrinology in 2020. It urges doctors to treat waist size as a vital sign, measured at every visit like blood pressure. The statement comes from a working group on visceral obesity, the deep belly fat linked to disease.

Decades of evidence show waist size predicts illness and death risk on top of what body mass index, or BMI, reveals. Yet clinics rarely measure it. The authors argue that BMI alone cannot capture the health risk of extra fat. They review the evidence in full and recommend that shrinking waist size become an explicit treatment target for patients with overweight or obesity.
openalex-w3045768331:
Diana Garibo, Hugo Borbón-Nuñez, Jorge Díaz de León, and colleagues published this study in Scientific Reports in 2020. It makes silver specks by a green route, using the sap of a Mexican tree, and tests how well they kill germs. The tree has long been used in folk care and is rich in germ-fighting compounds.

Tiny silver specks are prized for fighting microbes, but making them with harsh chemicals can cost much and leave toxic waste. Plant sap offers a cleaner path: it turns silver into specks and can boost their power. The team checked the specks with lab tools and tested their strength against microbes. The specks killed germs well, backing green methods as a sound way to make safer cleaning materials.
openalex-w4200137031:
Shruti Khare, Céline Gurry, Lucas Freitas, and colleagues describe the role of GISAID in pandemic response, in China CDC Weekly in 2021. GISAID is a global initiative that collects genome data on influenza, RSV, and the coronavirus behind COVID-19. Its shared platform lets tens of thousands of researchers deposit and compare virus sequences quickly. That speed matters when a new variant starts to spread.

Through GISAID, scientists track emerging variants, such as Delta, and estimate how common each is by country. A shared family tree of the virus shows how it evolves and travels. Health authorities have asked GISAID to extend its system to other dangerous pathogens. The authors argue that open, fast data sharing is now core pandemic infrastructure.
openalex-w4409288331:
Go Takeuchi and Mikio Eto examine a superconducting diode effect in a double quantum dot device. Their paper appeared in the Journal of the Physical Society of Japan in 2025. A superconducting diode lets current flow more easily one way than the other. Such devices could serve future low-power electronics.

The design joins two quantum dots to three superconducting leads. Because the dots share one lead, their bound states merge into an Andreev molecule. The authors show that the critical current into one lead then depends on its direction. That happens unless a second phase is set to special values. Notably, the effect needs no spin-orbit interaction, widening the materials that could host it.
openalex-w7204266731: The Sao Francisco Valley grows grapes under a blazing sun, and new varieties keep arriving. This study tested the BRS Vitoria grape: how fertilizer application affected yield and post-harvest quality. The authors measured what the new cultivar can do in local conditions. Practical viticulture for one of Brazil's most distinctive wine and table-grape regions.
openalex-w7204591731: Blood clots after surgery can kill, and tight stockings are a simple defense. This paper reviews the evidence on graduated compression stockings for preventing deep vein thrombosis after operations. The authors assess how well the mechanical squeeze works. A clinical review of low-tech prevention doing quiet, life-saving work.
openalex-w7204783531: Children with ADHD struggle to manage tasks and daily routines, and their parents struggle alongside them.
