This article presents MEMOIRS, a phone app concept designed to help such children organize their day. The authors lay out the design and the thinking behind it as a digital aid for young users. A tech-meets-care proposal aimed at making routine manageable for restless minds.
openalex-w7206178031: Maria Zenaide de Souza Carvalho, known as Zenaide Parteira, is a midwife and singer from Acre whose song Tarauaca tells the story of migration. This article reads her music as geography, showing how lived experience can become a form of knowledge about place and territory. The authors argue that songs like hers record how migration shapes identity and belonging. An unusual meeting of cultural studies, geography, and oral tradition.
openalex-w7208745231:
Bruno Acioly Coutinho, writing alone, analyzes the time rules that govern police entry into homes in Brazil, and what they mean for the Alagoas military police. The constitution protects the home, allowing entry under a court warrant or in narrow cases without one. Coutinho reads the constitutional text, the criminal procedure code, a 2019 abuse-of-authority law, and rulings of the two high courts, updated to August 2026.

Recent case law fixed the hours for serving home warrants to a daytime window running from early morning to evening. That change, he finds, did not widen the cases where police may enter without a warrant; it made the time requirement easier to check and enforce. Entry without a warrant stays bound to strict conditions. For police governance, the ruling turns timing into a point of proof that officers and commanders must plan around.
openalex-w7212033231: Eliza Furst Klafke leads a team of seven authors studying what nursing teams know about adverse reactions to antimicrobials in children, published in 2026 in the journal Research, Society and Development. Harm from these drugs is a known risk for child patients, made sharper by frequent off-label use and by how young bodies handle medicines. The sample gives the study's aim, to assess the nursing team's knowledge, but not its results.
openalex-w7212186931:
Jose Augusto Melo Ribeiro leads a team that asks families what a police youth plan did for their homes in Castanhal, Para. The plan is PMZITO, a state police scheme that works with kids and teens to stop harm before it starts. The local arm runs from a peace hub in the town. The team gave forms to the carers of the young who took part, and read the replies with care.

Each home in the poll saw a gain in family life. Four in five saw a big shift in the young: more order, more self-rule, and more calm. The plan's core, they say, joins good acts, pride in one's place, and clear rank. Home life, in these tales, took that core in. The study backs the plan as a tool of peace at the root level, where crime has yet to start.
openalex-w7214099431:
Tales Paulino Guimarães de Sales and colleagues analyse child-centred play therapy and gamification together. Their 2026 narrative, theoretical review rests mainly on Carl Rogers and Virginia Axline, plus studies of games and child development. The setting is the person-centred approach to child psychotherapy.

Play therapy and gamification are distinct ideas that can meet in clinic, they argue. In play therapy, play lets the child express and work through experience. Gamified elements, borrowed from games, aim to raise participation and engagement. Such resources fit child-centred practice only when they protect autonomy, spontaneity, and the child's lead. Gamification may complement therapy, they conclude, if it stays subordinate to the therapeutic relationship.
openalex-w7214649631: Nature builds complex molecules with enzyme tools, and this paper studies one of them. The authors investigated KwwB, a P450 enzyme from a Kitasatospora bacterium, showing it can stitch an unusual chemical bond in cyptides, a growing family of modified peptides. They mapped what the enzyme accepts. A biochemistry study of nature's molecule-making machinery.
openalex-w7220931631:
Bianca De Castro Souza Santos and three colleagues counted congenital anomalies, birth conditions present from the start of life, among babies born in the Brazilian state of Paraná between 2012 and 2022. Their 2026 cross-sectional study drew on the national live-birth information system and compared mothers, pregnancies, and newborns.

Of well over a million births, a small share, under one percent, involved an anomaly. Rates ran higher for mothers over forty, Indigenous and Black mothers, and mothers with little schooling or no prenatal care. Multiple pregnancies, early birth, very low birth weight, and low Apgar scores also carried higher rates. The authors argue the pattern strengthens the case for prenatal care and steady birth surveillance.
openalex-w7220974031:
Juliana Lubiano Nunes and Rozineide Iraci Pereira da Silva reviewed theory and official documents on diversity and inclusion in the first years of Brazilian elementary school, publishing in 2026. Their focus is classroom practice: how teaching itself can turn the legal promise of inclusion into real participation and learning for every child.

Twenty-one sources mixed academic work with laws and official guidance. They were sorted into four themes: inclusive planning, participatory methods, adapted activities and resources, and school-family-community teamwork. Their synthesis says access alone is not inclusion. It takes teacher mediation, accessible teaching, institutional conditions, and shared responsibility to make the promise hold.
openalex-w7220997331:
Maria Teresa Borges Ferreira Cardoso and three co-authors reviewed new tools for vaginal rejuvenation in a 2026 article. They compared radiofrequency devices with ablative lasers. The team gathered clinical studies from 2016 to 2024. Each study had to report measured results. Effects, safety, and how each tool works on tissue all counted.

Both approaches improved tissue structure and function. Gains showed in moisture, stretch, and sexual function. Change-of-life symptoms eased too. Lasers also helped mild to moderate stress incontinence. Against these gains, the authors flag weak rules and few long-term trials. Trained staff are scarce as well. They advise caution and close follow-up before such treatments spread.
openalex-w7221074231:
Danthi Barbosa Lima and Diemerson da Costa Saquetto wrote a 2026 essay on teaching the humanities in school, joining that tradition to a second theme: students' mental health. They argue that how humanities teaching was built, and what its curricula aim at, shapes whether school can support a freer, more humane education.

Drawing on historians of schooling, curriculum thinker Sonia Kramer, and writer bell hooks, the essay follows humanities teaching from its historical roots to today's classroom. A broad, critical idea of mental health runs through the argument. The authors invite readers to rethink practice starting from the individual and reaching the collective, turning liberating pedagogy into concrete action fitted to each school.
openalex-w7221128731:
Daniel Sebastião Celestino and five co-authors surveyed early childhood teachers in Angola about play-based learning and mathematical thinking, in a 2026 study. Thirty teachers answered a closed questionnaire about how they use games and play, what mathematics those activities carry, and what holds the practice back.

Teachers placed play at the center of their work, using it mostly for numbers and quantities, shapes, space, measures, classification, and patterns. They credited games with building mathematical thinking in young children. Shortages of materials, specific training, and planning time stood out as the persistent obstacles. The authors conclude that playful mathematics needs prepared teachers and real classroom conditions, not goodwill alone, to flourish.
ouspensky-new-model-of-the-universe-1931:
Ouspensky summed up his thought in A New Model of the Universe, printed in 1931. Science, faith, and esoteric lore are woven into one scheme in its pages. The Russian thinker had spent decades on the road between East and West.

His method is what he calls psychological: study the world by first studying the mind that meets it. The book takes up time, sex, myth, the Gospels, and the fourth dimension in turn. It states his mature view of man as a being not yet awake. Readers who want Ouspensky whole come to this summa.
paley-works-complete-1831:
William Paley, an English clergyman and Cambridge teacher, wrote the books that a generation of students learned their morals and their faith from. The complete Works in one volume, Philadelphia, 1831, gather his Life, his Moral and Political Philosophy, and his Evidences of Christianity. His Natural Theology stands with them, along with the Horae Paulinae, his Tracts, Sermons, and the Clergyman's Companion.

Paley writes with a gift for the clear example and the homely comparison that any reader can follow. His watchmaker argument for God's design, from Natural Theology, became the most famous of its kind. His moral philosophy grounds duty in God's will and human happiness. One volume here holds a whole curriculum of Georgian faith.
plos-pbio-0020031:
Yi Tang, Taek Soon Lee, and Chaitan Khosla reported a bioengineering feat in PLOS Biology in 2004. Certain soil microbes build useful drugs, like the antibiotic tetracycline, with huge enzymes called polyketide synthases. These enzymes link small building blocks into ring-shaped products, step by step.

The team rebuilt the system with two-part enzymes so they could steer where changes land on the final product. Controlled changes are the hard part of making new versions of old drugs. Their success shows that these assembly lines can be reprogrammed with care. That opens a path to custom compounds that nature never made, some of which might beat drug-resistant germs.
plos-pbio-0020131:
Michael S. Kobor, Shivkumar Venkatasubramanyan, and their team studied a histone-swapping machine in yeast for PLOS Biology in 2004. DNA wraps around proteins called histones. A variant spool, H2A.Z, takes the place of the standard one at certain genes and changes how they behave.

The study names the protein complex that loads H2A.Z into place. Its core is an enzyme called Swr1p, kin to a family of DNA-moving motors. Knowing the machine explains how cells place the variant with care rather than at random. H2A.Z placement affects gene activity across many species, including humans. The yeast work gives a parts list that other fields can build on.
plos-pbio-0020231:
James M. Holaska, Amy K. Kowalski, Katherine L. Wilson, and their team studied a nucleus protein in PLOS Biology in 2004. Emerin sits in the inner membrane of the cell nucleus. Mutations in emerin cause a form of muscular dystrophy that also harms the heart.

The team found that emerin caps the pointed end of actin filaments, the thin rods that give cells shape. That job hints at a network of actin right against the nucleus. Such a network could help the nucleus hold its form and place. The finding gives a fresh angle on how emerin faults weaken muscle cells. It also adds the nucleus to the map of the cell's inner scaffolding.
plos-pone-0000031:
Ivan Nagaev, Maria Bokarewa, Andrej Tarkowski, and co-authors redefined a hormone-like protein called resistin in work published in 2006. Resistin was first studied in fat tissue and linked to insulin resistance. The human version, this team showed, behaves differently: it is a systemic, immune-derived proinflammatory cytokine, a body-wide alarm signal made by immune cells.

They found resistin targets both leukocytes, the white blood cells, and adipocytes, the fat cells. That makes it a messenger running between the immune system and fat tissue, two systems medicine once treated as separate. Inflammation that involves both helps explain diseases like diabetes and heart disease, and resistin sits at that crossroads in humans.
plos-pone-0000131:
Sara O. Dean and James A. Spudich published this cell division study in PLOS ONE in 2006. Using Drosophila S2 cells, a fruit fly cell line, they examine how the motor protein myosin is recruited to the cell's equator during division. The focus is on an enzyme called Rho kinase and the chemical tag it places on myosin's light chain.

As the title states, Rho kinase's job in this recruitment is to phosphorylate that light chain, switching myosin on at the right place. Getting this step right is what lets a dividing cell pinch in two. The paper clarifies one link in the machinery of mitosis, the process behind growth and tissue repair.
plos-pone-0000231:
Tianshou Zhou, Jiajun Zhang, Zhanjiang Yuan, and colleagues published this theory paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Many natural systems tick in rhythm, from firing neurons to flashing fireflies, and outside stimuli can push groups into shared rhythm. The authors study how external stimuli mediate such collective rhythms and propose artificial control strategies for them.

Controlling group rhythm matters in fields from power grids to brain stimulation. The authors model when an outside signal can steer a population of oscillators. Their strategies offer a handle on synchronization, the same phenomenon that can help a system work or, in a brain, produce a seizure.
plos-pone-0000331:
Jeffrey Shaman and Jonathan F. Day published this mosquito ecology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Mosquito populations breed in phases tied to reproduction. The authors show that these populations lock their reproductive phase to the frequency of rainfall, syncing breeding pulses with how often rain falls.

Rain creates the standing water mosquitoes need, so syncing to its rhythm is adaptive. The authors model and document that phase locking. Predicting mosquito pulses matters for controlling diseases they carry, from dengue to West Nile, because control works best timed to breeding. That rhythm gives control programs a clock to work against.
plos-pone-0000431:
Ulrike Böer and colleagues watched stress rewrite gene activity in mouse brains, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The mice were engineered so that genes driven by the CRE/CREB system light up, making their activity visible. Under chronic social stress, that system drove gene expression up, and the team tested whether antidepressant treatment could reverse the change.

The authors report that antidepressant treatment did reverse the stress-driven rise. A visible readout of a stress-sensitive gene system lets researchers screen how stress and drugs interact in the living brain. The findings support the idea that long-term stress reshapes brain chemistry in ways that treatment can push back.
plos-pone-0000531:
Qi Wang and Yuan-Ping Pang tested a docking program's accuracy on a large set of known structures, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Computer docking predicts how a small molecule fits into a protein, a key step in drug design. The EUDOC program reproduced 161 small-molecule complex crystal structures accurately, and the authors proposed expanding its use to supramolecular chemistry.

Reproducing known answers is how a prediction tool earns trust; 161 successes is a serious benchmark. Supramolecular chemistry, the chemistry of molecules binding each other, uses the same fitting logic beyond drugs. A validated program serves both fields, and papers like this are the receipts.
plos-pone-0000631:
Elías Barquero-Calvo, Esteban Chaves-Olarte, David S. Weiss and co-authors explored how Brucella abortus slips past first-line defenses, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Brucella causes brucellosis and can set up chronic, long-lasting infections. The question was how it manages that at the very start of infection.

The team found the bacterium did not trigger proinflammatory responses early on. White blood cells were not recruited, and blood showed no humoral or cellular changes. In short, the innate immune system barely noticed its arrival. That stealth at the onset helps explain how Brucella gains the foothold it needs to persist.
plos-pone-0000731:
Ana Hrus, Gordon Lau, Harald Hutter and colleagues characterized the worm version of a junction protein, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Agrin is a basement membrane protein crucial for building and maintaining the neuromuscular junction in vertebrates, where nerves meet muscle. The C. elegans genome harbors a candidate agrin gene, agr-1. The team cloned its cDNA to determine the protein's structure and where it is expressed.

Their title reports expression in the pharynx, in IL1 neurons, and in distal tip cells. It also reports a negative: worm agrin does not genetically interact with genes for synaptogenesis or muscle function. A clear negative result steers the field away from assuming the worm protein does the vertebrate job.
plos-pone-0000831:
Bruce E. Deagle, Nick J. Gales, Karen Evans and co-authors read penguin menus from droppings instead of stomachs. The usual way to study seabird diet is to flush the stomach and sort what comes up. That is hard on the birds, and hard to arrange on remote islands. The team tested DNA-based analysis of faeces as a kinder route, in a study in PLOS ONE in 2007.

Their test case was macaroni penguins raising chicks. DNA in droppings can name prey that digestion would else hide. If the method works, scientists can sample often, across whole colonies, without handling a single bird. Diet data of that depth feed straight into fishery and wildlife choices in the far south seas.
plos-pone-0000931:
Daniel Kelley, Richard Davidson, Jamie Elliott and colleagues found a key signaling chain altered in fragile X syndrome, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Fragile X is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and autism. It comes from a repeat expansion in the fmr1 gene, which lowers a protein the brain needs.

The team focused on the cyclic AMP cascade, a relay that helps nerve cells respond and adapt. Their report says the relay runs differently in the fragile X nervous system. A defined chemical fault gives drug research something concrete to aim at. It also helps explain how one gene change can ripple across learning and behavior.
plos-pone-0001031:
Maja Adamska, Sandie Degnan, Kathryn Green and colleagues found embryo patterning signals at work in a sponge, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Animal development rests on cells sticking together, signaling and cooperating. Sponges sit at the base of the animal tree, so their toolkits hint at what the first animals had.

The team report expression of Wnt and TGF-beta signals in the sponge Amphimedon queenslandica. Both families guide embryonic patterning in later animals. Finding them active in a sponge embryo pushes the origin of patterning to the very start of animal life. The work gives the deep root of development a concrete gene list.
plos-pone-0001131:
A healthy brain notices when a pattern breaks, even when nobody is paying attention. Erich Schröger and colleagues studied that ability in hearing for a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their brain recordings show that violations of abstract sound rules are processed even when the sounds are ignored.

The team tested rules that go beyond single tones, such as patterns spanning several sounds. Subjects did another task while the sounds played, yet their brains still registered rule-breaking events. Encoding rules and catching violations outside focused attention is vital for adaptive behavior. As the authors note, it lets an organism react to change without watching for it.
plos-pone-0001231:
Biologists increasingly struggle to agree on what a gene is. Evelyn Fox Keller and David Harel take up that disarray in a 2007 PLOS ONE article titled Beyond the Gene. The classical concept, a neat stretch of DNA coding for one product, has been eroded by decades of findings.

After reviewing the problems, the authors propose an alternative to both the concept and the word. Their essay is a piece of conceptual analysis rather than an experiment. It matters because how scientists define the gene shapes how genomes are annotated, taught, and discussed in public.
plos-pone-0001331:
Theiler's virus is a mouse picornavirus that infects neurons and, unusually, passes from their axons into the surrounding myelin sheath. Jean-Pierre Roussarie and colleagues studied that transfer in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Earlier work had shown the virus trafficking from the axon of infected neurons into myelin.

When this traffic is interrupted, as in the shiverer mouse, which carries a mutation in the myelin basic protein gene, the infection's course changes. The authors examine axon-to-myelin transfer of a non-enveloped virus, a route without obvious machinery. Theiler's virus is also a model for multiple sclerosis, which gives the work a second audience.
plos-pone-0001431:
Joan Company and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on climate and life in the deep sea. Life on the deep floor was thought to live on scraps that sink from the sunlit zone. Side flow of scraps from land edges may matter too, but was less known. The team tracked deep sea numbers against climate shifts.

They found that climate swings shape deep populations in a clear way. Shifts in wind and rain change the flow of food to the depths. That link makes deep life less cut off from the world above than once thought. It also means climate change may reach the deep sea faster than expected.
plos-pone-0001531:
Antonio Pacheco and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on causes of death in HIV patients in Brazil. Brazil was the first developing land to give free HIV drugs to all in 1996. Deaths fell, but how the mix of causes shifted was not logged. The team assessed death records in the drug era.

They found a rise in deaths from ills not tied to AIDS itself. As HIV care lets people live longer, heart, liver, and other ills take a larger share. Care plans must thus widen past HIV alone. The study marks a shift in what clinics in Brazil now most need.
plos-pone-0001631:
Jason R. Gerstner, Quentin Z. Bremer, William M. Vander Heyden, and their co-authors tracked a brain protein across the day in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The protein is Fabp7, short for brain fatty acid binding protein. It plays a role in early growth of the nervous system. In adult brain it is found in support cells called astrocytes and in young nerve cell precursors.

The team reports that levels of the Fabp7 gene's message in adult mouse brain rise and fall over a 24-hour cycle. A related protein, Fabp5, does not show the same pattern. The full text gives the time-course data from the hippocampus and other brain areas. Daily rhythms in brain support cells may shape how the brain handles fats, sleep, and the birth of new nerve cells.
plos-pone-0001731:
Ying Yu and co-authors measured DNA methylation in chickens bred to resist or suffer tumors, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Chickens carry inherited endogenous viruses called ALVE, retrovirus-like elements built into their DNA. These elements correlate negatively with disease resistance, and changes in methylation, chemical tags that silence DNA, may affect susceptibility to neoplastic disease.

The team quantified methylation patterns for the ALVE and TVB genes in susceptible and resistant chicken lines. The full text gives the measurement method and the pattern differences between the lines. Methylation differences that track with resistance could become markers for breeding healthier flocks, and a model for how silent virus copies influence cancer risk.
plos-pone-0001831:
Sune Frankild, Rob J. de Boer, Ole Lund, and their co-authors modeled T cell cross-reactivity in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Cytotoxic T cell cross-reactivity is believed pivotal for immune responses. In it, one T cell responds to several different peptides, but its extent and mechanisms were largely unknown. Some studies suggested T cell clones recognize highly diverse peptides, some sharing no obvious similarity.

The team argues that amino acid similarity accounts for cross-reactivity and for 'holes' in the T cell repertoire, targets no T cell can see. The full text gives the model and its tests. Explaining both phenomena with one measure helps vaccine design, since a vaccine peptide must fall inside the repertoire.
plos-pone-0001931:
Brian Slaughter and co-authors watched protein parts link up inside living cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The parts are SAM domains, small units found in proteins from yeast to humans. They let proteins stick to each other, in pairs or in larger groups, for tasks from signal relay to RNA binding.

Faults in SAM domains can cause disease, so how they group matters. The team used a glow-based method that tracks tiny shifts in living cells to see grouping as it happens. Seeing groups form in real time, rather than in dead extracts, gives a truer view of how these units work in health and in illness.
plos-pone-0002031:
Stephane Cauchi and co-authors followed up genome scans for type 2 diabetes genes, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Large genome-wide association studies in European groups had lately found and confirmed new gene variants tied to the illness. The team asked whether those markers hold in other European and non-European groups.

They also tested whether variants interact, so that pairs of genes raise risk more than each alone. As the title states, they found gene-gene interaction and high predictive value in the follow-up. Strong joint effects hint that risk scores built from many variants may one day flag diabetes early.
plos-pone-0002131:
Janet May and co-authors studied a herpesvirus protein in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. They used a mouse virus as a stand-in for its human kin. Murid herpesvirus 4 is a gamma-herpesvirus that is easy to work with in the lab. Its glycoprotein M spans the virus membrane. It is one of only four such proteins the virus cannot do without when it copies itself.

The authors tested which end of the protein does the key work. They found that the near end of its inner tail is vital for infection, while the far end is not. Small details like these help explain how herpesviruses build new copies of themselves.
plos-pone-0002231:
Liqun Jiang, Mingyi Wang, Jing Zhang, and co-authors studied an enzyme that may drive artery aging, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. As arteries age, their smooth muscle cells migrate more and the vessel wall takes on inflamed traits. Signals from angiotensin II, a hormone that tightens blood vessels, are part of that change, including the switch-on of a matrix-cutting enzyme, MMP2.

The team reports that activity of the enzyme calpain-1 rises in aging aortas and mediates the angiotensin signal in these muscle cells. Naming the middleman in age-linked vessel change points to a fresh place where drugs might slow arterial aging.
plos-pone-0002331:
Melanie Massaro, Amanda Starling-Windhof, and James Briskie watched a New Zealand bird, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. It changed how it cares for its young after foreign predators arrived. Introduced mammals have driven many island birds to extinction. Survivors might be expected to evolve habits that lower the new predation risk, but whether island birds can respond fast enough was untested.

The team studied parental care in an endemic bird living with introduced mammalian predators. Parents adjusted their behavior in ways that reduce danger at the nest. Evidence of a rapid behavioral answer matters for conservation: it shows some native birds can adapt their habits even when evolution has had little time.
plos-pone-0002431:
Townsend led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Simon W. Townsend, Tobias Deschner, Klaus Zuberbühler, among others. Its subject is female Chimpanzees Use Copulation Calls Flexibly to Prevent Social Competition. The adaptive function of copulation calls in female primates has been debated for years.

One influential idea is that copulation calls are a sexually selected trait, which enables females to advertise their receptive state to males. The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002531:
Lee and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Dong W. Lee, Michael Freitag, Eric U. Selker, among others. Its subject is a Cytosine Methyltransferase Homologue Is Essential for Sexual Development in Aspergillus nidulans. The genome defense processes RIP (repeat-induced point mutation) in the filamentous fungus Neurospora crassa.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002631:
Stefan Koelsch and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was effects of unexpected chords and of performer's expression on brain responses and electrodermal activity. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Stefan Koelsch, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. There is lack of neuroscientific studies investigating music processing with naturalistic stimuli, and brain responses to real music are, thus, largely unknown. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002731:
Elin B. Begley and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was willingness of men who have sex with men (MSM) in the united states to be circumcised as adults to reduce the risk of HIV infection. The catalog record names Elin B. Begley first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Circumcision reduces HIV acquisition among heterosexual men in Africa. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002831:
Joseph Ahlander and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was the N-Terminal domain of the drosophila retinoblastoma protein rbf1 interacts with ORC and associates with chromatin in an E2F independent manner. Authorship is credited in the record to Joseph Ahlander and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. The retinoblastoma (Rb) tumor suppressor protein can function as a DNA replication inhibitor as well as a transcription factor. It goes on to note a further point. Regulation of DNA replication may occur through interaction of Rb with the origin recognition complex (ORC). The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002931:
R. Alexander Pyron, Frank Burbrink and Timothy Guiher challenged warnings about invasive pythons spreading across the United States in 2008. A geological survey report had suggested Burmese pythons in the Everglades could spread widely where climate suits them. Warming trends were said to widen that range further.

Using ecological niche models, which map where climate fits a species, the authors found the claims contradicted. Their models pointed to a far smaller suitable area. Published in PLOS ONE, the dispute shows how choice of model can swing invasion forecasts, and why managers should check the method behind a headline.
plos-pone-0003031:
Fuli Wang, Elvira Grigorieva, Jingfeng Li and co-authors tested two candidate tumor suppressor genes in 2008. The team had mapped two regions on chromosome 3, called LUCA and AP20, that are often lost in lung, breast, and other cancers. Each region seemed to hold several suppressor genes.

Two of them, HYAL1 and HYAL2, inhibited tumor growth in living animals but not in lab dishes, per the title. That contrast is the lesson: dish tests alone can miss suppressors that need a whole tissue setting. Published in PLOS ONE, the genes stay on the suppressor list.
plos-pone-0003131:
Yanchun Li, Cintia M. Coelho, Tian Liu and colleagues present a statistical model for seed growth in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A seed grows well only when its three parts signal to each other in a coordinated way. One part is the mother's outer layer, and the other two are the embryo and the tissue that feeds it.

Their model estimates how mother and offspring interact, and how parent-of-origin effects act at gene sites that shape seed traits. Readers get a formal tool for a hard genetics problem. Plant breeders and geneticists can use it to separate effects that are often tangled together.
plos-pone-0003231:
Kenji Hashimoto, Shingo Nishiyama, Hiroyuki Ohba and colleagues test a brain imaging ligand in monkeys in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The alpha7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors play an important role in the pathophysiology of neuropsychiatric diseases such as schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease. However, no positron emission tomography, or PET, tracer fit for imaging those receptors existed at that time.

The team test a compound called [11C]CHIBA-1001 as a novel PET ligand for alpha7 receptors in conscious monkeys. Readers get an early check of a brain scan tool. A working ligand would let doctors watch a key receptor in living patients.
plos-pone-0003331:
Christine Moussion, Nathalie Ortega and Jean-Philippe Girard locate a cytokine in normal tissues in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Interleukin-33 is an IL-1-like cytokine ligand for the IL-1 receptor-related protein ST2, which activates mast cells and Th2 lymphocytes and induces production of Th2-associated cytokines in vivo. The team initially discovered IL-33 as a nuclear factor abundantly expressed in certain cells.

The title reports that IL-33 is constitutively expressed in the nucleus of endothelial and epithelial cells in vivo, and asks whether it is a novel alarmin. Readers see a stored signal waiting in barrier tissues. An alarmin role would make IL-33 a first alert of tissue damage.
plos-pone-0003431:
David A. Shoham and colleagues linked sugary soda to a kidney warning sign in this 2008 study. Kidney failure rates rose after high fructose corn syrup spread through American food. Soda sweetened with sugar is a main source of fructose. The team used a large national health survey from 1999 to 2004.

They looked for albuminuria, protein leaking into urine, an early sign of kidney damage. Soda intake and that warning sign moved together in the data. The link was statistical, from survey records, not a trial. Still, it adds weight to concerns about fructose and kidney health.
plos-pone-0003531:
Gabriela Durcova-Hills and co-authors turned germ cells back into stem cells in this 2008 paper. Primordial germ cells are the early source of eggs and sperm. They begin as flexible epiblast cells, then lock into the germ line. A complex with Blimp1 helps set and keep that locked state.

Yet germ cells can be induced to reopen their options. The team reprogrammed them into pluripotent stem cells. Such cells can form many body tissues, not just gametes. The conversion offers a new route to versatile lab stem cells. Stem cells from germ lines may dodge some of the moral debates over embryos.
plos-pone-0003631:
René C. W. Mandl, Hugo G. Schnack, Marcel P. Zwiers, and colleagues published this brain imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Standard scans show which gray matter areas switch on during a task. They say little about activity along the white matter tracts that link those areas.

The team measured changes in fractional anisotropy, a sign of how water moves along nerve fibers, while people did tasks. Those changes tracked activity along the tracts themselves. The method, called functional diffusion tensor imaging, opens a way to watch the brain's wiring at work, not just its hubs.
plos-pone-0003731:
John P. Norman, Seth W. Perry, Holly M. Reynolds, and colleagues published this brain study in PLOS ONE in 2008. HIV-1 causes neurologic disease that modern drug therapy cannot fully cure. The virus is never fully cleared from the central nervous system, and normal neural signaling gets disrupted there.

The team studied Tat, a protein the virus makes, in neurons. Tat switched on ryanodine receptors, releasing calcium inside the cells. That set off the unfolded protein response and pushed mitochondria into an abnormal state, a chain that helps explain lasting brain injury in HIV.
plos-pone-0003831:
Susanne Hartmann, John H. Missimer, Cornelia Stoeckel, and colleagues published this brain imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Telling objects apart by touch is an essential human skill. It relies on communication between motor, touch, and higher-order brain areas. Such spread-out networks are hard to study with simple subtraction methods.

The team used principal component analysis on fMRI data from a tactile discrimination task. That approach extracts the connected patterns behind performance. Their analysis shows tactile knowing as a conversation across the brain, not the job of a single touch area.
plos-pone-0003931:
Elise Drouyer, Ouria Dkhissi-Benyahya, Christophe Chiquet, and co-authors studied glaucoma and the body clock in 2008. Glaucoma is a common eye disease and a major cause of blindness. It slowly destroys the optic nerve and the retinal cells that feed it. Most study had focused on vision loss itself.

Their PLOS ONE article asks what the disease does to daily timing. Retinal cells also send light signals that set the circadian clock. Damage to them could disturb sleep and daily rhythms in patients. The work widens glaucoma care beyond eyesight alone. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004031:
Caterina I. Fanello, Corine Karema, Pamela Avellino, and co-authors flagged a malaria drug risk in 2008. G6PD deficiency is the most common inherited enzyme defect in humans. It gives some protection against malaria itself. It also makes red cells break down under oxidant drugs.

Their PLOS ONE article reports high risk of severe anemia after one drug mix. The mix was chlorproguanil-dapsone plus artesunate. Patients carrying the G6PD A- variant faced the danger. The warning argues for screening or drug choice changes in such patients. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004131:
Jung Joo Hong and colleagues published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. CD8 T cells are white blood cells that help control viral infections. The team wanted to know exactly where virus-specific T cells sit inside the tissues of monkeys infected with SIV, the monkey form of HIV.

Using MHC class I tetramers, lab tools that tag T cells matching a chosen virus piece, they mapped the cells in lymph and genital tissues. They found distinct local groups of these T cells, including some with low CD8 levels, inside lymphoid follicles and the genital lining. Knowing where the cells gather helps explain how the body fights the virus at its entry points.
plos-pone-0004231:
Roxane Chiori and colleagues published this evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Hox genes pattern the body along its head-to-tail axis in most animals. How early they took on that role, and whether the Hox and ParaHox clusters began before two-sided animals existed, has been hotly debated.

The team studied the hydrozoan jellyfish Clytia hemisphaerica, a cnidarian from a lineage that split off early. They present evidence on whether its Hox genes are involved in axial patterning. A patterning role in such an animal would push the job's origin deep into animal history.
plos-pone-0004331:
Alessandro Bartolomucci and colleagues published this obesity study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Social and psychological factors interact with genes and diet in determining obesity, yet few pre-clinical studies address psychosocial factors in metabolic disorders. The team's own earlier work in male mice had shown chronic social stress changing body weight.

Here they examined the metabolic consequences of that stress and the mice's vulnerability to diet-induced obesity. Stressed males facing rich food model a very human situation. The study asks whether social defeat makes the body store fat differently, before any new drug is considered.
plos-pone-0004431:
Plague bacteria disarm immune cells with a weapon called YopH. Maria Luisa de la Puerta, Antonio Trinidad, Maria del Carmen Rodriguez, and co-authors mapped more of its targets in PLOS ONE in 2009. YopH is an enzyme of a class called tyrosine phosphatases, and it is among the most active known. The plague bacterium Yersinia pestis needs it to cause disease.

YopH works by cutting signal chains inside immune cells, which blunts the body's defense. Only a few of its target proteins had been described before. The team set out to characterize new targets and show how the enzyme acts on them. Each new target adds detail to the picture of how plague shuts down immunity, and where drugs might step in.
plos-pone-0004531:
Breast tumors grow in different soil in African-American and European-American patients, report Damali Martin, Brenda Boersma, Ming Yi, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. African-American patients die of breast cancer at higher rates than European-American patients, even though they get the disease less often. The team tested whether intrinsic differences in tumor biology help explain that gap.

They focused on the tumor microenvironment, the mix of cells and signals around the cancer itself. Using tumor samples from both groups, they looked for differences in that surroundings. Biology is only one part of a health disparity that also involves care and access. But if the soil differs, treatments and screening plans may need to account for it.
plos-pone-0004631:
How white blood cells force tumor cells into an unusual form of death is dissected by Neil Hoa, Michael Myers, Thomas Douglass, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The death pathway is paraptosis, a programmed cell death that leads to cellular necrosis. Earlier, the team had shown that monocytes and macrophages kill glioma cells bearing a surface factor through paraptosis, but the molecular mechanism was unknown.

Here they work out the mechanisms of paraptosis induction. The aim reaches beyond mechanism: they discuss implications for a non-genetically modified tumor vaccine. If the body's own killer cells can be prompted to use this pathway, tumors might be attacked without engineering the patient. The paper links a cell death curiosity to a practical cancer strategy.
plos-pone-0004731:
Philippe Ravassard and colleagues offered a new way to make working insulin producing cell lines, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Human cell lines help study cell life and screen drugs and toxins. They may also serve in future cell therapy, yet working human beta cell lines are very scarce.

Beta cells in the pancreas make insulin, and their loss causes diabetes. The team moved genes into early pancreas cells to grow lines that still make insulin well. Good lines would speed drug tests and diabetes research. They could also form a base for cell based care one day.
plos-pone-0004831:
Amanda Wilson and colleagues reported that media reporting of health interventions shows signs of improvement but major problems persist, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Studies persistently show deficiencies in medical reporting by mainstream media. The team monitored accuracy and comprehensiveness of medical news in Australia since mid 2004. Analyzing more than a thousand stories across print, television, and online outlets.

Comparison over time reveals modest gains alongside gaps. Benefits are overstated and harms understated too often. Better reporting helps public decisions about treatments. Journalists need accessible expert sources. Future studies can use these results to refine both methods and theory. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0004931:
Inside each cell, sensor proteins called Nod-like receptors watch for invading germs. When they detect trouble, they recruit helper proteins. Those helpers process alarm chemicals and switch on immune genes. Roland Wagner and co-authors mapped part of this system in PLOS ONE in 2009. They studied how the receptors' effector domains interact.

Effector domains are the plugs and sockets of the inner alarm network. By testing which domains bind which partners, the team charted the wiring. The chart links detection to response step by step. It helps researchers understand immune signaling. It may also reveal points where future drugs could adjust that signaling.
plos-pone-0005031:
Furin is a protein-cutting enzyme. It is born with a safety lock, an extra piece called a prodomain. The lock blocks its own cutting site. Katarzyna Gawlik and colleagues detailed the unlocking in PLOS ONE in 2009. Furin must cut off its prodomain itself. That self-activation is called autocatalytic.

The study shows activation needs one more step. The emerging enzyme's N-terminus must leave the active site. Only then can furin act on other proteins. The work reveals the exact order of the self-unlocking. Many protein-cutting enzymes share this kind of birth. Understanding furin's version helps explain the whole family.
plos-pone-0005131:
Radiation breaks DNA strands. Double-strand breaks are emergencies for the cell. A protein called ATM detects them and sounds the alarm. Kazunari Mouri and colleagues modeled that detection mathematically in PLOS ONE in 2009. ATM tags itself with phosphates when breaks appear. That autophosphorylation is the detection signal.

Their model follows breaks, repair proteins and the complexes they form. It reproduces how ATM's self-tagging reports break numbers. The model captures detection logic in equations. Such models turn a molecular alarm into predictable math. They can be tested against experiments and refined. Understanding break detection matters for cancer and radiation medicine. Cells that misread breaks can turn malignant.
plos-pone-0005231:
Tumor suppressor genes help keep cell growth in check, and cancers often disable them. Kashuba and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 that two such genes, RASSF1 and RBSP3, change at unusually high rates in cancer. RBSP3 is also known by the name CTDSPL.

Cancer cells carry many kinds of gene damage, from single-letter changes to lost chunks. A high mutation rate in guard genes can speed a tumor's growth and spread. Flagging these fragile guards helps explain tumor behavior and may point to markers worth testing in patients.
plos-pone-0005331:
Photosynthetic cells make oxygen, which can damage the very machinery that produces it. Flavodiiron proteins help bacteria and archaea detoxify oxygen and nitric oxide. Zhang and colleagues asked what these proteins do in cyanobacteria, reported in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Cyanobacterial versions carry an extra domain compared with other forms. Two of them, Flv2 and Flv4, protect photosystem II, a core part of the light machinery, in the species Synechocystis. Guarding that machinery keeps photosynthesis running under bright, stressful light. Green cells that guard their own light gear can keep making food in bright sun. Crop science would love to copy that trait into plants that feed the world at large scale.
plos-pone-0005431:
Jon Dobson and co-authors raised a safety question about strong MRI scanners in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. MRI machines are now common in hospitals, and the strongest types are used more and more. At the same time, European rules were moving to limit how much time staff spend near high fields.

The team asked whether strong magnetic fields could pull on tiny iron oxide particles that occur in the human body. They weighed the forces involved and what they could mean for health. Their work helps set safe limits for patients and for staff who work near scanners every day.
plos-pone-0005531:
Shanmugalakshmi Sadagopal and co-authors worked on improving the tuberculosis vaccine in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The BCG vaccine once protected strongly against lung tuberculosis in early trials. Its protection has faded in many places, though it still guards young children against the worst forms.

The team weakened the vaccine germ's own defences against oxygen damage, both in output and release. A vaccine germ that defends itself less may provoke a stronger immune response. The hope is a BCG strain that protects adults against lung disease as well as the old one once did.
plos-pone-0005631:
François Casas and co-authors studied a thyroid hormone receptor in muscle in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. A form of the thyroid hormone receptor sits inside mitochondria, the cell's energy centres, and boosts their activity. The team had shown earlier that it raises both mitochondria numbers and their gene activity.

When the receptor was overproduced in mouse skeletal muscle, the muscle wasted as the animals aged. More energy machinery did not mean stronger muscle. The surprising harm warns that hormone paths in mitochondria need careful balance. Thyroid hormone paths are tempting drug targets in aging muscle, and this result urges caution with them.
plos-pone-0005731:
Mazen Habayeb, Jens-Ola Ekström, and Dan Hultmark reported in 2009 that a lasting virus infection in fruit flies slips past the flies' main antiviral weapon. Fruit flies are a key model for innate immunity, the built-in first line of defense. But lasting virus infections in flies were barely studied.

The virus, called Nora virus, sets up a quiet, persistent infection. The team found the RNA interference machinery, normally a strong virus killer, does not curb it. That gap raises the question of what, if anything, keeps such viruses in check. The answer may reshape views of insect immunity.
plos-pone-0005931:
Airborne diseases spread through everyday meetings between people. Mirjam Kretzschmar and Rafael Mikolajczyk set out in 2009 to map those meetings across eight European countries for PLOS ONE. Their study records who meets whom, how often, and how contact rates differ by age and place.

Such contact profiles feed the math models used to forecast epidemics. Better maps of mixing mean better guesses about how fast a flu-like illness will move and whom it will hit first. The eight-country data give modelers a shared base, and they show that contact habits are a core part of public health planning.
plos-pone-0006031:
In lupus, the immune system attacks the body's own tissues, and the kidneys often take the hit. Kenneth Scalapino and David Daikh tested a cell-based calm-down in lupus-prone mice in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper transfers regulatory T cells, grown and expanded outside the body, into mice of the NZB/NZW strain, whose kidneys inflame as lupus advances.

The title reports success: the transferred cells suppressed glomerulonephritis, the kidney inflammation that can end in organ failure. Lab-grown peacekeeper cells thus hold promise as a treatment, not just a lab curiosity. The study supports a path where a patient's own regulatory cells are grown in number and returned to quiet the attack.
plos-pone-0006131:
Electric fields run quietly through healing tissue, and cells can steer by them. Nurdan Özkucur, Thomas Monsees, Srikanth Perike and colleagues watched the first steps of that steering in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies osteoblast-like cells, bone-building cells, under direct current electric fields, which are known to induce directional migration in development and regeneration.

Local calcium rises and cell elongation come first, launching the guided motility, the title reports. Knowing the opening moves tells engineers which signals to amplify in a healing scaffold. The work links a physical cue to a chemical one, calcium, that cell biology already knows how to measure and tune.
plos-pone-0006231:
Simple repeated DNA stretches offer a clean window on how selection shapes genomes. Andrew Dalby compared those repeats across malaria parasites, the plasmodia, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Repeats inside coding regions change the proteins themselves, so their effects show up directly in the organism.

Protein surveys revealed that different parasite lineages favour different amino acid repeats. That lineage-specific pattern bears the mark of selection, not random drift alone. Reading the repeats helps trace how malaria parasites diverged. It may also flag protein regions that matter for survival, and thus for drug or vaccine work.
plos-pone-0006331:
A yeast phosphatase system that drives cell division has close counterparts in human cells. Helena Morales-Johansson and colleagues swapped human parts into budding yeast in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. In yeast, the phosphatase Sit4 and four Sap partners mediate cell cycle progression and signals from the TOR growth cascade.

Human PP6 regulatory subunits provided Sap function that depended on Sit4 and stayed sensitive to rapamycin, an TOR-blocking drug. Cross-species rescue shows deep conservation of the machinery. It also gives a simple yeast testbed for studying human phosphatase parts.
plos-pone-0006431:
Georgette Stern, Julia Beel, Béla Suki, and co-authors tracked body temperature in healthy babies for a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Breathing, heart rate, and temperature control are linked in infants. Unstable temperature control can add to breathing pauses and even life-threatening events. Spotting such problems matters most in the first six months of life.

The team studied rectal temperature swings as babies mature. They looked for long-range patterns in the ups and downs over time. Patterns like these can reveal how control systems are developing. The work may help clinicians tell normal variation from early warning signs in young infants.
plos-pone-0006531:
Christophe Carnoy and Claude-Alain Roten reviewed chromosome resolution systems in bacteria for PLOS ONE in 2009. In E. coli, a share of growing bacteria produce dimeric chromosomes during DNA replication. Two joined copies result when recombination crosses the wrong way. These dimers are resolved by XerC and XerD, two tyrosine recombinases that target a site called dif.

Without resolution, cells cannot divide their DNA properly. The authors survey the dif/Xer recombination systems across Proteobacteria, a large bacterial group. Comparing systems shows which parts are universal and which vary. That knowledge feeds both basic microbiology and efforts to disrupt bacterial growth.
plos-pone-0006631:
Jeremiah Bernier-Latmani, Alessandra Baumer, and Phillip Shaw tested a candidate gene in Silver-Russell syndrome in PLOS ONE in 2009. Silver-Russell syndrome is a genetically and clinically heterogeneous disease of growth restriction. Although no protein coding gene defects had been reported in patients, about half of cases involve imprinting control regions. The team looked at the CTCFL/BORIS gene in patients with IGF2/H19 imprinting defects.

Their title states the result: no evidence for mutations of CTCFL/BORIS in these patients. Excluding a strong candidate focuses the search on other regulators of imprinting. Negative genetic results are essential for accurate counseling.
plos-pone-0006731:
Akihiko Mougi and Kinya Nishimura modeled how invasion order shapes evolution in a food web in PLOS ONE in 2009. Experiments had shown that invasion history matters for communities. Species arriving earlier can steer how later species evolve. Few theory studies had focused on that history effect. The authors built a model with three feeding levels.

Their tri-trophic food web tracks predators, prey, and their food. Species invade in sequence, and coevolution follows each arrival. Different arrival orders produced different evolutionary outcomes. The model shows history is not a detail but a driver. That insight helps interpret real invasions and community assembly in nature.
plos-pone-0006831:
Alexander Samoshkin and his team showed that a packing crew for chromosomes is a must at the centromere in PLOS ONE in 2009. The crew is condensin, which coils chromosomes tight for cell division. Man and most backboned beasts have two forms of it. Take the crew away, and the centromere, the chromosome's waist, goes wrong. Why that link holds was not known.

The team cut condensin down in human cells. The waist of the chromosome then failed to form right. The twin grips that haul chromosomes apart also aimed the wrong way. Bad aiming can send chromosomes to the wrong side. Such faults can drive disease and failed growth.
plos-pone-0006931:
Kristi Bennett, Todd Romigh, and Charis Eng examined a cancer-linked protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein, AP-2α, takes part in many normal body processes. Its levels rise as several squamous cell cancers progress. Earlier work found it overexpressed in roughly seven in ten head and neck squamous cell carcinomas.

The authors link that excess to the silencing of tumor suppressive genes. They describe silencing done by epigenetic means, which switch genes off without changing the code. They also connect AP-2α with microsatellite instability in these tumors. The work suggests a route by which one protein helps this cancer grow.
plos-pone-0007031:
Guang-Hui Liu and Larry Gerace studied a fat-processing protein in nerve cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Lipin-1 does two jobs in the cell. It works as an enzyme in fat metabolism, and it acts in the nucleus as a gene coactivator. How its move into the nucleus is controlled was unknown.

The pair showed that a small tag, called sumoylation, regulates that location. Adding the tag shifted where lipin-1α sits in neuronal cells. Location decides which of its two jobs the protein performs. The result links a tagging system to both metabolism and gene control.
plos-pone-0007131:
Ya-Lan Guo, Dan-Qing Liu, Zhen Bian, and colleagues studied platelet loss in a foodborne infection in PLOS ONE in 2009. Shiga toxin producing E. coli can cause hemolytic uremic syndrome. Platelet depletion is a key feature of that syndrome. Why platelets vanish was not fully understood.

Working with the O157:H7 strain, the team tracked a platelet surface protein called CD47. Its levels fell during infection-induced platelet loss. This first demonstration names a concrete change on the platelet surface. That change may mark platelets for removal, and blocking it could protect patients.
plos-pone-0007231: Ludmila Prokunina-Olsson, Lee M. Kaplan, Eric E. Schadt, and colleagues wrote a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on a diabetes-linked gene. The gene is TCF7L2, one of the strongest known genetic links to type 2 diabetes. Their study concerns alternative splicing, where one gene yields several different message forms. They compare those forms in two fat depots, omental fat inside the abdomen and subcutaneous fat under the skin, and relate the patterns to diabetes risk.
plos-pone-0007331:
Jeffrey A. Wilson, Claudia A. Marsicano, and Roger M. H. Smith reinvestigated an early dinosaur tracksite in Lesotho in 2009. The Moyeni tracksite dates to the Early Jurassic. It preserves tracks on an ancient point bar, a river deposit with varied sediment that recorded dinosaur movement in unusual detail.

The authors combine sedimentology and ichnology, the study of tracks. They draw new insights into behavior and locomotor dynamics of early dinosaurs. Trackways show how these animals moved and turned at different speeds. Their PLOS ONE work extracts dynamic capabilities from footprints rather than from bones alone.
plos-pone-0007431:
Haleh Yasrebi and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on predicting cancer survival from gene activity data. Profiling which genes are switched on in a tumor biopsy is now common in clinical research. Machine learning tools can search such data for patterns tied to patient outcomes. The team asked whether combining several data sets improves those predictions.

Single studies are often small, which limits what their models can learn. Merging gene expression data sets gives the algorithms more patients to learn from. The authors tested whether the merged forecasts actually held up better than single-study ones. Their work speaks to a practical problem in cancer research. Combining data promises stronger predictions, but only if the combined signal stays reliable.
plos-pone-0007531:
Corina Hayano-Kanashiro and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how Mexican maize landraces cope with drought. Dry spells are one of the top limits on crop yields around the world. Landraces are the old local corn types, kept by farmers for many years. They carry mixed ways of handling thirst. The team read gene activity in three landraces while water was withheld, then again after the plants were watered.

Gene activity shifted in clear patterns as water ran out and then came back. Types that bear drought well answered in ways the weak types did not. Watching the recovery matters too, since to live through drought a plant must restart growth. These gene maps are raw stock for plant breeders. Corn that stands up to dry spells is prized as the climate dries. The study reads that know-how straight from old Mexican corn.
plos-pone-0007631:
Alberto Riva and Graziano Pesole published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on a naming problem in genetics. Through alternative splicing, one gene can produce many transcript variants. Research keeps showing how fundamental that variety is in higher organisms. Yet there was no standardized, consistent, unique identifier for each variant. Databases and papers name them in clashing ways. The authors propose a system to fix that.

A unique, stable identifier would let every study point at exactly the same variant. Confusion in databases slows research and breeds errors. Shared naming is unglamorous infrastructure, but science runs on it. The proposal aims at consistency across genomes and over time. If adopted, splicing research gains a common language. The paper is a plea, with a working scheme attached.
plos-pone-0007731:
Angelo Gamez-Pozo and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It uses protein profiling to sort human lung cancer into subtypes. Knowing a tumor's subtype guides treatment choices. A method called MALDI mass spectrometry can read protein patterns from tissue quickly.

The hard part is that raw samples mix many cell types. The authors worked out a profiling approach that copes with that mix. Their patterns separated lung cancer subtypes from each other. Reliable protein fingerprints could one day help doctors classify tumors from small samples. That would support faster, more personal cancer care.
plos-pone-0007831:
Patrick Kiefer and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It explains why adding a plasmid can slow a bacterium's growth. Plasmids are small DNA circles that labs insert into cells. Cells carrying them often grow more slowly, for unclear reasons.

The test bacterium, Methylobacterium extorquens, lost about half its growth rate. The team profiled the cell's metabolites to find the bottleneck. Carrying the plasmid left the cells short of cobalt, a needed trace metal. Profiling chemistry inside the cell exposed a hidden cost. Such knowledge helps engineers design hardier industrial microbes.
plos-pone-0007931:
Antje Willuweit and colleagues built a new mouse model of Alzheimer's disease and described it in PLOS ONE in 2009. The mice carry changed forms of two genes tied to the disease, in both copies rather than one. Older models often grew brain plaques slowly or unevenly.

In these mice, amyloid plaques, the sticky clumps that mark the disease, formed early and in force. That speed and strength make the model handy for lab work. Drug ideas can be tried sooner and judged on clearer results, which may speed the search for treatments that slow the human illness.
plos-pone-0008031:
Srinagesh Koushik and colleagues caught light energy moving in an odd way between glowing molecules in PLOS ONE in 2009. The process, called FRET, passes energy from a lit donor molecule to a nearby acceptor without light escaping. Standard theory treats one donor and one acceptor at a time.

With several acceptors in range, the team measured more energy transfer than theory allows. Real samples crowd molecules together, so the gap matters. FRET is widely used as a ruler for tiny distances inside cells; if the ruler bends in crowds, many past readings need a second look.
plos-pone-0008131:
Elena Izquierdo and colleagues watched what anti-TNF therapy does to blood vessels in arthritic joints in PLOS ONE in 2009. Rheumatoid arthritis feeds on new vessel growth in the joint lining, which brings in more inflammatory cells. Young vessels in such tissue are often leaky and unfinished.

After anti-TNF treatment, the unfinished vessels were the ones that vanished, while mature vessels stayed. Pruning the leaky supply lines may be part of how the drug calms the joint. The selective loss also gives doctors a tissue sign that the therapy is working as hoped.
plos-pone-0008231:
Michael L. Robbins and colleagues studied a maize color gene in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. The pericarp color1 gene controls brick-red pigments called phlobaphenes. It encodes a myb-like protein that regulates pigment production. Color patterns on the kernel coat and cob depend on which gene versions a plant carries. Some versions show patchy, tissue-specific patterns.

The team traced those patterns to epigenetic changes driven by gene structure. Gene shape itself influenced how the gene was silenced or expressed. The result is mosaic coloring in specific tissues. The study shows how DNA structure can steer inherited traits without changing the code.
plos-pone-0008331:
Marc A. Carrasco, Anthony D. Barnosky, and Russell W. Graham measured mammal losses in PLOS ONE in 2009. Earth has seen five major extinction events in the past era of complex life. Many scientists suggest a sixth is now under way, driven by human impacts. Quantifying the real extent of current losses has been difficult. A fair measure needs a pre-human baseline for comparison.

The team quantified North American mammal extinction relative to that baseline. Their numbers show how severe the modern episode already is. A solid count helps conservation focus where losses run deepest. It also grounds debate about the sixth extinction.
plos-pone-0008431:
Philippe Pascua and co-authors tested flu shots in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on the pandemic H1N1 virus of 2009. That virus spread from person to person around the world. It also spread back from people to pigs. Such spread gave it chances to change into more harmful forms. The team asked if recent shots could help.

They check shots made for people and shots made for swine. They test how well each shot guards against the new virus. They also test if a shot for one strain guards against the other. The results help guide which shots to use in a pandemic.
plos-pone-0008531:
Qin Li and co-authors study how nickel and low oxygen break down c-Myc in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Nickel compounds can cause cancer in humans and animals. They also transform normal cells in culture dishes. Part of that effect runs through stabilization of HIF1a, a low-oxygen factor. That factor switches on downstream signaling. Recent studies reported effects on c-Myc, a growth control protein.

The team trace mechanisms by which nickel and hypoxia degrade c-Myc. Degradation means the cell destroys the protein faster than usual. Understanding that loss helps explain nickel toxicity. It connects metal exposure, oxygen sensing, and growth control in one pathway.
plos-pone-0008631:
Margaret Carrel and co-authors trace bird flu evolution in Vietnam in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Vietnam is one of the countries most affected by H5N1 avian influenza. The virus was first identified there in poultry in 2001 and in humans in 2004. It has since caused many human cases and deaths. The team analyze the spatiotemporal structure of its molecular evolution. They map how viral lineages move through space and time.

Their analysis shows distinct regional patterns in how H5N1 evolved. Trade and poultry movement shape those patterns. Understanding spread routes helps target surveillance and culling. Vietnam's data inform control of highly pathogenic avian influenza regionally.
plos-pone-0008731:
James Gregory, Eric Becker, James Jung, and colleagues built a tool that tags genes with light. Their methods report appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The tool, called TAGIT, rides on a jumping piece of DNA named Tn5. It drops a green glowing gene into random spots of a germ's chromosome. Good tools must not wreck the gene groups they land in.

The modified jumper was designed to respect local gene organization. Selection markers show which cells received a working insertion. Tagged proteins glow, so their place and amount become visible. The tool speeds up studies of germ genes whose jobs are still unknown.
plos-pone-0008831:
J. Jeff McConnell, Larry Bragg, Stephen Shiboski, and colleagues studied how HIV-positive men adjust their sex lives. Their cohort study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Seroadaptation means choosing partners or acts based on HIV status. Health officials track infections to judge risk behavior. Seroadaptation can distort those readings badly. A man may take fewer risks than raw infection counts suggest.

Following a cohort of men who have sex with men revealed clear adaptive patterns. Their choices lowered transmission risk in ways surveillance can miss. Prevention programs should measure behavior with seroadaptation in mind. Sex research gains a needed correction factor.
plos-pone-0008931:
Kelly Lei and colleagues asked why male prairie voles are such loyal partners, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Prairie voles are small rodents famous for forming lasting pair bonds. The team studied a receptor for the hormone estrogen in one small brain region. That region, called the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, helps steer social behaviour.

Males with fewer estrogen receptors in this region tend to act more sociable. The researchers changed receptor levels there and watched how the voles behaved with partners and strangers. Raising receptor levels made the males less keen to huddle with other voles. The finding ties a single brain spot to how much company a male vole seeks.
plos-pone-0009031:
Lisette Leliveld, Marina Scheumann, and Elke Zimmermann played calls to mouse lemurs to test their ears, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The grey mouse lemur is one of the earliest primates still living. Primate brains usually process their own species' calls mostly on the left side. But meaning, emotion, and who is calling may shift that balance.

The team varied caller traits and watched which way the lemurs turned. Head turns reveal which side of the brain takes the lead. Caller identity and the call's social weight changed the response. Even in early primates, listening is not one-sided in a simple way.
plos-pone-0009131:
Masaki Tomonaga and Tomoko Imura tested whether a chimpanzee spots a staring face in a crowd, in PLOS ONE in 2010. People find a direct gaze among averted faces very fast. Faces looking away vanish into the crowd more easily. Chimpanzee eyes differ from human eyes in shape and colouring.

The chimp searched photographs for human faces with different gaze directions. The team measured whether direct gaze popped out for her too. Her search pattern tested how deep the stare-in-the-crowd effect runs. Shared sensitivity would hint the skill predates the human-chimp split.
plos-pone-0009231:
Gerald Falkenberg and colleagues published this bird sense study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Birds can read Earth's magnetic field to find their way, but the sensor behind that ability stayed mysterious. Earlier work on homing pigeons pointed to the upper beak. There, the skin lining holds branching nerve cells packed with iron minerals.

The authors checked whether those iron-rich dendrites appear in other birds too. They report that the elaborate structures seem to be a common feature of birds. A shared sensor across species strengthens the case that the beak houses a magnetic sense. It gives researchers a concrete structure to test against bird navigation behavior.
plos-pone-0009331:
Chung-Chien Hong and Mingzhou Song published this genetic engineering paper in PLOS ONE in 2010. Engineers often want to delete several genes at once to boost a desired product. Choosing the best set of deletions is a hard puzzle. Computer models of metabolism now make it possible to search for that set in advance.

The authors present a method based on nonlinear programming. It picks target genes whose removal should raise or lower the activity of chosen downstream genes or products. A smart search avoids the trial and error of testing every combination in the lab. The method gives bioengineers a shortlist worth building.
plos-pone-0009431:
Morad Zahid and colleagues described a new light tool for brain work in PLOS ONE in 2010. Light can free trapped chemicals that then excite nerve cells. Past tools could hit one cell well, but they were poor at hitting many cells at once. The team worked with thin slices of mouse hippocampus, a brain area tied to memory.

By shaping light into a pattern, like a hologram, they could excite a chosen set of cells at the same time. The method gives fast, exact control over which cells fire. Brain researchers can use it to probe how small groups of cells work together. That is hard to do with a single spot of light.
plos-pone-0009531:
Kevin Miranda, Fiona Karet, and Dennis Brown tackled naming in cell biology in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells use a pump called V-ATPase to control acidity inside and outside their compartments. The pump is built from many parts. Several parts come in variant forms, made by swapping pieces of their gene messages. Names for those parts and forms had grown messy in print.

The authors propose an extended, orderly naming system for the genes and their variants. One clear name per part ends mix ups between labs. Shared names matter more as data sets grow and computers link them. This housekeeping paper quietly supports a whole field's work.
plos-pone-0009631:
Brahm Segal and co-authors studied an enzyme that both fights and calms lung infection in mice in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme, NADPH oxidase, lets immune cells make reactive chemicals that kill germs. People born without it suffer repeated infections and excess inflammation. That odd pairing raised a question. The team examined what the enzyme does to innate immune responses in mouse lungs.

Mice lacking the enzyme showed stronger and longer inflammation in the lungs. So the enzyme also acts as a limit on the response it helps start. That dual role explains the excess inflammation in the human disorder. It reframes an old enzyme as a regulator, not just a weapon.
plos-pone-0009731:
Real-time PCR is a lab workhorse for counting how many copies of a gene a sample holds. Robert Rutledge and Don Stewart assessed a streamlined version of the method in PLOS ONE in 2010. The assays rest on LRE, short for linear regression of efficiency.

Absolute quantification means putting an exact number on gene copies, not just a relative one. The authors tested how well LRE-based assays handle that demanding task. Honest performance checks keep a widely used method trustworthy. Labs counting genes for medicine or research depend on such checks.
plos-pone-0009831:
DNMT1 is an enzyme that copies DNA methylation marks when cells divide. Leonardo D'Aiuto and colleagues took apart one end of the mouse version to see what it does. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The part under study is the N-terminal domain, the front section of the protein. The team used regional frame-shift mutagenesis, small targeted changes that shift how the code is read. Changing pieces one region at a time maps structure to function. The map clarifies how the enzyme keeps methylation patterns stable. Methylation marks help decide which genes stay silent.
plos-pone-0009931:
A protein's address inside the cell decides what jobs it can do. Kuo-Chen Chou and Hong-Bin Shen updated a predictor that guesses those addresses for eukaryotic proteins. The method, Euk-mPLoc 2.0, appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Eukaryotic cells are the complex cells of animals, plants, and fungi.

Subcellular localization means which compartment of the cell a protein lives in. Some proteins sit at a single site, others at multiple sites at once. The new method predicts both cases. Reliable address guesses help biologists interpret the flood of new protein sequences.
plos-pone-0010031:
The authors were Ertugrul Dalkic, Xuewei Wang, Neil Wright, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study treated cancer drugs as a network. Earlier network work mapped drugs, targets, and diseases on a huge scale. A smaller network lets analysts look closely at each link and member.

The team built that focused view of links between cancer drugs and their targets. Patterns in the map can hint at new uses for known drugs or risky drug pairings. The approach shows how math from network science can guide cancer research choices. Readers get both the map and the reasoning behind it.
plos-pone-0010231:
The authors were Gabriela Gutierrez-Reyes, Maria Garcia de Leon, Gustavo Varela-Fascinetto, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study examined livers from very sick children. In adults with cirrhosis, worn-out liver cells that have stopped dividing, called senescent cells, are common. The team asked whether the same is true in children with end stage liver disease.

They studied livers from five children aged three years or less. They measured how often senescent cells appeared and checked cell cycle control points. Finding early cell aging in young livers could change how doctors read the course of childhood liver disease.
plos-pone-0010331:
Kelvin Wong offered a fresh look at bargaining in a 2010 PLOS ONE article on game theory. Bargaining problems ask how two sides can split gains fairly. Wong used geometry, the math of shapes and positions, to frame the question. He sought the outcome where no other deal makes everyone better off at once. In his setup, a balance point is a set of choices with a special property.

At that point, no single player can switch choices and raise the total payoff for the group. The approach gives negotiators a clean way to judge proposed deals. It also links a social problem, dividing gains, to a visual method. Readers get a new lens on an old puzzle in economics and strategy.
plos-pone-0010431:
Ville Härmä and colleagues built a broad set of 3-D prostate models for lab research in PLOS ONE in 2010. Prostate cells grown flat on plastic behave unlike cells in a real gland. Balls of cells grown in three dimensions act more like tissue. Such spheroids suit studies of growth, invasion, and drug response. The team assembled the most complete panel of them yet.

Their panel covers normal and cancer prostate cells alike. A shared panel lets different labs compare results on the same footing. Drug tests in 3-D models predict patient responses better than flat cultures. The resource could speed the search for prostate cancer treatments. Building shared tools is quiet work, but it lifts a whole field.
plos-pone-0010531:
Kashif Ahmed and co-workers mapped the openness of DNA packaging in early mouse embryos in PLOS ONE in 2010. Embryonic stem cells keep their DNA loose and open, a state tied to their ability to become anything. Setting up that state may also be required when adult cells are reprogrammed.
