They add a new label, vampire articles, next to the known idea of zombie articles, which are retracted papers that keep being cited.

A vampire article must meet two tests: its result cannot be reproduced, and it is still cited with approval in policy, papers, or private messages. The authors sort repeat attempts into four types and suggest how many failed repeats should trigger action. Two cases, on shooting coyotes from the air and on predicted overfishing, show the harm. They urge sharper retraction rules.
pmc-13267531:
Mario Romeo and colleagues present a 2026 case report on treating a bowel cancer spread in the liver. Their patient was a 52-year-old woman whose rectal cancer had been treated with drugs, radiation, and surgery. One liver spot, about 17 millimeters wide, sat near a large vein and bile ducts in a liver full of cysts, making standard imaging unclear.

A contrast ultrasound scan showed rim brightening and fast washout, signs of living tumor. Surgery and heat-based burning were judged poor fits for the spot's position. Doctors instead used electric pulses, a method that kills cells without heat, guided by ultrasound. The scan right after showed full coverage. Six months later, scans showed no leftover or returning disease in the liver.
pmc-13267731:
Yucui Ding and colleagues report a 2026 study of a nano-sized drug carrier built to overwhelm breast cancer cells with calcium. Drug resistance and spread limit chemotherapy for breast cancer. The carrier wraps a plant compound, oridonin, in a manganese-based mineral sheet inside a fat shell aimed at tumors. Once inside a cell, it sets off a self-feeding loop of stress.

Stress in the cell's protein workshop forces calcium into its power plants, which then fail and burst out damaging oxygen chemicals. Manganese adds more of those chemicals and wakes an immune alarm pathway. Immune cells inside the tumor shifted to an attacking mode, and killer T cells moved in. In mice, the carrier strongly shrank tumors with no clear whole-body harm.
pmc-13267831:
Ji-Seong Jeong and colleagues present a 2026 rat study of silica nanoparticles breathed in during pregnancy. These tiny particles are among the most made nanomaterials, used in industry, medicines, and consumer goods. The nose and lungs are a main entry route, yet pregnancy risks were little studied. Pregnant rats received the particles through the nose daily in mid-to-late pregnancy, at four dose levels including none.

Treated mothers showed mild inflammation and healing changes in the breathing passages. No mothers died, and no general poisoning appeared. Checks of the litters and unborn young found no harm to development at any dose. The authors say the particles hurt only the surfaces they touched under these conditions. They still urge more studies, since particle types and exposure patterns vary widely.
pmc-13268231:
Mehmet Beler and Yusuf Bilal Çelenk present a 2026 study of insomnia in people aged 80 and over. This oldest group grows fast yet is rarely studied for sleep. The team enrolled 419 patients at a Turkish city hospital's advanced age unit in late 2025, using a standard insomnia severity questionnaire; a score of eight or more counted as insomnia.

About 38 percent had insomnia. It was more common in women and in those with low income. Past falls, high blood pressure, diabetes, and taking many medicines all linked to insomnia. Severity rose with the number of chronic diseases and the number of drugs taken. The authors argue insomnia at this age is not normal aging but a treatable problem, and that routine sleep checks belong in care of the very old.
pmc-13268631:
Xingyu Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 machine learning study predicting lab test orders in emergency departments. Lab testing guides emergency care, but overuse wastes money and time. The team analyzed 13,115 adult emergency visits from a 2021 national US survey. They built models from structured record data, from free-text complaint notes converted by a language model, from both together, and from an averaged ensemble.

The combined model predicted test ordering best, clearly beating either data type alone. The ensemble also did well but did not top the combined model. Older age, ambulance arrival, abnormal vital signs, and chronic illness predicted testing; injury visits predicted less testing. The authors say joining structured and text data could power decision support that trims unnecessary tests without missing needed ones.
pmc-13269031:
Celina Wojciechowska and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on death risk after removing heart device leads. They tested two simple scores, first built to judge stroke risk, as tools to predict death after the procedure. The scores add points for age, sex, and common health problems.

The study followed 3,822 patients treated between 2006 and 2023 at busy centers. Patients scoring three or more died more often at 30 days, one year, and three years. That cut point caught 80.6 percent of later deaths, with 62.3 percent exactness for survivors. Each extra point on the newer score raised death risk by 11.7 percent overall.
pmc-13270031:
Long Jing and co-authors published a case report and literature review in 2026 about a 50-year-old woman treated for a brain aneurysm, a bulge in a brain artery. She had a stent-assisted coiling procedure through blood vessels, which went smoothly. The next day she developed continuous seizures, a medical emergency called status epilepticus.

A brain scan showed mild swelling on the right side, pointing to brain injury from the imaging dye used in the procedure. Prompt seizure drugs and supportive care followed. She recovered fully, with no lasting deficits. The authors summarize how this dye reaction presents when seizures dominate, to help clinicians spot and treat it early.
pmc-13271331:
Shuang Liu is lead author of a 2026 journal article on FTL008.16, a bispecific antibody designed to switch on T cells only inside tumours. Drugs that activate the 4-1BB receptor on T cells can fight cancer but have been limited by liver damage. This antibody also binds 5T4, a protein found on tumour cells, so activation needs both targets.

In cell tests, the antibody boosted T cell growth, signal release, and tumour killing only when 5T4 was present. In two mouse tumour models it beat a standard 4-1BB antibody, fully clearing tumours in one model. In monkeys, even a high dose caused no rise in liver enzymes, suggesting a safer profile.
pmc-13271431:
Ticiana De Francesco is lead author of a 2026 multicentre study comparing two tiny drainage devices for glaucoma, the Xen63 gel stent and the Preserflo microshunt. Both lower eye pressure by draining fluid. Both were implanted alone, with a drug to limit scarring, in this study looking back at past cases.

At twelve months, complete success was about sixty-two percent for Xen63 and about seventy-four percent for Preserflo. Complete success meant pressure controlled without glaucoma medicines under strict rules. That gap was not statistically clear. Complications were more frequent with Xen63, at about sixty-two percent against about twenty-nine percent. Reoperations were also more common, at about seventeen percent against four percent. Pressure reduction and medicine burden were otherwise comparable.
pmc-13272231:
Riccardo Maria Borgo is lead author of a 2026 cross-sectional study linking retinal damage to cognition in multiple sclerosis. In that disease, immune attacks on nerves cause brain shrinkage and disabling thinking problems. Eye scans called OCT measure retinal layer thickness quickly and cheaply. They offer a possible window on brain degeneration.

One hundred people with multiple sclerosis had thinking tests, brain MRI scans, and retinal scans of several layers. Thinner retinal layers tracked with smaller brain volumes and lower cognitive performance. One layer, the ganglion cell layer, showed the strongest links, especially with processing speed and executive function, and was the only retinal predictor left in statistical models. Patients with impaired cognition had thinner ganglion and nerve fibre layers.
pmc-13272731:
Kendra Rodeghiero leads a 2026 longitudinal study of bacteria in the lower airways of pigs, comparing animals with and without lung lesions. The lesions matched infection with Mycoplasma hyopneumoniae, a common swine pathogen. Samples of airway mucus and lung tissue were taken from nursery through slaughter.

Pigs without lesions showed richer and more diverse bacterial communities during finishing, while pigs with lesions had lower diversity and less change over time. Only 18 bacterial variants appeared in all phases in both groups. Two candidate marker types were flagged for each group, but the authors treat those links as preliminary and specific to this data set, needing further checks.
pmc-13273631:
Khan and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on cutaneous leishmaniasis in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. This skin disease is spread by sand fly bites. The study links hospital records with a household survey. It asks where cases cluster and which habits raise risk.

The team counted 5,123 confirmed patients at 17 district hospitals during 2020. They also surveyed 576 households about schooling, family size, knowledge, and spray use. Big families, low schooling, and poor knowledge were tied to more cases. Spray use was tied to lower risk. The authors tested new sticky traps for sand flies. Most flies were caught 30 to 121 centimeters above the ground. That height detail can guide where teams place traps and spray.
pmc-13274131:
Siyao Liu and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a fat-handling protein that helps an aggressive breast cancer grow. HER2-positive breast cancer spreads readily, and disordered fat use inside tumors may fuel it. The protein STARD10 moves lipids within cells, but its role in this cancer was unclear.

STARD10 levels were higher in HER2-positive tumors and marked a poorer outlook for patients. In two lab cell lines, extra STARD10 sped growth, movement, and invasion, and fat droplets built up. In mice it sped tumor growth and spread to the lungs. The effect ran through a signaling chain named cAMP, PKA, and CREB1, which the authors propose as a drug target.
pmc-13274831:
Ahadul Hassan Bhuiyan Konok and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on adverse birth outcomes across Bangladesh. Using the national Demographic and Health Survey, the team analyzed pregnancy outcomes for 10,254 ever-married women. They counted four problems: stillbirth, early birth, low birth weight, and death in the first month of life.

Low birth weight was commonest at 14.3 percent of pregnancies, followed by early birth at 8.9 percent, with stillbirth and newborn death each at 1.3 percent. The authors report about one in seven births involved at least one problem. Twin births, household wealth, place of delivery, and the mother's wish for the child recurred as linked factors. They recommend equity-focused maternal care and stronger women's decision-making power.
pmc-13275531:
Yves Moreira Ribeiro and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on how the natural estrogen estrone, a pollutant in farm runoff and sewage, harms fish reproduction. Zebrafish were exposed for forty-nine days to three estrone levels found in real surface waters, from twenty to two thousand nanograms per liter. The team then examined ovaries, hormone levels, and spawning success.

Exposure reshaped the ovary: more immature egg cells and withered follicles, more inflammation, and fewer support cells. A related hormone and a growth factor signal rose at the lower doses, while a nitrogen stress marker climbed at the higher ones. Egg production fell in every exposed group, and fertilization rates dropped significantly at the two higher doses, even at common environmental levels.
pmc-13275631:
Luis Parmenio Suescún-Bolívar and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on tiny plastic bits in water and the germs they may carry. The team studied recycled PET, the plastic used in drink bottles, cut into microplastics. They asked how Escherichia coli, a common gut bacterium, sticks to and changes on these plastic surfaces.

The team checked the plastic with light-based tests and microscopes before and after contact with the bacteria. The tests found nine clear chemical bands for PET, and neither cleaning nor bacteria changed the plastic much. Microscope views showed bacteria clinging to the surfaces and forming biofilms, thin layers of living cells. Colonies also fermented lactose, a milk sugar, less well. The authors propose their setup as a model for tracking how plastics move microbes in water.
pmc-13276231:
Wang Yi and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a better endoscopic fix for bleeding-prone veins in the stomach. Gastric varices are swollen veins caused by liver cirrhosis, and their bleeding can be deadly. Standard banding treatment often grips the vein incompletely, so rebleeding is common.

At one Chinese hospital, ninety-nine patients had either standard banding or banding assisted by a metal clip. The clip method cleared the veins in a single session for about seven in ten patients, versus about half with standard care. Early rebleeding hit none of the clip group but about one in eleven of the standard group. Death rates and side effects were similar. The authors caution that the rebleeding benefit is exploratory and want larger, forward-looking trials to confirm it.
pmc-13276531:
Mariana Arino and co-authors present a 2026 case report on a rare, poorly understood degeneration of the cornea's edge. Peripheral nodulocystic corneal degeneration forms clear blister-like nodules around the cornea's rim. Only one similar case had been reported before, leaving its course and treatment undefined.

Their patient was a fifty-two-year-old woman with joint aches throughout her body and a past history of LASIK eye surgery in both eyes. She reported worsening dryness and discomfort in the left eye. Examination found multiple blister-like nodules in both eyes, mostly along the upper and outer edges. Scans showed cyst-like spaces under the surface layer and mild loss of the cornea's inner cells. She declined surgery, and symptoms eased with anti-inflammatory and lubricant eye drops plus a pressure-lowering drop. The authors discuss how degeneration, body-wide inflammation, and prior surgery may interact.
pmc-13393331:
Herrera-Luna and colleagues developed a light-driven method in 2026 to make aryl boronate esters, building blocks prized for assembling new molecules and medicines. Their recipe uses visible light alone, with no light-absorbing catalyst and no metal, and runs inside a gel open to the air. The starting materials are common aryl halides, ring compounds carrying a halogen atom that is easy to swap.

Lakens offers a practical primer on calculating and reporting effect sizes for common statistical tests. Effect sizes, he argues, matter more than any other outcome of empirical studies. They communicate the practical significance of results, beyond whether an effect merely exists.

For working scientists, effect sizes prove most useful because they let findings accumulate across studies. Lakens walks readers through computing them for t-tests and ANOVAs, with reporting advice. The primer is widely used in psychology teaching, pushing the field from yes-or-no significance toward measured magnitudes. pmc-3965031:
Lombard, Ramulu, Drula, and their colleagues updated the CAZy database in a 2014 report. CAZy sorts enzymes that build, change, and break down sugars and related chains. Its web site gives free access and is kept up to date as new data arrive.

Each family in CAZy is grouped by protein sequence, and that grouping is tied to what the enzyme acts on and to its three-dimensional shape. pmc-4134331:

pmc-4521131:
Herrett, Gallagher, Bhaskaran, and their co-authors profiled the Clinical Practice Research Datalink in 2015. Known as CPRD, it is an ongoing primary care database of anonymized medical records from general practitioners. It covers millions of patients from hundreds of practices across the United Kingdom.

Because the records come from real daily care, they show illness and treatment as they occur in the population. Researchers use CPRD to study drug safety, disease rates, and outcomes at large scale. Its size gives power to detect rare effects that trials miss. The profile explains coverage and limits so new users can judge whether the data fit their question.
pmc-5664031:
Susan Hewlings and Douglas Kalman reviewed curcumin and human health in 2017. Curcumin is the main active compound in turmeric, a spice long used in cooking and folk medicine. Interest in it has grown among both scientists and home cooks.

The review gathers evidence on how curcumin may help with swelling, joint pain, and damage caused by unstable oxygen molecules. It also notes weak points, such as poor absorption from the gut and small study sizes. Readers get a balanced look at what is known and what is still unproven. That makes it useful for anyone weighing turmeric supplements.
pmc-7005631:
Ygor Silva, Andressa Bernardi, and Rudimar Frozza reviewed gut-brain communication through microbial fatty acids in 2020. Gut microbes govern much of the body's metabolic, hormone, and immune balance. Their role in brain signaling has gained strong recognition.

When microbes ferment fiber they release short-chain fatty acids. These compounds reach the brain directly and through immune and nerve routes. They can affect appetite, mood circuits, and brain inflammation. The review weighs animal evidence against the thinner human record, and marks where diet-based brain claims outrun the proof. The authors also discuss fatty acids made as drugs, and how they differ from the microbial products.
pmc-7672931:
Hisham Kadry, Behnam Noorani, and Luca Cucullo gave an overview in 2020 of the blood-brain barrier, the tightly sealed wall that guards the brain. This barrier controls which substances move between the blood and brain tissue. Its sound structure is essential for the brain's chemical balance and for healthy nerve cell function.

The authors describe how the barrier is built, how it works, and the ways it can break down in injury and disease. They also review the marker molecules that signal whether the barrier is intact or leaking. That knowledge matters far beyond anatomy, since the same wall that protects the brain also blocks most medicines, and judging its state helps doctors assess brain injury and illness.
pmc-8387231:

The statement fixes a definition and scope, distinguishing true postbiotics, preparations of inanimate microbes that benefit health, from neighboring products that had borrowed the label. Friedrich Spee was a German Jesuit priest who heard the last words of many women judged as witches. In 1631 he put out Cautio Criminalis in Latin, with no name on the title page. The book was the first strong Catholic attack on the witch trials. Spee risked his post and his life to write it.

Spee shows how torture forces false claims from weak and strong alike. He asks judges to test proof with care and to doubt paid witch finders. His calm case helped slow the trials in parts of Germany. Few books of the age speak for the accused with such force.
spee-cautio-criminalis-latin-1631:
Friedrich Spee, a Jesuit priest, published the Cautio Criminalis in Latin in 1631, without his name. Spee had served as confessor to condemned witches in Würzburg, hearing their last words before the fire. What he learned in that cell produced a searing attack on the trials and their tortures.

He argues that torture makes every accusation true by force. Germany, he warns, will burn its whole population if the process runs unchecked. The book is the moral turning point of the persecution. Its anonymity protected a man whose order and church ran the trials he condemned. Few braver books came out of the burning times.
the-lock-and-key-library-classic-mystery: This edition of Julian Hawthorne's classic mystery anthology gathers the founders of detective fiction: Poe, Doyle's predecessors, and the French masters. Every story a landmark of the genre. The essential history of the whodunit in one volume.
the-lock-and-key-library-the-most-intere: Still another edition of the "most interesting stories" anthology: Hawthorne's world tour of great short fiction. Each story a gem, each nation represented. No state may use or threaten force in its dealings, in space as on earth, the Charter's rule recalled here. The 1978 disarmament session had held that fresh steps are needed to bar an arms race in space. This yearly vote keeps that guard in place.

They were to keep in mind the interests of the territory's people. Britain was asked to speed the process and report back before the next session.

It reaffirms that the existing legal regime alone does not guarantee against an arms race there. It calls on all states, especially major space powers, to work toward that goal and refrain from contrary actions. It invites the Conference on Disarmament to set up a working group on the subject during its 2015 session. The group would pursue negotiated agreements, including verification measures.

United Nations Security Council Resolution 1031 put the Dayton peace agreement for Bosnia into force. The Council adopted it on 15 December 1995, one day after the agreement was signed in Paris. The war in Bosnia had killed many thousands and driven many more from their homes.

The text welcomes the peace deal and calls on all sides to keep their promises. It lets member states set up a NATO-led force, called IFOR, to guard the deal. The Council extends the observer mission, called UNOMSIL, until 13 June 1999. The mission should move back into Freetown as soon as safety allows. More military observers and human rights staff will join it. The text condemns rebel abuse of women and children and the use of child soldiers. All states must honor the arms embargo on rebel forces.
un-sc-res-1331:
Council members took up Cyprus and unanimously adopted Resolution 1331 on Cyprus on 13 December 2000. The peacekeeping force on the island had served since 1964. Cyprus had agreed the force should stay past mid-December. New limits placed on its patrols that June had raised concern.

It urged both parties to cooperate fully and quickly with the mission and to guard its staff. Final duty for applying the Algiers Agreements and the boundary ruling rested with the two governments, the Council stressed. It backed the special envoy's good offices and pressed both sides to open a direct air route between Asmara and Addis Ababa. Delays, it noted, were raising the mission's costs.
un-sc-res-1631:

The Council voiced its resolve to deepen cooperation with regional and subregional organizations. All states and bodies were urged to give money and skills to build their capacity, above all in Africa. Regional strategies inside the United Nations system had to grow. The Council stressed what regional bodies can do in settling disputes, peacekeeping, and rebuilding after war. It meant to hold regular meetings with the heads of regional organizations. un-sc-res-1731:

A new forestry law had passed, and the ban on timber exports had been lifted. Yet the Council judged that other reforms still fell short.

The text renews the arms and travel bans for twelve more months. The ban on rough diamond exports runs six more months, with a review after four. Liberia must build a clear origin scheme for its diamonds and join the Kimberley Process. The expert panel that checks the sanctions stays on until 20 June 2007.

The Council condemned all violence inside Somalia and acts meant to block a peaceful political process. It stressed the need for disarmament and reintegration of fighters.

The Council renewed the authorization of African Union member states to run AMISOM for a further six months. The mission could take all necessary measures to carry out its mandate under resolution 1744 (2007). The arms embargo terms of resolution 733 (1992) would not block supplies meant for the mission. African Union states were urged to send more troops, and all member states were asked for money, staff, and equipment. The Secretary-General was encouraged to keep working with the African Union on plans for a possible United Nations force to follow.
un-sc-res-1931:

The Council restated that persons indicted by the tribunal must face trial. It noted the need for the tribunal to be staffed well enough to finish. The terms of the permanent trial judges were extended to 31 December 2011, or to the end of their cases if sooner. Appeals judges' terms ran on in the same way, to the dates set out in the text. Ad litem judges gained matching extensions. Named ad litem judges were allowed to sit past their terms to finish the cases before them.

The Council reaffirmed its Cyprus resolutions, reaching back to Resolution 186 of 1964. The parties were urged to show the utmost restraint. They were also told to keep working together toward the Council's goals. The force's stationing was extended for six months, ending on 26 June 1967. The Council hoped that enough progress toward a settlement would be made by then. Such progress might at last allow the force to leave the island.
un-sc-res-31:

It had also pointed them toward a peaceful settlement. One part of that text let the parties ask for the Council's help. Resolution 31, adopted on 25 August 1947, makes that offer in form.

The Council resolved to tender its good offices to the parties. In plain terms, it offered its own help to bring about a peaceful settlement of the dispute. If the parties asked, the help would come through a small committee of the Council. The committee would have three members. Each party would choose one member, and the two chosen would name the third. The offer put the Council's mediation on the table, ready for the Dutch and the Republic of Indonesia to use.
un-sc-res-331: With a catalog date of 1973, Resolution 331 records a decision of the UN Security Council. The Council asked the Secretary-General to appoint a special representative for Namibia. His task was to secure the territory's early independence through free elections under United Nations supervision and control. The Secretary-General also had to report at the earliest date with advice on putting the settlement proposal into effect under resolution 385. All concerned were urged to do their best to bring Namibia to independence as soon as possible. The special representative's work became the core of the settlement effort the Council pursued from that summer on.
un-sc-res-631:
United Nations observers were watching the Iran-Iraq ceasefire in early 1989. On 8 February 1989 the Security Council renewed their mission, UNIIMOG. The Secretary-General had reported on the observer group two days before. The Council took note of his observations. It also recalled resolution 598, the text that had demanded an end to the war.

The renewal ran for seven months and twenty-two days. It ended on 30 September 1989. The Council called on both parties to carry out resolution 598 without delay. The Secretary-General owed a report at the end of the period. It would cover events on the ground and steps taken toward a settlement.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
The Dayton peace deal for Bosnia and Herzegovina is put into force by Resolution 1031, adopted on 15 December 1995. The General Framework Agreement had been signed in Paris the day before by Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. A London conference had set up a Peace Implementation Council to guide the work ahead.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes a multinational implementation force, IFOR, under unified command, with power to use all needed measures to enforce the military parts of the deal. It ends UNPROFOR's mandate once authority passes to IFOR. It backs elections run by the OSCE, the right of refugees to go home, and full cooperation with the war crimes tribunal. It also endorses a High Representative to oversee the civilian side of the settlement, agreeing to the designation named in the text.

Sierra Leone's observer mission is extended and sent back to the capital in Resolution 1231, adopted on 11 March 1999. The situation remained fragile after the recent escalation of violence. The Secretary-General's fifth report of 4 March 1999 recommended the move. Reports persisted that rebels were receiving arms and mercenaries, in particular from Liberian territory.

The Council extends the mandate of the United Nations Observer Mission in Sierra Leone, UNOMSIL, until 13 June 1999. It welcomes the plan to re-establish UNOMSIL in Freetown as soon as possible with more military observers and human rights personnel, subject to strict attention to security. It condemns rebel atrocities against civilians, especially women and children, including recruiting children as soldiers, and demands full humanitarian access. It reaffirms the Resolution 1171 (1998) arms embargo, commends ECOMOG, and asks the Secretary-General to report by 5 June 1999 with recommendations on UNOMSIL's future deployment.

Guinea's break with France brought its bid to the Council within weeks in 1958. On 9 December, it adopted Resolution 131. Guinea had voted that autumn for instant freedom in a referendum. It was the only French colony to choose that path in 1958. A republic was proclaimed at once under its new leaders.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit the Republic of Guinea. Admission followed days later. Guinea's arrival marked an early sign of the wave to come. African decolonization would reshape the UN's ranks and its politics within a few short years.

Cyprus, again, is the real subject of Resolution 1331. Some digests mislabel it as a Golan Heights text. In fact it was adopted unanimously on 13 December 2000, after the Secretary-General's report on the Cyprus operation. UNFICYP peacekeepers had guarded the island's buffer zone for decades.

The Council extended UNFICYP's mandate to 15 June 2001. It asked for an implementation report by 1 June. It also pressed the Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces on a sore point. Restrictions imposed in June 2000 had hampered the peacekeepers. Members demanded those limits be lifted. They wanted the former military position restored at Strovilia, a village inside the buffer zone.

Short-term judges come to the Rwanda war crimes tribunal in this text of 14 August 2002. The tribunal's president had asked for the change so trials could finish sooner. A similar ad litem system already existed at the tribunal for the former Yugoslavia.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council amended the Rwanda tribunal's Statute to create the pool, and adjusted related articles of the Yugoslavia tribunal's Statute too. The Secretary-General is asked to arrange the election of 18 ad litem judges for Rwanda as soon as possible. Staff and facilities for the new judges were to follow, so the extra courtroom capacity could actually be used.

Resolution 1531, adopted unanimously on 12 March 2004, voices frustration at a peace process stuck between Ethiopia and Eritrea. The boundary commission had reported in February that it could not move ahead with marking the border under present conditions. The Council blamed the impasse mainly on missing progress in demarcation, and singled out Ethiopia's refusal to accept key parts of the binding ruling, and its weak cooperation.

The Council kept UNMEE, the UN mission in both countries, in place for a further six months. It restated support for the Algiers Agreements and the commission's 2002 ruling, which both sides had accepted as final. The text warned, in effect, that a peace both governments had signed was being undone by delay.

How the UN should work with regional bodies on peace and security is the theme of Resolution 1631, adopted on 17 October 2005. It rests on Chapter VIII of the UN Charter, which covers regional arrangements. The 2005 World Summit had urged a bigger role for regional groups, and a new Peacebuilding Commission was about to be created.

The Council invites regional and subregional groups with peacekeeping skill to place that strength in the UN Standby Arrangements System. It urges states to help build up such groups, above all in Africa, with people, training, and money. It stresses fast deployment in support of UN missions and the role of regional groups against the illegal small arms trade and terrorism. It also plans regular meetings with regional heads and asks for a report on the chances and problems in this teamwork.

Liberia's sanctions are renewed in Resolution 1731, adopted on 20 December 2006. The new government had made real progress since January 2006, passing a forestry reform law, and the timber measures had already been lifted. Diamond controls were not yet in place, though work toward the Kimberley Process was under way. The expert panel found that the conditions for ending the remaining measures were not yet met.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms embargo and travel ban for 12 months, with an exemption for non-lethal equipment for vetted, trained Liberian police and security forces. It renews the rough-diamond ban for six months, with a review after four, to give Liberia time to build a transparent certificate-of-origin regime. The asset freeze from Resolution 1532 stays in force. The Panel of Experts is extended to 20 June 2007, reporting by 6 June 2007.

Resolution 1831, passed on 19 August 2008, keeps the African force in Somalia for six more months. The force, AMISOM, was small and based in Mogadishu. It worked in the midst of a fierce revolt. The Council condemned bids to block peace talks by force. It deplored fresh calls to arms and fresh attacks on aid staff and peace staff alike.

The force won six more months of cover from the Council. Calm in Somalia, the text says, needs arms laid down and ex-fighters brought back to civil life. The Council restated its respect for the land's unity and its borders. It also wove this grant into its web of past texts on guards for the weak, for children, and for aid teams.

Resolution 1931, adopted on 29 June 2010, deals with the judges and timetable of the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. The tribunal had been told to finish its work in 2010, but its own report said that goal could not be met. Skilled staff were leaving, and a string of trials and appeals still had years to run.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the terms of the appeals judges until 31 December 2012 and of the trial judges until 31 December 2011, or until their cases end. It lets nine short-term ad litem judges serve past the usual three-year limit. It presses states, above all those of the former Yugoslavia, to help the tribunal and arrest those still indicted. It also urges the tribunal to finish its work as fast as it can.

The Central African Republic had held elections in 2011, but armed groups still controlled much of the country outside the capital. One of them, the Lord's Resistance Army, crossed borders to raid villages. Resolution 2031, adopted on 21 December 2011, concerns BINUCA, the United Nations peacebuilding office in the country.

The Council extended BINUCA's mandate until 31 January 2013. It pushed the government to set up a permanent, independent body to run future elections. The electoral code also had to be revised. The office would keep backing the peace agreement process and disarmament work. Regional efforts against the Lord's Resistance Army received support as well. The aim was to help the state extend its authority beyond the capital.

A year of Cyprus renewals closed with one more in December 1966. On the fifteenth, the Council adopted Resolution 231 without dissent. The Secretary-General's report held that the force was still needed to keep peace. The Cyprus government agreed it should stay past late December.

The text restates the long list of earlier Cyprus decisions. It urges all parties to show the utmost restraint. It also asks them to keep working together toward the Council's goals. The posting then runs on for a further period. By late 1966, the pattern was fixed. The force could neither solve the Cyprus problem nor leave it.

Mediation, not troops, was the Council's offer in the Indonesia dispute of 1947. On 25 August, it adopted Resolution 31. Eight members voted yes and none voted no. Three members held back from the vote. Three weeks before, Resolution 27 had called for a halt to the fighting.

The Council now tenders its good offices to both sides. It offers help through a panel of three Council members. Each party would pick one member of the panel. Those two would then choose the third. The offer grew into the Committee of Good Offices. That body walked with Indonesia toward full independence in 1949.

Egypt's foreign minister addressed the Council on the Middle East in April 1973, and Resolution 331 followed on 20 April. The short text asks the Secretary-General for a full report. The report had to cover every effort the United Nations had made on the Middle East situation since June 1967. It was to reach the Council as early as possible. Once the report arrived, the Council would meet to examine the situation. The Secretary-General's special envoy for the region was to be on hand to assist during that debate.

Resolution 431, adopted on 27 July 1978, puts a negotiator in charge of Namibia's road to independence. A settlement proposal for the territory, prepared by five Western governments and circulated that April, was on the table. The Council's 1976 resolution had already laid down the goal: a free Namibia, chosen by its own people.

The Council asked the UN chief to name a special envoy for Namibia. His task was to make sure independence came early, through free elections under UN supervision and control. The Secretary-General also had to report back as soon as possible with recommendations for carrying out the proposal. The appointment set up the UN operation that, after long delays, finally ran Namibia's founding election in 1989.

An odd, precise span marks this Iran-Iraq observer renewal of 1989. On 8 February, the Council adopted Resolution 631. The observer group had watched the truce line since August 1988. The peace text behind it, Resolution 598, was still not carried out. The Secretary-General's February report grounded the step.

The text calls once again on the parties to act on Resolution 598 at once. It renews the mandate for seven months and twenty-two days. The term ends on 30 September 1989. A report on the state of play is due from the Secretary-General then. The odd end date matched the UN planning calendar, not a round half-year.
widger-s-quotations-from-the-project-gut: David Widger gathers the best lines of Lord Chesterfield. The Earl’s worldly wit shines briefly. His counsels delight in small doses. A treasury for Chesterfield fans, David Widger, Chesterfield, Earl, wit, treasury, lines, best.
